# Homelab Documentation

> GitOps-driven Kubernetes homelab on bare metal, running Flatcar Container Linux, Kubeadm, Cilium, Rook-Ceph and ArgoCD.

Bare-metal Kubernetes on Flatcar Container Linux. Ansible and a PXE boot
server bring the nodes up; Argo CD owns everything after that. The pages are
reference material: architecture decisions, one page per platform component,
operations runbooks and the contribution workflow.

# Get started

# Flatcar Homelab

![Homelab Logo](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/assets/images/logo.png>)

A rack of machines and a pile of YAML: a bare metal Kubernetes cluster that provisions itself over PXE, keeps its entire state in Git, and is documented here so that nothing has to be re-derived at 02:00.

## Start here

- **I want to build this**

  ---

  [Adapt It to Your Cluster](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/adapting/index.md>) first — the repository URL, domain and addresses are hardcoded — then the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>). Set aside an afternoon.
- **I know Kubernetes, not this repo**

  ---

  [Architecture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md>) for how it fits together, [Design Decisions](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md>) for why, and [Known Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>) for what it does not do.
- **I am learning Kubernetes**

  ---

  These pages assume you can use `kubectl`; the [Kubernetes basics tutorial](<https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics/>) gets you there. Then [Core Concepts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md>) for the five ideas underneath this cluster and the terms the other pages use.
- **Something is broken**

  ---

  [Operations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/index.md>) has the health check and the symptom-to-cause table. If it is a stalled install, the [PXE troubleshooting table](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#troubleshooting-pxe-boot>).
- **I am making a change**

  ---

  [Development](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/index.md>) for the checks a pull request must pass, [GitOps Strategy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>) for what a merge does to the cluster, and the [repository layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md#repository-layout>) for where things live.

## The stack in one table

Each choice had a simpler alternative that was rejected on purpose; the reasoning and what each one costs is in [Design Decisions](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md>).

| Layer | Choice | Why it is not the obvious one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OS | [Flatcar Container Linux](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md#flatcar-container-linux>) | Read-only `/usr`. You cannot `apt install` your way out of a problem, which turns out to be the feature |
| Cluster | Kubernetes via kubeadm | Stock upstream, so the upstream docs apply verbatim |
| Network | [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) | eBPF, no `kube-proxy`, no iptables archaeology. Also supplies Gateway API and the LoadBalancer addresses bare metal does not come with |
| Storage | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) | Replicated block storage across the nodes, and the component most likely to teach you humility |
| Secrets | [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) | Nothing sensitive in Git, at the price of a manual unseal after every reboot |
| Delivery | [ArgoCD](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>) | If it is not in Git it is not real, and it will not survive the next reconcile |

The sections follow the reader's journey: [Get Started](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/adapting/index.md>) to build it, [Architecture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md>) to understand it, [Platform](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md>) for each of the components, [Operations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/index.md>) to run it, and [Development](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/index.md>) to work on the repository.

# Core Concepts

Five ideas carry this cluster besides Kubernetes itself. Read this before the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>) if any of the names below are new; the [Terms](<#terms>) table defines the words the other pages assume.

| Concept | What it is | What it costs you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Flatcar Container Linux](<#flatcar-container-linux>) | An immutable OS with a read-only `/usr` and A/B partition updates | No `apt install`. Anything unusual has to arrive another way |
| [Ignition & Butane](<#ignition-and-butane>) | First-boot provisioning from a JSON config | It runs *once*. Changing a template means rebuilding the node |
| [Systemd sysexts](<#systemd-sysexts>) | Read-only images that extend `/usr` at boot | Upgrading Kubernetes means swapping an image and rebooting |
| [PXE boot](<#pxe-boot>) | Booting a machine off the network instead of its disk | Needs a DHCP server you control and a host on the same segment |
| [GitOps](<#gitops>) | Git is the desired state; a controller reconciles to it | If it is not committed, it does not exist |

## Flatcar Container Linux

[Flatcar](<https://www.flatcar.org/>) is an immutable, minimal Linux distribution designed for running containers. The root filesystem is read-only — you cannot install packages or modify system files at runtime — which forces all configuration to happen declaratively, at first boot, through Ignition. A read-only `/usr` makes undocumented drift between "identical" nodes impossible rather than merely discouraged.

Updates are downloaded in the background onto the passive half of an A/B partition pair, so a bad one can be rolled back and nothing changes until the machine restarts. [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>), not Flatcar's `locksmithd`, drains and reboots one node at a time — see [Updates & Upgrades](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md>).

## Ignition and Butane

**Ignition** is Flatcar's first-boot provisioning system. It reads a JSON config and applies it: creates users, writes files, partitions disks, enables systemd units.

**Butane** is the human-writable YAML that compiles to that JSON. Ansible renders Butane from Jinja2 templates on the deployment host and transpiles it; the boot server serves the result.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Ignition runs once, in the initramfs, before the real root is mounted**
>
> Change a template and the node has to be *reprovisioned* to care — which here means arming it with `make reinstall` and network-booting it, wiping the disk on the way in. The config is embedded into the OEM partition at install time, so an installed node reads it from its own disk rather than from the network.

## Systemd sysexts

Because `/usr` is read-only, software the base image does not ship — only `kubernetes`, in this cluster — arrives as a **system extension**: a read-only squashfs image overlaid onto `/usr` at boot, managed by `systemd-sysupdate`. Nodes fetch it from the HTTP boot server on their first boot from disk. containerd is part of the base image and is deliberately not replaced: a sysext-bakery build would run a containerd Flatcar has not tested.

Upgrading Kubernetes on these nodes is therefore not `apt upgrade`; it is swapping an image and rebooting. See [Updates & Upgrades](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md>).

## PXE boot

**PXE** (Preboot Execution Environment) lets a machine boot from the network instead of a local disk. The NIC asks DHCP where to go, fetches a bootloader over TFTP, and the bootloader fetches everything else. In this project:

1. An external DHCP server hands out the boot server's IP and a syslinux filename.
2. TFTP serves the syslinux bootloader and a per-MAC boot menu.
3. Syslinux fetches the Flatcar kernel and initrd over HTTP, passing the Ignition config URL as a kernel parameter.

The full sequence is in [Boot & Bootstrap Process](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md>).

## GitOps

Everything the cluster runs is described in this repository under `payload/`, and [ArgoCD](<https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/>) continuously reconciles the cluster to match; a change made by hand is put back on the next sync.

## Terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| [ApplicationSet](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#structure>) | An ArgoCD object that generates an `Application` per matching file, so a component is a directory |
| [CNI](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) | The plugin that gives pods their network; Cilium here |
| [CRD](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-convergence>) | A custom resource type a component adds to the Kubernetes API |
| [eBGP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>) | The routing protocol the control planes announce the Gateway addresses to the router with |
| [ExternalSecret](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) | A resource that copies an OpenBao value into a Kubernetes `Secret` |
| [Helm chart](<https://helm.sh/docs/>) | A packaged, templated set of manifests, rendered by ArgoCD |
| [OSD](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#disks>) | The Ceph daemon that owns one disk partition |
| [Seal, unseal](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#unsealing-after-a-restart>) | OpenBao starts locked and opens only with a threshold of key shares |
| [Sync policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#sync-policy>) | Every `Application` syncs automatically, reverts drift and retries |
| [Sync wave](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#workloads-sync-alongside-the-platform>) | An annotation that orders resources within one Application |
| [VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>) | The floating address the API server answers on, whichever control plane holds it |

# Quickstart

![Homelab Logo](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/assets/images/logo.png>)

Bring up the bare metal Kubernetes cluster from scratch, using [Flatcar Container Linux and Kubeadm](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md>). Set aside an afternoon: step 7 depends on your DHCP server behaving.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Read this first if the cluster isn't mine**
>
> Node names, IP addresses, the `wlkr.ch` domain, and the Git repository URL are hardcoded throughout `payload/`. Following the steps below verbatim gives you a cluster whose ArgoCD syncs from **this** repository and whose certificates are issued for a domain you don't control. Work through [Adapting This for Your Cluster](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/adapting/index.md>) **before** step 1.

## Hardware Requirements

At least four machines: three workers, because Ceph keeps three copies on three different hosts and puts no OSD on a control plane, and one control plane, or three for an etcd that survives losing one — see [Cluster layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md#cluster-layout>). Size their memory by the [platform's limits rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>). Each node must have:

- A NIC that supports PXE booting, with network boot first in the firmware's [boot order](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#boot-order>)
- An NVMe drive, or a different `install_disk` in `inventory.yaml`
- Enough disk for Flatcar and the root filesystem. On workers the root partition is capped (`size_mib` in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2`) and Rook-Ceph takes the remainder as OSD storage; control planes keep the whole disk
- At least 4 GB of RAM: the installer runs from a RAM disk and streams the Flatcar image straight to disk

The deployment host (the machine running Ansible and the boot server) must be on the same L2 network segment as the nodes.

## Prerequisites

### Tools on the deployment host

| Tool | Used by | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `make` | every step | Xcode CLT / `build-essential` |
| `git` | cloning this repository | your package manager |
| `uv` | Ansible and the boot server | `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh \\| sh` |
| `butane` | transpiling Butane YAML to Ignition JSON | `brew install butane` or the [Flatcar docs](<https://www.flatcar.org/docs/latest/provisioning/config-transpiler/>) |
| `gpg` and `gpgv` | checking the signatures on the Flatcar and syslinux checksums in `make download` | `brew install gnupg` or your package manager |
| `kubectl` | steps 8 onwards | [kubernetes.io](<https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/>) |
| `helm` | `make install-cilium`, `make install-argo` | [helm.sh](<https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/>) |
| `jq`; day 2 also `argocd`, `bao`, `velero`, `aws` | step 12; the runbooks in [Argo CD](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#cli-access>), [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#authenticating-locally>) and [Backups](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>) | your package manager |

### Other requirements

- **SSH Key**: An Ed25519 key at `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` (or edit `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` and `butane_installer_config.yaml.j2` to use a different path/key)
- **External DHCP Server**: Must point PXE clients at the deployment host and give every node a fixed address:

  - Option 66 (`next-server`): IP of the machine running `make serve`
  - Option 67 (`filename`): `lpxelinux.0` for BIOS, `syslinux.efi` for UEFI
  - A reservation per `mac_address` handing out exactly that host's `ansible_host`. Nothing in the node config sets a static address; the API server's `advertiseAddress`, the etcd peer URLs kubeadm derives from it and the metrics listeners are all rendered from `ansible_host`, so a node that leases a different address joins with the wrong one or not at all.
- **Outside accounts**: `make bao-secrets` (step 11) asks for what the cluster cannot generate: DNS provider keys for cert-manager and external-dns, an SMTP login for alert mail, the BGP session password, and the logins some workloads need. The list is at the top of `scripts/bao-secrets.sh`; what a fork drops is in [Adapting](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/adapting/index.md>).

> [!TIP]
>
> **Consumer routers and PXE**
>
> Many home routers accept options 66 and 67 and then serve neither. If step 7 produces silence in the boot server log, prove the DHCP side first with `tcpdump -i <iface> port 67 or port 68`.

## Setup

1. **Clone Repository**:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab.git homelab
   cd homelab
   ```
2. **Configure Inventory**: Edit `ansible/inventory.yaml` to define your target nodes and settings.

   Every variable, and the `make` target that bakes it into `output/`, so you know what to re-run after an edit:

   | Variable | Why it matters | Read by |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `boot_server_ip` | **Most commonly missed.** Baked into the generated PXE menu as the URL for the kernel, initrd, and Ignition config. If this isn't the IP of the machine that will run `make serve`, nodes load the bootloader and then hang. | `make config`, `make serve` |
   | `mac_address` (per host) | Selects which generated PXE menu a node picks up | `make config`, `make reinstall`, `make serve` |
   | `ansible_host` (per host) | The address the node's DHCP reservation hands out; rendered into the kubeadm and static pod configs | `make config`, `make reinstall` |
   | `install_disk` | Target disk for the Flatcar install, overridable per host for a node whose disk sits elsewhere. **Wiped completely** — partitions, GPT and a device-level discard — before the install | `make config` |
   | `control_plane_vip`, `control_plane_vip_interface` | The API endpoint kubeadm bakes into every certificate and kubeconfig, and the NIC kube-vip advertises it on; see [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>) | `make config`; the VIP also `make kubeconfig`, `make reinstall` |
   | `control_plane_endpoint_host` | The name or address nodes join through; a name only on a fresh build, see [Endpoint name](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md#endpoint-name>) | `make config`, `make kubeconfig`, `make reinstall` |
   | `pod_subnet`, `service_subnet` | kubeadm's cluster networks; change only on a collision with your LAN | `make config` |
   | `router_ip`, `router_asn`, `cluster_asn` | The eBGP peer the Gateway addresses are announced to; rendered into `output/router/frr-bgp.conf` for the router, and `payload/platform/cilium/bgp.yaml` must say the same; see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>) | `make config` |
   | `flatcar_channel`, `flatcar_version`, `syslinux_version` | The OS image and bootloader to fetch; `flatcar_version` also names the image the installer writes | `make download`; `flatcar_version` also `make config` |
   | `kubernetes_version`, `kubernetes_sha256` | The sysext image to fetch and the checksum `make download` verifies it against, so both move together; the version is also what kubeadm and sysupdate are rendered with | `make download`, `make config` |
   | `kube_vip_version` | The bootstrap static pod only; the running image is pinned in `payload/platform/kube-vip/`; see [Inventory](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md#inventory>) | `make config` |
   | `bootstrap_cluster` (`control_plane` group) | `true` for this first install, so the first control-plane node runs `kubeadm init`; back to `false` once the cluster is up — see [Inventory](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md#inventory>) | `make config`, `make reinstall` |
   | `control_plane` / `workers` membership | Decides the node role, and with it the partition layout and the kubeadm command | `make config` |
   | `ansible_user`, `ansible_ssh_common_args` (`k8s_nodes` group) | How the playbooks reach a running node for the kubeconfig and the join-credential renewal | `make kubeconfig`, `make config` |
3. **Initialize Environment**: Creates the `uv` virtual environment and installs dependencies:

   ```bash
   make setup
   ```
4. **Download Artifacts**: Fetches Flatcar, Syslinux and the Kubernetes sysext image into `output/http`:

   ```bash
   make download
   ```
5. **Generate Configurations**:

   ```bash
   make config
   ```

   Writes Ignition configs to `output/http` and PXE menus to `output/tftp`. Each host gets `ignition-<host>-install.json`, which the PXE environment runs to wipe the disk and install, and `ignition-<host>.json`, which `flatcar-install` embeds into the installed system — see [Boot & Bootstrap Process](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md>).

   Re-run this after **any** change to `inventory.yaml`; the values are baked into the generated files. `make artifacts` runs steps 4 and 5 together. Check that one PXE menu was generated per node:

   ```bash
   ls output/tftp/pxelinux.cfg/     # one 01-<mac> file per host
   ```
6. **Start Boot Server**:

   ```bash
   make serve
   ```

   On a Linux deployment host, lower `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` first, or TFTP cannot bind — see [Boot server](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#boot-server>). Leave this running through step 7 and keep the window visible: it names each node and logs one line per request. Its opening lines say what each node will do when powered on: a boxed `ARMED TO INSTALL` warning names the nodes that will wipe and install, and a node under *booting from disk* will not, however often you reboot it.

   ```console
     ⚠  ARMED TO INSTALL: odin, thor
   20:33:04  server                                                    booting from disk: freya, heimdall, loki, valkyrie
   20:34:17  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  collecting its boot menu -- armed, so it will install
   ```
7. **Arm the install, then boot the machines**:

   ```bash
   make reinstall
   ```

   The generated PXE configs default to booting the local disk; `make reinstall` flips them to `Install`, for `LIMIT=<node>` or, after a typed confirmation, for every host. The boot server disarms a node itself once it has delivered the OS image, so the reboot at the end of the install lands on the disk — see [Switching back to local boot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#switching-back-to-local-boot>).

   Then power on the nodes. No menu appears; each node does what it was armed to do, and the boot server log walks it through the fetches, then `switching to local boot`, then after the reboot the Ignition config again plus the sysext images. A node still shown by bare IP has not fetched a menu the server recognises.

   - **Leave the boot server running until every node is up.** The sysexts are fetched on the first boot from disk.
   - The nodes come up `NotReady`, as `kubectl get nodes` in step 8 shows, because no CNI is installed. This is correct; do not fix it yet.
   - If a node stalls, see [Troubleshooting PXE boot](<#troubleshooting-pxe-boot>).

   > **Watching an install**
   >
   > `journalctl -u flatcar-install -f` as `core@<node>` (`flatcar-install-uefi` on UEFI firmware) shows the wipe and the write (so does a monitor on the node). A failed install does *not* reboot — the node stays in the PXE environment with the journal intact.
8. **Retrieve Kubeconfig**: Once the first control plane has run `kubeadm init`, which this checks:

   ```bash
   ssh core@<node> sudo test -f /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf && make kubeconfig
   ```

   Every `make` target that touches the cluster reads `output/kubeconfig` (`make KUBECONFIG=<file> <target>` picks another); only `kubectl` in your own shell needs the export. Verify the cluster answers. `NotReady` is expected at this point:

   ```bash
   export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/output/kubeconfig"
   kubectl get nodes
   ```

   Once every node is listed, set `bootstrap_cluster` back to `false` in `ansible/inventory.yaml` and run `make config`; `make reinstall` refuses to arm a node while it is `true` and the cluster answers.
9. **Install Cilium** (CRITICAL):

   ```bash
   make install-cilium
   ```

   Installs the Gateway API CRDs, then Cilium via Helm — only what ArgoCD needs in order to run; everything else arrives through ArgoCD, at the versions pinned in each component's `application.yaml` (see [GitOps Strategy → Version pins](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#version-pins>) and [Cilium → Installation](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#installation>)). `make bootstrap` runs this step, `make install-argo` and `make bootstrap-apps` in one go.

   Nodes reach `Ready` once Cilium is up:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/cilium
   kubectl get nodes                  # all Ready
   ```
10. **Post-Installation**:

    - **Deploy ArgoCD**:

      ```bash
      make install-argo
      ```

      There is no way into the UI yet: the local admin is disabled in `payload/argocd/values.yaml` and Authentik arrives later through GitOps. Follow the bootstrap with `kubectl` instead.

      **Tip — the UI before Authentik exists:** re-enable the local admin with a patch. It holds only until the next step: right now ArgoCD is the plain Helm release `make install-argo` made, and `make bootstrap-apps` hands it to the self-healing `argocd` Application, whose first sync puts `admin.enabled` back to what `payload/argocd/values.yaml` says. After that the only way in is the pull request in [Authentik → When Authentik is down](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#when-authentik-is-down>). The restart is what generates the password Secret:

      ```bash
      kubectl -n argocd patch cm argocd-cm --type merge \
        -p '{"data":{"admin.enabled":"true"}}'
      kubectl -n argocd rollout restart deploy/argocd-server
      kubectl -n argocd rollout status deploy/argocd-server

      kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
        -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
      kubectl -n argocd port-forward svc/argocd-server 8080:80   # http://localhost:8080, user admin
      ```

      Nothing to undo: the handover reverts the patch.
    - **Hand the cluster over to ArgoCD**:

      ```bash
      make bootstrap-apps
      ```

      Applies the AppProjects, then the self-managing `argocd` Application, which brings the `platform` ApplicationSet and with it every component at once. They converge in the [order their dependencies allow](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#rollout-order>); watch them settle:

      ```bash
      kubectl -n argocd get applications -w
      ```

      **Everything that reads a secret stays Degraded, and that is expected.** No `ExternalSecret` resolves until step 11 — see [Bootstrap pauses at OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-pauses-at-openbao>).
    - **Gate on storage** before trusting anything that mounts a volume:

      ```bash
      make storage-check
      ```

      A `StorageClass` exists whether or not a CSI driver registered for it, so `rook-ceph-cluster` can go Healthy with no working provisioner. This asks for a volume the way a workload would and names the first broken link — see [Rook-Ceph → Is storage ready?](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#is-storage-ready>).
11. **Initialise the secret store**: OpenBao starts uninitialised, sealed and empty; every `ExternalSecret` stays Degraded until it is unsealed and `certificates` until it is populated, then everything converges on its own.

    ```bash
    make bao-init
    ```

    Initialises and unseals OpenBao, enables the `kv` v2 engine and the Kubernetes auth method, and writes the policy and role External Secrets authenticates with, then replaces the root token with an operator login. The keys land in `output/credentials/openbao-init.json`, the login in `openbao-operator.json` beside it.

    > **Move those keys before you do anything else**
    >
    > That file is a plaintext copy of the keys to every secret the cluster holds. Copy them into a password manager and delete it. Losing them means the data is unrecoverable. See [OpenBao → Bootstrap](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#bootstrap>).

    Then populate the paths the cluster reads:

    ```bash
    make bao-secrets
    ```

    It prompts, with input hidden, for every value that belongs to an account outside the cluster: the DNS, mail and other third-party logins listed at the top of `scripts/bao-secrets.sh`, each against a path in [OpenBao → KV layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kv-layout>). A required value has no skip; an optional one is issued by something that runs on the cluster and takes Enter until it exists. A fork without one of those accounts replaces that path's `decide` line with `WRITE_<NAME>=0`, which skips its prompt and its write; deleting the line fails the script, which runs under `set -u` and reads every flag. Everything random — `kv/authentik/config` with the OIDC client credentials ArgoCD and Grafana read back, Grafana's break-glass admin password — is not prompted for: a `PushSecret` writes it once the store validates, see [Generated secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generated-secrets>). On a running cluster it asks per path before overwriting — see [Rotating a credential](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#rotating-a-credential>). Paste values at the prompt: on a command line a `#` or `!` in one is silently mangled.

    Once the store validates, every `ExternalSecret` resolves, `certificates` issues the gateway certificates and the Gateways come up. The store is re-checked every few minutes, so that can take that long to start.
12. **Create the first administrator**: Authentik ships the built-in `akadmin` account, and the blueprints switch it off as soon as it exists — see [Bootstrap credentials](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#bootstrap-credentials>). Log in to OpenBao inside the pod with the operator password `make bao-init` wrote, read the `akadmin` password, and switch the account on:

    ```bash
    jq -r .password output/credentials/openbao-operator.json | \
      kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -- bao login -method=userpass username=operator password=-
    kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- \
      bao kv get -mount=kv -field=bootstrap-password authentik/config
    kubectl -n authentik exec deploy/authentik-server -c server -- ak shell -c \
      'from authentik.core.models import User; User.objects.filter(username="akadmin").update(is_active=True)'
    ```

    Log in at `https://auth.k8s.<your-domain>` as `akadmin`; the first login enrols a second factor. Create a personal account in *Directory → Users* and put it in `authentik Admins` and the groups listed in [Authentik → Groups and roles](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#groups-and-roles>) under *Directory → Groups*; the blueprints create them.

    ArgoCD's `policy.default` is empty, so an SSO login that lands on an ArgoCD with no applications means a missing group, not a broken integration. Then switch `akadmin` off again with the same command and `is_active=False`; when Authentik itself is unavailable, see [When Authentik is down](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#when-authentik-is-down>).

## Single-node clusters

One node does not run this platform: control planes get no Ceph OSD (see [Rook-Ceph → Disks](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#disks>)) and the block pool wants three hosts, so no volume binds and OpenBao stays Pending at step 11. The minimum is under [Hardware Requirements](<#hardware-requirements>).

## Reprovisioned nodes

The installer wipes the disk before `flatcar-install` runs, so a node armed with `make reinstall` hands Ceph an empty disk. If that wipe ever fails, the symptom is no `rook-ceph-osd` pods, a `CephCluster` still reporting `Ready`, and `openbao-0` Pending on an unbound PVC at step 11 — see [Rook-Ceph → No OSDs after reprovisioning](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#no-osds-after-reprovisioning>).

## Verifying the result

Run the [routine health check](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/index.md#routine-health-check>) and `make storage-check` once more. Once DNS points at the gateway addresses, the platform UIs answer — see [HTTPRoute Locations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#httproute-locations>). Next: [Adding a Workload](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/add-workload/index.md>).

## Troubleshooting PXE boot

Step 7 fails as a black screen with a blinking cursor and no error message. Read the `make serve` log instead of the node and ask how far it got.

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing after the startup lines; the node never appears | DHCP isn't handing out options 66/67, or the node isn't on the same L2 segment. Check the DHCP lease and that PXE is enabled in firmware. |
| Node comes up on an address other than its `ansible_host` | No per-MAC DHCP reservation, or one for the wrong NIC. The join uses the rendered address, not the leased one. |
| `PXE-E32: TFTP open timeout` | `make serve` isn't running, or a firewall is blocking UDP/69. On macOS, allow the Python interpreter through the firewall; on Linux, lower the [unprivileged port start](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#boot-server>). |
| Bootloader loads, then "Could not find kernel image" or a hang at the menu | `boot_server_ip` in `inventory.yaml` is wrong. It is baked into the menu's kernel/initrd URLs. Fix it, re-run `make config`, and reboot the node. |
| `no generated menu has that MAC` in the boot server log | The node's `mac_address` in `inventory.yaml` doesn't match its actual NIC. The log prints the MAC the node actually asked for; put that in the inventory and re-run `make config`. |
| `collecting its boot menu -- booting from its local disk` | The node is not armed. `make reinstall LIMIT=<node>` and boot it again. Expected after an install: the boot server disarms a node once it has the OS image. |
| Kernel boots, then Ignition fails | The node couldn't fetch `ignition-<host>-install.json` over HTTP (port 8000), or the Butane template references an SSH key path that doesn't exist. |
| `refusing to wipe active disk` on the first boot after an install | The installer's disk stanza reached the installed system. `wipe_table` belongs in `ignition-<host>-install.json` only — see [Wiping the disk](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#wiping-the-disk>). |
| Node installs but never joins the cluster | Sysext download failed, or the join unit errored. SSH in as `core` and check `journalctl -u bootstrap-k8s`. |

A machine with two NICs PXE boots from whichever it likes, and the MAC on the case is often not that one. A node that boots the menu and stalls right after is almost always a wrong `boot_server_ip`, not a broken image. A file missing from `output/` needs `make artifacts`.

# Adapting This for Your Cluster

This repository documents one homelab, built from the pieces in [Concepts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md>), with its node names, addresses, domain and Git URL hardcoded in `payload/` and `ansible/`. Make the changes below in your fork before step 1 of the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>), and push them: ArgoCD reads Git, not your working tree.

## 1\. Fork and repoint ArgoCD

Every ArgoCD `Application` points at this repository; until you change them, your own commits have no effect. The match ends in `.git`, so the workloads repository is left alone:

```bash
git grep -lz 'github.com/JanWelker/homelab.git' -- payload/ | \
  xargs -0 perl -pi -e 's|github\.com/JanWelker/homelab\.git|github.com/YOUR_USER/YOUR_REPO.git|g'
```

The workloads repository is a second URL, in `payload/platform/argocd-projects/projects.yaml` (the `apps` project's `sourceRepos`) and `payload/workloads/applicationset.yaml`. Point both at your fork of [homelab-apps](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab-apps>), and change the `repoURL` in every `*/application.yaml` of that fork too, or your cluster deploys the author's applications. Delete the application directories you will not run, with their prompts in `scripts/bao-secrets.sh`; what the platform names per workload is in [GitOps Strategy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#workloads-live-in-a-second-repository>).

A private fork also needs [repository credentials](<https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/declarative-setup/#repositories>) in ArgoCD.

## 2\. Choose your domain

Four hostname patterns carry traffic, each a listener in `gateway-api/gateways.yaml`, a zone in external-dns's `domainFilters` and, for HTTPS, a wildcard `Certificate` in `certificates/certificates.yaml`, all under `payload/platform/`:

| Pattern | Purpose | In a fork |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `*.k8s.<your-domain>` | user-facing workloads, via `apps-gateway` | rename |
| `*.infra.k8s.<your-domain>` | platform UIs (ArgoCD, Grafana, Hubble, OpenBao, Rook), via `infra-gateway` | rename |
| `*.ssh.<your-domain>` | the [SSH listener](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#ssh-listener>) for in-cluster agent sessions | rename, or delete the listener and the zone |
| `*.wollbi.ch` | a second site family on `apps-gateway`, with its own listener and certificate | delete `payload/platform/authentik/secrets-*-wollbi.yaml`, and the `wollbi` entries in the other files `git grep -l wollbi -- payload/` lists |

Replace the first three in one pass. It rewrites hostnames only, so label and annotation keys such as `homelab.wlkr.ch/backup-exempt` and `host-firewall.wlkr.ch/exempt` keep the names the workloads and the [lockout runbook](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall-lockout>) use:

```bash
git grep -lzE '(k8s|ssh)\.wlkr\.ch' -- payload/ | \
  xargs -0 perl -pi -e 's/\b(k8s|ssh)\.wlkr\.ch\b/$1.YOUR-DOMAIN.example/g'
```

You must own the domain: Let's Encrypt's DNS-01 challenge needs write access to its zone, so `.local`, `.lan` and made-up TLDs fail.

## 3\. Point DNS at the gateway IPs

Each Gateway asks for a fixed address in its `spec.addresses`, which must lie inside the Cilium pools in `payload/platform/cilium/lb-pools.yaml`, or the Gateway is never programmed:

| Gateway | DNS record |
| --- | --- |
| `apps-gateway` | `*.k8s.<your-domain>` |
| `infra-gateway` | `*.infra.k8s.<your-domain>` |

Change both pools and both `spec.addresses` to free LAN addresses outside the DHCP range, so the router never hands one out, then create the two wildcard `A` records. `apps-gateway` also carries an `external-dns.kubernetes.io/target` annotation, the public address external-dns publishes for its names: set your own, or delete it to publish the LAN address — see [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md#configuration>) and [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#configuration>). Two more things decide whether anything answers on those addresses:

- The `CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy` in `lb-pools.yaml` answers ARP for them from the control planes only, on interfaces matching a pattern: change its `nodeSelector` and `interfaces` to fit. L2 needs the addresses in the nodes' subnet.
- `payload/platform/cilium/bgp.yaml` also announces them to the router over eBGP, and its peer and ASNs must match the inventory (step 5). With no BGP router, delete it and `bgp-secret.yaml` beside it, and skip the `cilium/bgp` path in `scripts/bao-secrets.sh` as in [Quickstart step 11](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>).

## 4\. Set up the DNS-01 solver

`payload/platform/certificates/cluster-issuers.yaml` is written for **AWS Route53**. Update:

- `email:` — your address, on both issuers. Let's Encrypt sends expiry notices here.
- `region:` — the Route53 region.

DNS hosted elsewhere means more than the matching [cert-manager DNS-01 provider](<https://cert-manager.io/docs/configuration/acme/dns01/>): external-dns is configured for AWS too, and the egress policies of both admit only that API. `git grep -il route53 -- payload/ scripts/` lists every file, the credential prompts included.

> [!TIP]
>
> Switch `issuerRef` in `certificates.yaml` to `letsencrypt-staging` while iterating: production allows 5 duplicate certificates per week, and a broken solver burns through that in minutes.

## 5\. Describe your hardware

Edit `ansible/inventory.yaml`; every variable is listed under [Quickstart → step 2](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>). The ones a fork must choose rather than copy, and the payload settings that repeat them:

| Setting | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `control_plane_vip` | Free address on the nodes' subnet, outside DHCP and distinct from the LoadBalancer pools. Becomes the API endpoint in the cluster certificates. |
| `control_plane_vip_interface` | The NIC kube-vip advertises on; before provisioning, `ip -br link` on any live Linux booted on the machine usually shows the name Flatcar gives it. |
| `control_plane_endpoint_host` | Set a name on a fresh build, see [Endpoint name](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md#endpoint-name>); a running cluster keeps the VIP. |
| host entries | Each needs `ansible_host`, `mac_address` (the NIC that PXE boots) and a matching DHCP reservation — see [Quickstart → Other requirements](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#other-requirements>). |
| `router_ip`, `router_asn`, `cluster_asn` | `payload/platform/cilium/bgp.yaml` must name the same values, since the payload cannot read the inventory — see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>). |
| `providerRegex`, `providerIpPrefixes` in `payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/application.yaml` | Your node names and subnet, or every kubelet serving certificate is denied — see [metrics-server](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/metrics-server/index.md#verifying-the-kubelet-instead-of-trusting-it>). |

Then update `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml`:

- `k8sServiceHost` — `control_plane_vip`, from the start on a new build, where the bootstrap static pod holds it; a literal, because Cilium replaces `kube-proxy` and cannot reach the API through a Service — see [Design Decisions → Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#cilium-as-cni-replacing-kube-proxy>).
- `devices` — the interface prefix Cilium binds to, found the same way.

And `payload/platform/kube-vip/daemonset.yaml`, which cannot read the inventory either:

- `address` — the same value as `control_plane_vip`.
- `vip_interface` — the same value as `control_plane_vip_interface`.

A mismatch fails only at the first sync, when the DaemonSet replaces the static pods and advertises somewhere else.

Two more places carry the author's network and mail:

- `git grep -nE '10\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' -- payload/` lists the address literals, among them the etcd peers in the [host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) and the subnets Tetragon's tracing policies treat as internal.
- The mail relay is `smtp_smarthost` in `payload/platform/monitoring/alertmanager-config.yaml`, and its name a `toFQDNs` entry in `network-policies/monitoring.yaml` — see [Alerting](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#alerting>).

## 6\. Provisioning access

The SSH key in [Quickstart → Other requirements](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#other-requirements>) is the only way into the nodes: there is no password, no console login and no rescue path short of reprovisioning.

## 7\. The documentation site

To publish your own copy, set `site_url`, `repo_url`, `repo_name` and `copyright` in `zensical.toml` and your domain in `docs/CNAME` (delete it for none); `docs.yaml` then publishes to your GitHub Pages. Otherwise delete `.github/workflows/docs.yaml`.

## Parts tied to the author's accounts

| Component | Why | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arc-controller`, `arc-runners` | `githubConfigUrl` names a repository of the author's, and the runners register with a GitHub App installed there | [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md#github-app>) |
| `apps` project in `argocd-projects` | `sourceRepos` lists the author's chart registries | [ArgoCD → Projects](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#projects>) |
| Claude agents | `security/claude-agent-rbac.yaml`, the SSH listener and an Argo CD account serve the author's sessions | [Agent RBAC](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#agent-rbac>) |
| Repository settings | `.github/CODEOWNERS`, `reviewers` and the preset in `renovate.json`, and `ci-ok.yaml` name the author's account | [Maintenance](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/maintenance/index.md>) |

To drop a component, delete its directory under `payload/platform/`, the lines `git grep -n <namespace> -- payload/` lists for each of its namespaces, and its path in `scripts/bao-secrets.sh` as in [Quickstart step 11](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>).

# Architecture

# Architecture

A bare metal Kubernetes cluster on Flatcar Container Linux and kubeadm: a rack of machines, a network, and a deployment host that talks them into existence. The stack itself is summarised in [one table](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/index.md#the-stack-in-one-table>) on the home page, and the reasoning behind each choice in [Design Decisions](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md>).

This section assumes you know what Flatcar, Ignition, systemd sysexts, PXE and GitOps are; [Core Concepts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md>) covers all five.

## What is in this section

- **[Boot & Bootstrap Process](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md>)**

  ---

  One node from power-on to `kubectl get nodes`, arrow by arrow, and the boot server that serves each step. Start here when an install stalls.
- **[Ansible](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md>)**

  ---

  The playbooks that generate everything the boot server serves.
- **[GitOps Strategy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>)**

  ---

  The ApplicationSet, the sync policy every Application shares, and how a fresh bootstrap converges without an order.
- **[Design Decisions](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md>)**

  ---

  Each choice as *X, not Y*, with its cost. Read before proposing a simpler alternative.
- **[Security Posture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md>)** · **[Audit Logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>)**

  ---

  The trust boundary this cluster assumes, what is deliberately not enforced, and what the API server records.
- **[Known Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>)**

  ---

  What it does not do, in one table.

## Cluster Layout

The deployment host — the laptop running Ansible and the boot server — is **not** part of the cluster and nothing depends on it once provisioning is done.

| Role | Nodes | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control plane | odin, thor, loki | etcd and the API server; tainted, no workloads, no Ceph |
| Worker | freya, heimdall, valkyrie, baldur, tyr, frigg, bragi, idun | Everything else, and a Ceph OSD partition each |

Three control-plane nodes because etcd needs an odd number, and two is the worst answer: twice the hardware and quorum still lost when one dies. The API server is reached through a kube-vip virtual IP rather than any single node — see [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>). Addresses, the VIP and the pod and service subnets are in `ansible/inventory.yaml`. How a request reaches a pod from the Internet, the LAN or another VLAN is drawn in [Traffic Flow](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#traffic-flow>).

## Repository layout

`ansible/` describes the machines, `boot_server/` hands them their operating system, `payload/` is the platform the cluster runs on, and `output/` is generated — never edit anything in there, the next `make config` overwrites it. The applications the cluster exists to serve live in the separate [`homelab-apps`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab-apps>) repository; see [GitOps Strategy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#workloads-live-in-a-second-repository>).

```text
.
├── .github/workflows       # CI: linters, docs build and preview, argo-diff-preview -- see Maintenance
├── ansible                 # Inventory, playbooks and templates -- see Ansible
├── boot_server
│   └── serve.py            # TFTP + HTTP boot server
├── docs                    # This site
├── output                  # Generated; never edited by hand
│   ├── credentials/        # Bootstrap token, certificate key, etcd
│   │                       # encryption key, OpenBao unseal keys -- 0700
│   ├── http/               # Ignition, Flatcar artifacts, sysext images
│   ├── kubeconfig          # Admin kubeconfig
│   ├── router/             # FRR BGP config for the router
│   ├── tftp/               # PXE bootloader and menus
│   └── tmp/                # Readable copies of the rendered Butane and kubeadm configs
├── overrides               # Theme template overrides for the docs site
├── payload                 # Everything ArgoCD deploys
│   ├── argocd/             # ArgoCD itself: Application, ApplicationSet, values
│   ├── platform/           # One directory per component, each with one
│   │   └── ...             #   application.yaml -- see Platform
│   └── workloads/          # The handover to homelab-apps
├── scripts                 # What the make targets run: OpenBao bootstrap, storage check, fonts
├── tests                   # pytest for the boot server
├── Makefile                # Every operator command, one target each
├── renovate.json           # The version pins Renovate tracks -- see Maintenance
├── zensical.toml           # Documentation site configuration
└── README.md
```

`ansible/` and `boot_server/` matter only while a node is being built; `payload/` matters every day after that.

`output/credentials/` is generated once and read back on every later run; `make config` writes new values for anything missing, which a running cluster will not accept. `make clean` therefore prints that inventory and asks before deleting, and refuses without a terminal.

| Target | Removes | Keeps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `make clean-artifacts` | `output/http`, `output/tftp`, `output/tmp`, `output/router` | `output/credentials/`, `output/kubeconfig` |
| `make clean` | everything under `output/` | nothing — it asks first |

# Ansible Configuration

Ansible never configures a node here: it generates files on the deployment host, and Ignition applies them once, on a node's first boot.

It renders two Ignition configs per host from two templates — one the PXE environment [runs to install](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#3-install-bootstrap>), one `flatcar-install` embeds into the system it writes. Changing anything under `ansible/` therefore takes a rebuild of the affected node, not a reboot. The directory layout is in [Repository layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md#repository-layout>).

## Inventory

`ansible/inventory.yaml` is the single source of truth for the machines; every generated artifact comes from it, and the values are baked into the output rather than read at boot. The variables are described in [Quickstart step 2](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>). Every playbook targets the `k8s_nodes` group, the parent of `control_plane` and `workers`, which carries `ansible_user` and the SSH options.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every edit needs a regeneration, and some need two**
>
> `make config` re-renders the Ignition configs, PXE menus and router config from the inventory; `make download` fetches what `flatcar_channel`, `flatcar_version`, `syslinux_version` and `kubernetes_version` name. The Flatcar, Kubernetes and kube-vip versions are rendered into the configs too, so a version bump needs `make artifacts`, which runs both. Which target reads which variable is in the [Quickstart table](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>). An edit followed by neither changes nothing at all, silently.

`bootstrap_cluster` in the `control_plane` group decides whether the first control-plane host renders `kubeadm init` (`true`, the first install) or, like every other control plane, `kubeadm join --control-plane` (`false`, every rebuild). A rebuilt node that ran `init` would start a second cluster on the same VIP — see [Rebuilding a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>).

`kube_vip_version` only sets the bootstrap static pod that gives `kubeadm init` a VIP; once ArgoCD syncs, `payload/platform/kube-vip/` takes over and its image is what runs — see [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>).

## Playbooks

| Playbook | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `config.yaml` | Generates the bootstrap token, certificate key, etcd encryption key and each node's SSH host key into `output/credentials/` (mode `0700`), and `output/known_hosts` from the host keys; renders the Ignition configs via Butane into `output/http` (mode `0600`, the node config first: the installer config pins its sha512), the sysupdate config for running nodes beside them, the per-MAC PXE menus into `output/tftp/pxelinux.cfg/`, the router's FRR config into `output/router/frr-bgp.conf`, and a readable kubeadm config copy into `output/tmp/` |
| `download.yaml` | Fetches the Flatcar kernel, initrd, OS image and its detached signature, checked against the `.DIGESTS.asc` that `gpgv` verifies; the Kubernetes sysext image; and the syslinux bootloader files, checked the same way against `sha256sums.asc`. The signing keys are fetched and trusted through the primary fingerprints pinned in the playbook |
| `reinstall.yaml` | Rewrites `DEFAULT` in the generated PXE menus — `install` to arm, `localboot` to disarm. `make reinstall` and `make reinstall-cancel` are the two directions, both taking `LIMIT=<host>`. Arming refuses while `bootstrap_cluster` is `true` and the API VIP answers, or when an [endpoint name](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md#endpoint-name>) is not the one the cluster publishes. `make config` keeps each menu's `DEFAULT`, so an armed node stays armed. See [Switching back to local boot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#switching-back-to-local-boot>) |
| `kubeconfig.yaml` | Copies the admin kubeconfig over SSH to `output/kubeconfig`, mode `0600`, with the VIP as its `server` |

`config.yaml` is safe to re-run: the `password` lookup reads an existing credential file back, so the encryption key every control-plane node shares stays the one etcd's Secrets were encrypted with.

`config.yaml` renews the join credentials on the first control-plane host that answers with a running cluster, so the node being [replaced](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#replacing-a-failed-node>) may be any of them; it fails when none answers while `output/kubeconfig` exists, since a node booted then could not join, and skips the renewal only before the first bootstrap.

`kubeconfig.yaml` targets `control_plane[0]` — the first control-plane host in the inventory, with no fallback. If that node is down, copy `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf` off any other control-plane node by hand. Keep a copy of the result off the cluster: it is the credential you want when the web UIs are unreachable, and `output/` is exactly as durable as the laptop it is on.

# Audit Logging

The API server records who did what, to which object, and whether it was allowed. It is also the destination for the `audit` half of the Pod Security Admission labels in [`pod-security.yaml`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md>): without it, findings at the stricter audit level go nowhere.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Policy file | `/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml`, written by Ignition from `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` |
| Log file | `/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log` on each control-plane node |
| Durable copy | [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>), via the Alloy pipeline in `payload/platform/alloy/application.yaml`, on Ceph |
| Query it with | `{job="kubernetes-audit"}` in Grafana |
| Worst-case disk | Bounded by the rotation flags in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2`, see [Where the log lives](<#where-the-log-lives>) |

## Audit policy

`--audit-log-path` on its own does nothing: without `--audit-policy-file` the API server declines to open a log, silently. Rules are evaluated top to bottom and **the first match wins**, so the order is the design:

| Matched | Level | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/healthz*`, `/livez*`, `/readyz*`, `/version`, `/metrics`, `/openapi*` | `None` | Polled continuously by kubelets, probes and Prometheus; the majority of requests |
| Leases, Events | `None` | Renewed every few seconds by every component |
| Reads by the control plane and by `system:nodes` | `None` | Not the reads anyone looks for; dropping them makes the next row affordable |
| Secrets, ConfigMaps, TokenReviews | `Metadata` | Reads included: a *read* is the interesting verb |
| `pods/exec`, `pods/attach`, `pods/portforward` | `RequestResponse` | Which pod, as which user, running what |
| Everything else read-only | `None` |  |
| Everything that changes state | `Metadata` | Also the level that carries the Pod Security Admission annotations |

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Never raise the Secret rule above `Metadata`**
>
> At `Request` or `RequestResponse` the request body is recorded, and for a Secret the body *is* the credential. The audit log would become an unencrypted copy of every Secret in the cluster, in a flat file beside the etcd that was [encrypted at rest](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md#encryption-at-rest>) to prevent exactly that.

## Where the log lives

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Path | `/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log` |
| Filesystem | root, ext4 |
| Rotation | The `--audit-log-maxsize`, `--audit-log-maxbackup` and `--audit-log-maxage` flags in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2`; the product of size and backups bounds the footprint, and the age cap keeps a quiet cluster from holding a month-old rotation forever |

The root filesystem persists across reboots, so the log survives on the node. Alloy still tails it into Loki, which is the copy that matters: a log stored only on the node is unavailable in precisely the situation where the node is what failed.

## Reading it

Audit events reach Loki as JSON with `job="kubernetes-audit"`, plus `verb` and `audit_level` as labels, set by the Alloy pipeline in `payload/platform/alloy/application.yaml`. Everything else stays in the line, where `| json` can reach it:

```text
# Who read Secrets, and which ones
{job="kubernetes-audit"} | json | objectRef_resource="secrets"

# Every exec into a running container
{job="kubernetes-audit", verb="create"} | json | objectRef_subresource="exec"

# Pod Security Admission violations that were audited but not enforced
{job="kubernetes-audit"} |= "pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-violations"
```

The last query answers "what would break if I tightened `enforce` on this namespace" from evidence, for the whole retention window. Exec, Secret reads by a person, RBAC writes, 403 bursts and anonymous requests also fire alerts from Loki's ruler, defined in `payload/platform/logging/loki-rules.yaml`; see [Logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>).

## Applying it to a running cluster

Changing the templates changes what a **newly provisioned** node gets. A running control-plane node keeps the `kube-apiserver.yaml` static pod manifest kubeadm rendered at init time, and nothing rewrites it on its own.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Get the policy file there before you re-render the manifest**
>
> An API server started with `--audit-policy-file` pointing at a missing file does not start. Step 3 before step 4, one node at a time, confirming the API server comes back before moving on.

1. Regenerate the Ignition configs so a rebuild gets this too:

   ```bash
   make config
   ```
2. Create the directories on the node:

   ```bash
   ssh core@<node> sudo mkdir -p /etc/kubernetes/audit /var/log/kubernetes/audit
   ssh core@<node> sudo chmod 0700 /etc/kubernetes/audit /var/log/kubernetes/audit
   ```
3. Place the policy file. It is inline in the Butane template, so take it from the rendered copy:

   ```bash
   yq '.storage.files[] | select(.path == "/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml") | .contents.inline' \
     output/tmp/butane/butane-<node>.yaml > /tmp/policy.yaml
   scp /tmp/policy.yaml core@<node>:/tmp/policy.yaml
   ssh core@<node> sudo install -m 0600 /tmp/policy.yaml /etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml
   ```
4. Place the regenerated kubeadm config on the node and re-render the API server static pod from it:

   ```bash
   scp output/tmp/kubeadm/kubeadm-config-<node>.yaml core@<node>:/tmp/kubeadm-config.yaml
   ssh core@<node> sudo install -m 0600 /tmp/kubeadm-config.yaml /opt/kubeadm-config.yaml
   ssh core@<node> sudo kubeadm init phase control-plane apiserver \
     --config /opt/kubeadm-config.yaml
   ```
5. Watch the kubelet restart the static pod:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-<node> -w
   ```
6. Update the `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap in `kube-system` so the flags survive the next `kubeadm upgrade` or control-plane join — kubeadm reads the ConfigMap on those paths, not `/opt/kubeadm-config.yaml`:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap kubeadm-config
   ```

# Boot & Bootstrap Process

One node from the power button to `kubectl get nodes`. When an install stalls, the question is *which arrow did not happen?*

## 1\. Preparation (on the deployment host)

`make config` generates the per-host Ignition and PXE configs; `make serve` starts the [boot server](<#boot-server>). The [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>) has the exact sequence.

## 2\. Network Boot

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Node
    participant DHCP
    participant Server as Boot Server

    Node->>DHCP: 1. PXE request
    DHCP-->>Node: 2. IP, next-server, filename
    Node->>Server: 3. TFTP bootloader
    Server-->>Node: 4. syslinux + menu
    Node->>Server: 5. HTTP kernel, initrd
    Server-->>Node: 6. Flatcar kernel, initrd
```

The DHCP server is external and must hand out the boot server's IP as `next-server` and a syslinux filename — see the [Quickstart prerequisites](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#prerequisites>). Step 2 is where most first attempts die, silently: the firmware moves on to the next boot device.

## 3\. Install & Bootstrap

PXE boots the **installer**, and only on a node armed with `make reinstall`; the generated menu otherwise says `DEFAULT localboot`. The installer is a RAM environment whose only job is to write Flatcar to `install_disk` and reboot into it. Two templates, because two machines share a disk and nothing else:

| Template | Renders to | Runs in | `wipe_table` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `butane_installer_config.yaml.j2` | `ignition-<host>-install.json` | the PXE environment | `true` |
| `butane_node_config.yaml.j2` | `ignition-<host>.json` | the installed system, first boot | `false` |

The PXE menu points at the first. The installer fetches the second over HTTP, verifies it against the sha512 rendered into the first, and hands it to `flatcar-install -i`, which embeds it in the OEM partition of the system it writes. The boot server gives it only to the node's `ansible_host`, its DHCP reservation.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Keep the installer minimal**
>
> Anything in `butane_installer_config.yaml.j2` is downloaded into RAM on every install and discarded ninety seconds later. If it configures the node rather than the installation, it belongs in `butane_node_config.yaml.j2`.

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Node
    participant Server as Boot Server

    Node->>Server: 7. HTTP Ignition config
    Note over Node,Server: Only when armed with make reinstall
    Server-->>Node: 8. ignition-<host>-install.json
    Node->>Server: 9. HTTP ignition-<host>.json, sha512-checked
    Node->>Server: 10. HTTP Flatcar image + signature
    Note over Server: Server disarms the menu back to localboot
    Node->>Node: 11. Wipe disk, flatcar-install, reboot
    Note over Node: Now booting from disk, not the network
    Node->>Node: 12. Ignition partitions and writes /etc
    Node->>Server: 13. HTTP sysext image
    Server-->>Node: 14. kubernetes
    Node->>Node: 15. systemd unit runs kubeadm
    Note over Node: init on the first control plane, join against the VIP elsewhere
    Note over Node: Node is NotReady - no CNI yet
```

Between steps 10 and 11 the boot server rewrites the node's menu to `DEFAULT localboot` — see [Switching back to local boot](<#switching-back-to-local-boot>). From step 12 the node runs from disk and needs the boot server only for the sysexts in step 13, on this first boot. Step 15 runs `kubeadm init` only on the first control plane while [`bootstrap_cluster`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md#inventory>) is `true`. `NotReady` after it is expected: there is no CNI until `make install-cilium`.

### Wiping the disk

Step 11 is the point of no return, and the wipe has three parts:

| Wipe | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wipe_table: true` | `ignition-<host>-install.json` only | Destroys the GPT before the installer runs, so partition numbers and offsets come out the same whether the disk was empty or held the last cluster. Without it a rebuild inherits the old layout and `ignition-disks.service` fails on an `sgdisk` overlap |
| `blkdiscard` | installer | Returns the device to unwritten. Best-effort: SATA without TRIM declines |
| `wipe_filesystem: true` on `rook-osd` | `butane_node_config.yaml.j2` | Erases the old BlueStore signature, which `ceph-volume` reads instead of the partition table; a repartition alone can resurrect an OSD from a previous cluster |

The installed system's config must not wipe: Ignition refuses to touch the disk it booted from (`refusing to wipe active disk`), failing the first boot before anything is written. `storage.filesystems` follows the same split — `rook-osd` does not exist in the installer, and Ignition would block waiting for it.

Check `install_disk` first.

### Boot order

The install leaves the firmware's boot order alone (`flatcar-install -u`, which would put the disk first in `BootOrder`, is not passed). The nodes network-boot first and reach their disk through `LOCALBOOT`, so the generated menu decides every boot; a disk promoted ahead of PXE would make `make reinstall` rewrite a menu the firmware no longer reads. A node needs network boot first with a working `LOCALBOOT`, or the disk ahead of PXE — with neither it installs and then has nothing to boot.

## 4\. Post-Installation Bootstrap

Once kubeadm has initialised the control plane, `make bootstrap` installs only what ArgoCD needs to run, and ArgoCD itself; once the `argocd` Application is applied, the repository is in charge.

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant Admin as Operator
    participant Deploy as Deployment Host
    participant Cluster

    Admin->>Deploy: 1. make install-cilium
    Deploy->>Cluster: 2. Helm install Gateway API CRDs, Cilium
    Note over Cluster: Nodes become Ready
    Admin->>Deploy: 3. make install-argo
    Deploy->>Cluster: 4. Helm install ArgoCD
    Admin->>Deploy: 5. make bootstrap-apps
    Deploy->>Cluster: 6. Apply AppProjects + the argocd Application
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> **`make untaint` is not part of this flow**
>
> It removes the control-plane `NoSchedule` taint and applies only to a single-node cluster, where it goes *before* `make install-argo` — ArgoCD has no tolerations. The [documented layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/index.md#cluster-layout>) has dedicated workers; see [Single-node clusters](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#single-node-clusters>).

## Every boot after the first

The node boots from its own disk; the boot server should be off.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `/` | ext4 on partition 9, grown into it by `grow-root.service`: a fixed size on workers (`size_mib` in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2`) so the OSD partition gets the rest, the whole disk on control planes |
| Ignition | Runs **once**, on the first boot after the install |
| `/etc/kubernetes`, `/var/lib/etcd`, `/var/lib/rook` | On disk; survive a reboot |
| `rook-osd` | Partition 10 on workers, raw and unmounted — Ceph owns it |

`bootstrap-k8s.service` does not fire again: its `ConditionPathExists=!/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf` is no longer satisfied.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Why `grow-root.service` exists**
>
> Taking partition 9 over in Ignition stops Flatcar's stock `systemd-growfs-root.service`: an `x-systemd.growfs` mount option pulls it in, and a root mounted from `root=LABEL=ROOT` does not carry it. Without the unit the node keeps the image's \~1.6 GB filesystem inside a far larger partition. It runs the same binary and is a no-op once the filesystem fills the partition.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Two boot paths, and the menu picks the safe one**
>
> `PROMPT 0` boots whatever `DEFAULT` names. A new menu says `DEFAULT localboot`, so a node that network-boots lands on its own disk; `make config` keeps whatever a menu already says, so an armed node stays armed. `make reinstall` rewrites that one line to arm it; see [Rebuilding or repartitioning a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>). Holding Shift or Alt at boot forces the prompt, the escape hatch for a node armed by mistake.

## Boot server

`boot_server/serve.py` is a TFTP server and an HTTP server, installed by `uv sync` as the `boot-server` command. `make serve` runs it as you, never root, from the repository root (the document roots hang off `--root`, which defaults to the working directory): macOS denies Local Network access to a process that started as root and dropped it, so every TFTP reply would fail with *No route to host*. HTTP binds `boot_server_ip` from `ansible/inventory.yaml` — the address `make config` baked into every generated URL — and nothing else, because it serves the Ignition secrets; stalled clients time out. TFTP listens on every interface, the only way an ordinary user may bind port 69 on macOS; on Linux, lower `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` to 69. If no interface holds `boot_server_ip` it says so and names the variable; if port 8000 is taken it exits. A failed send ends that node's transfer, not the server. `--bind`, `--http-port` and `--tftp-port` override the address and ports, which is how tests and laptop dry runs avoid the privileged port.

| Server | Root | Serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TFTP, port 69 | `output/tftp` | `lpxelinux.0` (BIOS) or `syslinux.efi` (UEFI), and the menus in `pxelinux.cfg/` |
| HTTP, port 8000 | `output/http` | Kernel, initrd, OS image and signature, Ignition configs, sysext images. No directory listings |

Both roots are written by `make config` and `make download`; a missing file is fixed by `make artifacts`, not by the script.

Leave it in the foreground. It opens by naming what it serves and which nodes are armed — a boxed warning listing every disk about to be wiped, with `make reinstall-cancel` and its `LIMIT=<node>` form — then logs one line per request against the node that made it: role, name, address and MAC once the menu it fetched has identified it, dashes before. The file a node *stops* at is the diagnosis; see [Troubleshooting PXE boot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#troubleshooting-pxe-boot>).

```console
20:33:04  server                                                    http on 10.9.200.222:8000 from output/http
20:33:04  server                                                    tftp on every interface, port 69, from output/tftp

  ⚠  ARMED TO INSTALL: odin, thor

20:34:17  -             -        10.9.2.1        -                  collecting the bootloader (lpxelinux.0)
20:34:17  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  collecting its boot menu -- armed, so it will install
20:34:48  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  collecting its Ignition config
20:34:48  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  collecting the OS image (1.2 GB) -- this is the long one
20:36:12  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  OS image delivered -- switching to local boot, so the reboot lands on the disk
20:38:40  control-plane odin     10.9.2.1        fc:3f:db:0d:8f:5c  collecting the kubernetes sysext (61.4 MB)
```

A node is identified by MAC from the `01-<mac>` menu it fetches, and after the install by name from the `ignition-<host>.json` it asks for. Any other address is logged bare, and a request for another node's config is refused.

## Switching back to local boot

`make reinstall` writes `DEFAULT install` into a node's menu and nothing in the generated files writes it back, so firmware that network-boots first would reinstall forever. The boot server therefore disarms the node the moment it has delivered the whole OS image — the same edit `make reinstall-cancel` makes. A node that never fetched an Ignition config cannot be identified by name; the server says so and tells you to run `make reinstall-cancel` yourself.

Arming survives the boot server, because the menu is a file on disk. `Ctrl-C` therefore checks: if anything is still armed it offers `Disarm 2 node(s) now? [Y/n]`. Enter accepts; anything else leaves them armed and repeats the cancel command. Without a terminal on stdin it warns and leaves them armed.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **It disarms on delivery, not on success**
>
> The server sees a transfer complete, not whether `flatcar-install` then wrote the disk. An install that fails after the download leaves a disarmed node with no working disk — loud, because `flatcar-install.service` (`flatcar-install-uefi.service` on UEFI firmware) does not reboot on failure — and the fix is `make reinstall LIMIT=<node>` before the power cycle.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Stop it when you are done**
>
> While it runs, anything on the segment can fetch the Ignition configs, which embed the kubeadm bootstrap token and certificate key — together enough to join a control-plane node. The token expires by its `ttl` in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2`, the certificate key with kubeadm's uploaded certificates; `make config` re-arms both against a running cluster (`ansible/templates/renew_join_credentials.sh.j2`). The real mitigation is not leaving it running, and nothing needs it after a build. See [Security Posture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md#provisioning>).

# Design Decisions

Why each choice, and what it gives up. Every one has a reasonable alternative.

## Flatcar Container Linux, not Talos or a general-purpose distro

Flatcar is an immutable, minimal, container-focused OS with A/B updates and declarative first-boot provisioning through Ignition. Nothing is configured by hand on a node, so a node is disposable and reproducible from `inventory.yaml`.

Talos goes further — no SSH, no shell, an API-driven machine config — and would remove a whole class of drift. Flatcar keeps a conventional Linux underneath: `ssh`, `systemd`, `journalctl` and `kubeadm` work the way the upstream Kubernetes documentation assumes, which matters more for a cluster that is also a learning environment than the extra hardening does.

The cost is that Flatcar's read-only `/usr` forces everything unusual into [sysexts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/concepts/index.md#systemd-sysexts>), Kubernetes included, which is the source of the update behaviour in [Updates & Upgrades](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md>).

## kubeadm, not k3s or a managed distribution

kubeadm produces a stock upstream cluster: real etcd, standard control-plane components, and a topology that matches the Kubernetes documentation. k3s would have been far less work — a single binary, batteries included — at the price of a bundled, non-standard set of components.

The cost is that everything above the API server is this project's problem: CNI, ingress, storage and certificates are all installed and sequenced explicitly. Most of `payload/` exists because of this choice.

## Cilium as CNI, replacing kube-proxy

Cilium replaces `kube-proxy` with eBPF, removing the iptables and IPVS service-routing path. It also supplies Gateway API, L2 announcements for LoadBalancer addresses, WireGuard transparent encryption and Hubble for flow visibility — four things that would otherwise be four components on bare metal.

The cost is a hard bootstrap dependency: with no `kube-proxy`, Cilium needs a literal API server address in `k8sServiceHost`, the [control plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>) so no single node carries the CNI; an address that does not answer takes networking down everywhere.

## Gateway API, not Ingress

Ingress is effectively frozen, and its per-controller annotations are why Ingress manifests are rarely portable. Gateway API separates the cluster-owned `Gateway` from the app-owned `HTTPRoute`, which fits the split between this repository and the [workloads repository](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/add-workload/index.md>) exactly: the `Gateway` is platform, the `HTTPRoute` ships with the application.

The cost is a smaller ecosystem and more moving parts: CRDs must be installed before anything references them, which is why they are their own Applications that every consumer's sync retries against.

## Rook-Ceph, not Longhorn or local volumes

Every worker contributes a raw partition (the control planes keep their disk for etcd, see [Disks](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#disks>)), and Ceph turns them into replicated block storage that survives a node failure. Local volumes would be simpler and faster, but would go down with every [update reboot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md>). Longhorn is the closer alternative and easier to operate; Ceph was chosen for its maturity and because the same cluster also serves the S3 buckets the backups and Loki write to — see [Object storage](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#object-storage>).

The cost: Ceph is the heaviest component in the cluster, wants at least three nodes, and has its own failure modes and vocabulary. It also only provides `ReadWriteOnce` here, since CephFS is not deployed.

## OpenBao, not sealed-secrets or SOPS

Sealed-secrets and SOPS keep encrypted material in Git, so rotation is a commit and revocation is impossible after the fact — the ciphertext is in every clone, forever. OpenBao keeps secrets out of the repository and hands them to workloads as ordinary `Secret` objects through the External Secrets Operator.

The cost is a manual unseal after every restart, taken deliberately over an auto-unseal dependency outside the house — see [Unsealing after a restart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#unsealing-after-a-restart>).

## ArgoCD with an ApplicationSet, not Flux

Either would work. ArgoCD was chosen mainly for its UI, which makes sync state and drift legible at a glance — worth more in a homelab, where the operator is often re-learning the system after months away, than Flux's smaller footprint.

After a bootstrap of two `kubectl apply`s an ApplicationSet discovers everything else; see [GitOps Strategy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>).

## CloudNativePG for every database, not the chart's bundled one

Accepting each chart's PostgreSQL subchart is how a cluster ends up running four Postgres versions from four maintainers, each upgraded on someone else's schedule. The rule in the [workloads repository](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/add-workload/index.md>) is absolute: the subchart is disabled and the application points at a CloudNativePG `Cluster` in its own namespace. The operator generates the credentials into a Secret the chart consumes, so no database password is written down — not in Git, not in OpenBao.

The cost is a controller and a CRD to learn, and a major-version upgrade that is explicitly this project's problem rather than something arriving silently in a chart bump — see [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>).

## Trivy Operator, not Kubescape

Trivy Operator stores every finding as a plain CRD and scans with the same Trivy that CI uses, so a dashboard number can be checked with `kubectl`; the cost is Kubescape's runtime relevancy, which marked a finding as loaded.

## ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, not Kyverno or Gatekeeper

The admission rules are CEL that the API server evaluates itself, so nothing has to stay up for an apply to succeed; a policy engine is a webhook, and a `failurePolicy: Fail` webhook refuses every apply while its pods reschedule. The cost is CEL's reach: a rule sees the request and its namespace, and nothing generates resources — see [Admission policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>).

## Tetragon, not Falco

Both record syscalls through eBPF and alert.
