The `PushSecret` in `secrets.yaml` writes `kv/authentik/config` once — see [Generated secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generated-secrets>) — with the secret key, the bootstrap password and the ArgoCD and Grafana client pairs; its `Password` generator's `secretKeys` is the list of keys. A workload's client credentials go in the workload's own path, read by its own `secrets-<workload>.yaml` mounted `optional`: rewriting `kv/authentik/config` would rotate the secret key that signs every session and token, and External Secrets fails an `ExternalSecret` whole when one key is missing, so a shared one would leave a cluster without the workload with no `AUTHENTIK_SECRET_KEY` either.

The first administrator is created through `akadmin`, switched on for the occasion as in [Bootstrap credentials](<#bootstrap-credentials>); the steps are in [Quickstart step 12](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>).

### Adding an application

1. Generate its client credentials into OpenBao with a `PushSecret` beside the workload's own `ExternalSecret`, and read them here with an `ExternalSecret` mounted `optional`, like `secrets-dependency-track.yaml`. A public client (PKCE, as OpenCloud's web and native clients) has no credentials: its client IDs are fixed by the client and sit in the blueprint in clear, so this step and step 3 do not apply.
2. Add the provider and application as a key of `blueprints-workloads.yaml`: an OAuth2 provider with `grant_types`, or a proxy provider added to the outpost's `providers:` list in `blueprints.yaml`.
3. Hand the worker the credentials: in the same file, a `secretRef` to `authentik-secrets-<workload>` with `optional: true` under `global.envFrom`, and bump `homelab.wlkr.ch/secret-generation`.
4. For a proxied application, point its `HTTPRoute` at `authentik-server`, add its namespace to `referencegrant.yaml`, and add a `toEndpoints` rule for its pods to the `authentik-server` policy in `payload/platform/security/network-policies/authentik.yaml`: the outpost dials the backend, and without the rule the login succeeds and the request after it times out.
5. Bind `infra-users` to an infra application in the blueprint, as an `authentik_policies.policybinding` with the application as `target`. An application with no binding is open to every Authentik account.

### Adding a user

1. Create the account under **Directory → Users**.
2. Add it to `infra-users`, or to a role group from [Groups and roles](<#groups-and-roles>), under **Directory → Groups**. Membership is not blueprinted because that would put a username in the repository, and only a superuser passes the bindings without it.

## Health check

When every login fails, in this order:

1. Server and worker are Ready and the database is healthy:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n authentik get pods,clusters
   ```
2. The discovery document names the one hostname as `issuer`:

   ```bash
   curl -s https://auth.k8s.wlkr.ch/application/o/argocd/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .issuer
   ```
3. The embedded outpost is healthy (`Outposts` in the admin UI, or):

   ```bash
   kubectl -n authentik logs deploy/authentik-server | grep -i outpost | tail
   ```
4. The worker applied the blueprints — a failed one names its file:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n authentik logs deploy/authentik-worker | grep -i blueprint | tail
   ```

## Pitfalls

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A new client credential needs the worker restarted**
>
> `envFrom` injects `authentik-secrets` **once, when the pod starts**. A blueprint reading a newly added credential through `!Env` on a running worker gets an empty string and creates a provider that answers 404 on its discovery endpoint. Bumping `secret-generation` restarts the worker in the sync that adds the credential; `kubectl rollout restart` fixes a running cluster but leaves nothing for the next one.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A blueprint is code with admin rights**
>
> The worker applies a blueprint with full access to Authentik's models, so one can create a superuser or add someone to `argocd-admins`. That is why every blueprint lives here and the workloads repository cannot write into `authentik`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **OAuth2 providers must name their grant types**
>
> `grant_types` defaults to an empty list. A provider that omits it serves no grants, and every login fails with `invalid_request: The request is otherwise malformed`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **The outpost entry replaces its provider list**
>
> `authentik_outposts.outpost` sets `providers` wholesale. Every proxied application must be listed there; adding one and forgetting the list silently unassigns the others, which fail open.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Home Assistant and Umami are the exceptions**
>
> Each has a login of its own and upstream ships no OIDC provider to replace it, so the outpost sits *in front of* it: browser users authenticate twice. Home Assistant's companion apps and webhooks hold a long-lived token and cannot complete an interactive login, so `skip_path_regex` lets `/api/`, `/auth/token` and the external-auth callback through; Home Assistant's own accounts are the only thing guarding those paths, and revoking an Authentik account does not revoke a Home Assistant token. Umami's tracker script and collect endpoint are loaded by every visitor of every site that embeds it, so `/script.js` and `/api/send` pass the same way; the rest of the dashboard and API stays behind the login.

## Recovery

### When Authentik is down

Single sign-on is a single point of failure for logging in at all. Every step needs a working `kubectl`, so keep a kubeconfig off-cluster; selfHeal reverts a `kubectl patch`, so each switch is a pull request, which ArgoCD syncs without a login. Revert them once Authentik is back.

1. ArgoCD: merge `admin.enabled: "true"` in `payload/argocd/values.yaml`, restart the server, which generates `argocd-initial-admin-secret`, and read the password as in [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md#setup>).

   ```bash
   kubectl -n argocd rollout restart deploy/argocd-server
   ```
2. Grafana: the admin account works through the API as it is. For the UI, merge `auth.disable_login_form: false` under `grafana.ini` in `payload/platform/monitoring/application.yaml` and log in as `admin` at `/login?disableAutoLogin=true` with the password from OpenBao, see [Resetting the Grafana admin password](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#resetting-the-grafana-admin-password>).

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao kv get -mount=kv -field=password monitoring/grafana-admin
   ```
3. Proxied dashboards have no bypass; port-forward instead.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system port-forward svc/hubble-ui 8080:80
   ```

### ArgoCD's API key account

Disabling the local admin also removes its `apiKey` capability. If a token is needed, add an account scoped to what the token is for rather than re-enabling admin:

The `claude` account is one, for the in-cluster agents; see [Agent account](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#agent-account>). The shape:

```yaml
configs:
  cm:
    accounts.mcp: apiKey
  rbac:
    policy.csv: |
      p, role:mcp, applications, get, */*, allow
      g, mcp, role:mcp
```

# cert-manager

TLS certificate automation via Let's Encrypt, using DNS-01 challenges through AWS Route53. DNS-01 because these hostnames resolve to RFC1918 addresses that Let's Encrypt cannot reach, and because it is the only way to get a wildcard: one per Gateway listener, in `payload/platform/certificates/certificates.yaml`, covers every hostname that listener serves.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `cert-manager`; the wildcards land in `kube-system` beside the Gateways, the agent sessions' in their own namespace; see [SSH listener](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#ssh-listener>) |
| Depends on | [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) for the Route53 credential, so transitively on [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) |
| If it is down | Nothing immediately. Certificates stop renewing, and the failure surfaces weeks later as an [expired certificate](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#pitfalls>) |
| Health check | `kubectl get certificate -A` → all `READY=True` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/cert-manager/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/cert-manager>), [`payload/platform/certificates/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/certificates>) |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Issuers and certificates in their own `certificates` Application | Kept with cert-manager, the controller reads Degraded until OpenBao holds the Route53 credentials — see [Bootstrap convergence](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-convergence>) |
| Three sync waves inside `certificates`: `ExternalSecret`, then the ClusterIssuers, then the Certificates | One wave orders custom resources alphabetically, exactly backwards, and an issuer applied before its Secret stays `Ready=False` with `InvalidSolver` |
| `gatewayAPI.enabled: true` in `values.yaml` | Turns on the shim that issues from `cert-manager.io` annotations on a Gateway. Nothing uses it: every certificate here is an explicit `Certificate` |
| `ServiceMonitor` rendered unconditionally | The chart cannot sync until the Prometheus operator CRDs exist, which is why they are the separate `prometheus-operator-crds` Application — see [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#crds>) |
| More than one webhook replica, a PodDisruptionBudget and a hostname spread | The webhook's `failurePolicy` is `Fail`, so a lone replica rescheduling through a drain refuses every apply — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#replica-placement>) |
| `letsencrypt-staging` and `letsencrypt-prod` | Use staging first: production allows five duplicate certificates per week and a misconfigured solver retries until they are gone |

The IAM policy is the [Route53 policy](<https://cert-manager.io/docs/configuration/acme/dns01/route53/#set-up-an-iam-policy>) cert-manager documents, narrowed to `_acme-challenge` TXT records so a stolen key cannot repoint a hostname. `ListHostedZonesByName` stays because the issuers do not set `hostedZoneID`. It lives in AWS, so a change is applied there by hand:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "route53:GetChange",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:route53:::change/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/<zone-id>"],
      "Condition": {
        "ForAllValues:StringEquals": {
          "route53:ChangeResourceRecordSetsRecordTypes": ["TXT"]
        },
        "ForAllValues:StringLike": {
          "route53:ChangeResourceRecordSetsNormalizedRecordNames": ["_acme-challenge.*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "route53:ListResourceRecordSets",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/<zone-id>"]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "route53:ListHostedZonesByName",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

List one `hostedzone/<zone-id>` ARN per zone a Certificate names.

### Issuer scope

`certificate-issuer-scope` lets only `kube-system`, and `claude-<session>` for `<session>.ssh.wlkr.ch`, use a ClusterIssuer, which signs any name in the zones; see [policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>).

### Pods from the controllers

`controller-pod-limits` refuses pods from the cert-manager controller, which solves DNS-01 only, and host access for CloudNativePG's. Confining those to namespaces holding a `Cluster` is not expressible in a policy.

## Usage

Once OpenBao and ESO are up, `make bao-secrets` prompts for the credentials, or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/cert-manager/route53 \
  access-key-id="YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID" \
  secret-access-key="YOUR_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
```

ESO creates the `route53-credentials` Secret within its `refreshInterval`, or [immediately on request](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md#adding-a-secret>).

## Health check

Work down the chain of custody; the answer is nearly always further back than the `Certificate`:

```bash
kubectl describe certificate -n kube-system <name>
kubectl get certificaterequest,order,challenge -A
kubectl -n cert-manager logs deploy/cert-manager --tail=100
```

A `Challenge` stuck in `pending` is a DNS problem: the credentials cannot write to the zone, or the resolver has not caught up. `dig +short TXT _acme-challenge.<host>` settles which.

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A sealed OpenBao means no renewals**
>
> Until OpenBao is unsealed and the secret stored, nothing issues or renews; how that surfaces is in [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#pitfalls>).

# Cilium

Cilium is the CNI: it replaces `kube-proxy`, terminates ingress through Gateway API, hands out LoadBalancer addresses on a network with no cloud load balancer, encrypts node-to-node traffic, and shows what is talking to what; [why Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#cilium-as-cni-replacing-kube-proxy>).

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` |
| Depends on | The Gateway API and Prometheus operator CRDs it renders against, and a `k8sServiceHost` that answers |
| If it is down | Everything. No CNI, no service routing, no ingress, no LoadBalancer addresses |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium status --brief` |
| UI | `hubble.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` (Hubble); the same flows in 3D across namespaces at [Flowscape](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/flowscape/>) |
| Files | [`payload/platform/cilium/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/cilium>) |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `kubeProxyReplacement: true` | Service routing in eBPF. `proxy.disabled` in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2` keeps `kube-proxy` out at init and on every `kubeadm upgrade apply` |
| `k8sServiceHost` as a literal IP | With `kube-proxy` gone Cilium cannot reach the API server through a Service, so it names the [control-plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>) — see [Pitfalls](<#pitfalls>) |
| Gateway API | Replaces an Ingress controller — see [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md>) |
| `lb-pools.yaml` | One address each for the apps and infra Gateways, announced over L2 ARP so the LAN can find them |
| `bgp.yaml` | The same two addresses as `/32` routes over eBGP from every control-plane node to the router. The router sends traffic from other VLANs, VPN clients and port forwards to all three nodes and drops a dead one after the hold time, where L2 moves one lease. L2 stays because LAN hosts ARP for the addresses and never ask the router. The ASNs and timers are in `bgp.yaml`. The router side is FRR on the UDM Pro: `make config` renders it from the inventory's `router_*` variables into `output/router/frr-bgp.conf`, so a firmware reset is recovered by pasting that file with the [password](<#bgp-session-password>) added |
| `encryption.type: wireguard` | Pod-to-pod only; `nodeEncryption` is deprecated |
| Hubble, behind the [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md>) proxy outpost | Hubble has no authentication of its own; the HTTPRoute points at the outpost through a ReferenceGrant in `payload/platform/authentik/` |
| Hubble metrics labelled by namespace | The chart's Hubble dashboards show nothing without them; namespace keeps the series count to the square of the namespace count. The HTTP metric adds workloads, but only for the Gateway's proxied traffic. |
| `hubble.export.static` | Every flow with a `DROPPED`, `ERROR` or `AUDIT` verdict, and every HTTP request a policy proxies at L7, goes to a file on the node that [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) tails into Loki, with a field mask that keeps identities, ports and the request line. Hubble's own buffer is minutes deep; this is the record the L7 rules are tightened from. Other forwarded flows are too many to export. |
| `hubble.redact` | Every header except `User-Agent` and `Content-Type`, and the password of a basic-auth URL, is replaced before a flow leaves the agent, for the export file and Relay alike. L7 rules proxy requests that carry credentials: `X-Vault-Token`, bearer tokens, signed S3 requests, cookies. The method, path and query survive |
| `hostFirewall.enabled: true` | Filters traffic to the node's own addresses, which is every host-networked port, through `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` objects that select nodes. Nothing is denied on IPv4 until a policy selects the node; IPv6 differs, see [Pitfalls](<#pitfalls>). Rollout and policy in [Host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) |
| `policyAuditMode: false` | Policies are enforced. On, verdicts are logged and not enforced for a rollout's observation week — see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#rollout>). Cluster-wide, and blind to L7 rules |
| `rollOutCiliumPods` and the four `rollOutPods` | The agent, Envoy, the operator, Relay and the UI read their ConfigMap once, at startup. With a checksum of it on the pod template, a merged value rolls the pods and is live within minutes, and a value the agent refuses fails at merge time, not at the next unrelated restart. The price is that every change to `cilium-config` rolls the CNI on every node: running pods keep their networking, policy updates pause per node while its agent is down, and the [`k8sServiceHost` pitfall](<#pitfalls>) bites at merge, not later |
| `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 1` | The chart default restarts the agent on two nodes at once, which can be two of the three control planes that hold the L2 leases and BGP sessions; one at a time keeps every Gateway address announced |
| `operator.replicas` above one | The operator owns Gateway API reconciliation, LoadBalancer IP allocation and the `cilium-secrets` sync: with one replica, a drain or crash of its node stalls all three until the reschedule. The chart's hostname anti-affinity keeps the replicas apart, so the standby is already running — see the [operator pitfall](<#pitfalls>) |
| The operator's cluster-wide Secret read | The chart grants `get`, `list` and `watch` on all Secrets whenever Gateway API or `bgpControlPlane` is on, with no value to narrow it: the operator copies the certificate Secrets a Gateway names, in any namespace, into `cilium-secrets`. The [log alert](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>) allowlists it |
| `lb-pools.yaml` on `cilium.io/v2` | The storage version for `CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool`; `v2alpha1` is served as deprecated and warns on every sync. `CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy` has no `v2` yet and stays |
| `cilium-agent` memory limit | It is the one process whose death takes pod networking with it; sized by the [platform rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md>) |
| `trustCRDsExist: true` | The chart otherwise refuses to render while `monitoring.coreos.com/v1` is missing: at bootstrap, before `prometheus-operator-crds` has synced, and in the diff preview |

## Usage

### Installation

Cilium is installed twice, in a sense. `make install-cilium` installs it by Helm, because no pod runs without a CNI and ArgoCD is a pod; ArgoCD then adopts the release. The version comes from `targetRevision` in `application.yaml` — see [Version pins](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>).

The bootstrap install uses the same `values.yaml`, and has to: the pods roll whenever `cilium-config` changes, so a slimmer bootstrap config would restart every agent the moment ArgoCD adopts the release. The Gateway API CRDs go in first, see the [operator pitfall](<#pitfalls>). The one difference is the three `serviceMonitor.enabled` flags, which `make` turns off because the Prometheus operator CRDs arrive through ArgoCD; ArgoCD adds the monitors back on adoption, rolling the agent and operator once.

### BGP session password

The session is TCP MD5 authenticated with a typed password, since the router needs the same one. Setting or rotating it breaks BGP, and both Gateways with it, until both ends match; L2 still announces them to the flat LAN.

1. `make bao-secrets`, answering for `kv/cilium/bgp`.
2. On the router, in the live FRR and `output/router/frr-bgp.conf`, then `clear bgp *`:

   ```text
   neighbor cilium password <password>
   ```
3. Check the session as in the [Health check](<#health-check>).

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium status --brief
```

It prints `OK`. The BGP session on each control-plane node, `established` with two routes advertised; only control planes peer, so ask that node's agent:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec "$(kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l k8s-app=cilium \
  --field-selector spec.nodeName=<control-plane> -o name)" -- cilium shell -- bgp/peers
```

Hubble answers *what did I just break?* during a network policy rollout — see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#usage>). The `hubble` CLI talks to Relay through a port-forward on its default port:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward deploy/hubble-relay 4245:4245 &
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --follow
```

The same verdicts, for the whole Loki retention window, in Grafana:

```text
{job="hubble", verdict="DROPPED"} | json | flow_drop_reason_desc="POLICY_DENIED"
```

## Pitfalls

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **`k8sServiceHost` pointed at an address that does not answer takes the cluster down**
>
> Every Cilium pod loses the API server at once, and cluster networking goes with it. The change ordering is in [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **An operator that starts without the API server leaves the Gateways without certificates**
>
> cilium-operator checks for the Gateway API CRDs once at startup; if that check fails it runs without its Gateway controller until the next restart, and `cilium-secrets` empties. Envoy then resets the TLS handshake on every node without a cached copy, so clients fail depending on the node the router hashes them to. `CiliumGatewayCertificatesMissing` fires; `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy/cilium-operator` recovers it.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A chart default that disappears stays in `cilium-config`**
>
> The bootstrap install's `helm` field manager still co-owns every `cilium-config` key it wrote, so ArgoCD's server-side apply cannot delete one the chart stops rendering: the old value stays live while the rest of the chart assumes the new one. `envoy.xdsMode` is pinned for that reason. Pin such a value in `values.yaml` rather than relying on the default.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **The host firewall drops all node IPv6, with or without a policy**
>
> With `enable-ipv6: false` the datapath has no IPv6 branch, so on the native device and `cilium_host` every IPv6 packet is dropped as `DROP_UNKNOWN_L3` in both directions, before any policy or audit mode ([upstream](<https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/47307>)). A client that does not fall back to IPv4 stalls until the node's SLAAC address expires. The drops reach Loki as `DROPPED` flows with a reason other than `POLICY_DENIED`, so `HubblePolicyDrops` and `HostFirewallDrops` stay quiet.

# CloudNativePG

CloudNativePG is one operator in `cnpg-system` and a `Cluster` resource per database, [instead of each chart's bundled PostgreSQL](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#cloudnativepg-for-every-database-not-the-charts-bundled-one>).

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `cnpg-system` for the operator; each database in its workload's namespace |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for the database volumes and the backup writers; [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for the backup plugin's gRPC certificates |
| If it is down | Running databases keep running; failover, upgrades and new clusters stop |
| Health check | `kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A` → `Cluster in healthy state` |
| Backups | Continuous WAL and a nightly base backup per database, to its own prefix of `offsite` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/cloudnative-pg/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/cloudnative-pg>) |

## Configuration

A `Cluster` is not a StatefulSet with a nicer name:

| It handles | Instead of |
| --- | --- |
| Primary election and failover between instances | A single pod that takes the database down with it |
| `-rw` and `-ro` Services that follow the primary | Hardcoding a pod name and being wrong after a restart |
| Rolling minor-version upgrades, replicas first | A `StatefulSet` image bump and hope |
| A metrics exporter per instance and an upstream Grafana dashboard | No visibility until something is already wrong |

Major-version upgrades are declarative too, but offline: ArgoCD reports Degraded while one runs and the workload is down for its duration. Read [the upstream guide](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/postgres_upgrades/>) before merging one.

Databases claim `rook-ceph-block`, so Ceph's replicas already sit under every database and a single-instance `Cluster` is a defensible default: the data survives a node loss even when the process does not. Where a workload cannot tolerate the restart, more `instances` are the change, as [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#database>) and the workloads repository's `advent-wollbi` and `shot-bridge` show.

The operator and the backup plugin each run several replicas, spread per [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#replica-placement>), so a Kured drain stalls neither: the operator serves the `Cluster` and `ScheduledBackup` webhooks with `failurePolicy: Fail` and calls the plugin on every `Cluster` reconcile. Leader election keeps one of each reconciling; neither chart ships a PodDisruptionBudget.

### Backups

The [Barman Cloud plugin](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/plugin-barman-cloud/>) runs beside the operator and injects a sidecar into every instance that names an `ObjectStore`. The sidecar archives each WAL segment as PostgreSQL closes it and takes the base backups a `ScheduledBackup` asks for, so a database restores to any second inside the retention window, not just to last night.

| Choice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The plugin, not `spec.backup.barmanObjectStore` | The in-tree field is deprecated upstream and is removed in a later release |
| One [backup writer](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>) per database, in its own namespace | Its keys exist only there and reach only its prefix of `offsite`, so a compromised workload can read or delete its own backups and nobody else's |
| `https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, not the plain RGW Service | Backups hold every row of the database; the Gateway's TLS is the same path Velero uses |
| Base backup nightly, after Velero | The two never contend for the object store; WAL archiving covers the hours between |
| `retentionPolicy` equal to `schedules.ttl` in `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml` | One window to reason about: what Velero can no longer restore, the WAL archive cannot either. Change the two together: each `backup.yaml` restates the value |
| No opting out by omission | The `cnpg-cluster-backed-up` and `cnpg-objectstore-offsite` [admission policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) refuse a `Cluster` without the WAL archiver and a store outside `offsite`; a database rebuilt from elsewhere, like a preview, carries `homelab.wlkr.ch/backup-exempt` with the reason |

`ObjectStore` is a namespaced resource with no cluster-scoped counterpart, so the per-database part is a short, identical stanza (below); everything else is shared: the plugin, and the `cnpg-backups` policy in `payload/platform/security/network-policies/cluster-wide.yaml` that lets any CloudNativePG pod reach the object store.

## Usage

### The contract

**Every workload that needs PostgreSQL gets a CloudNativePG `Cluster`. No chart-bundled database, ever.** A bundled Postgres moves when the application's chart decides — a major version jump inside someone else's patch release; a `Cluster` moves when its `imageName` changes, a Renovate PR with a human in front of it. Most bundled subcharts are also Bitnami's, whose registry terms keep changing. The rule for the [workloads repository](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/add-workload/index.md>):

1. Disable the subchart (`postgresql.enabled: false` or `internalDatabase.enabled: false`) and point the chart at the `Cluster`.
2. Never copy the password. CloudNativePG writes `username`, `password`, `host`, `port`, `dbname` and a ready-made `uri` to `<cluster-name>-app`; charts take those through an `existingSecret` block, and applications without one read `uri` as an environment variable. Nothing goes into Git or OpenBao — nothing outside the cluster ever needs this secret.
3. Put the `Cluster` in the workload's namespace, not `cnpg-system`, so the namespace's `CiliumNetworkPolicy` governs port 5432 and deleting the namespace takes the database with it.
4. Set `enablePDB: false` on a single-instance `Cluster` only. Its `<cluster>-primary` PodDisruptionBudget refuses the eviction, so a node drain hangs on it until [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) gives up and never reboots the node; without the budget the instance is down for the move to another node. A `Cluster` with replicas keeps the budgets: the operator sees the drain, switches the primary over to a replica in seconds, and the drain continues. Without them the drain deletes the primary, and the failover waits for its smart shutdown, up to `smartShutdownTimeout` while clients hold connections.
5. Set `smartShutdownTimeout: 15`, and on a `Cluster` with replicas `primaryUpdateMethod: switchover`. A smart shutdown refuses new connections and waits for the open ones to close, and every application here holds a pool, so the default's 180 seconds only lengthen every restart, move and failover; after 15 seconds the instance manager shuts down fast, rolling back open transactions, and the clients reconnect. The default update method restarts the primary in place on a spec change, leaving no writer for the whole shutdown; a switchover promotes a replica first.
6. Back it up with the [stanza below](<#backing-up-a-database>). Velero's nightly PVC snapshot is crash-consistent and restores only to the night it was taken; the WAL archive restores to any second.
7. Scrape it with its own `PodMonitor`, like Authentik's `podmonitor.yaml`; upstream deprecated `enablePodMonitor`.

### Backing up a database

Next to the `Cluster`, in the same namespace, with `<db>` the cluster's name. The S3 user writes `offsite/<namespace>.db/` and nothing else; a second database in the namespace gets a user with its own suffix. The sync wave puts the user and the store ahead of the `Cluster` that names them.

```yaml
---
apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephObjectStoreUser
metadata:
  name: <namespace>.db
  namespace: <namespace>
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
spec:
  store: object-store
  clusterNamespace: rook-ceph
  displayName: <namespace> database backups
---
apiVersion: barmancloud.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ObjectStore
metadata:
  name: <db>
  namespace: <namespace>
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
spec:
  retentionPolicy: 14d   # Velero's schedules.ttl
  configuration:
    destinationPath: s3://offsite/<namespace>.db/
    endpointURL: https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch
    s3Credentials:
      accessKeyId: {name: rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-<namespace>.db, key: AccessKey}
      secretAccessKey: {name: rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-<namespace>.db, key: SecretKey}
    wal:
      compression: gzip
    data:
      compression: gzip
---
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: ScheduledBackup
metadata:
  name: <db>
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  schedule: "0 0 3 * * *"   # after Velero's daily schedule
  immediate: true
  backupOwnerReference: self
  cluster:
    name: <db>
  method: plugin
  pluginConfiguration:
    name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
```

And in the `Cluster`:

```yaml
  plugins:
    - name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
      enabled: true
      isWALArchiver: true
      parameters:
        barmanObjectName: <db>
```

`enabled: true` is the webhook's default; written out, ArgoCD's diff matches the live object, since `plugins` is compared as a whole list. Adding the plugin restarts every instance to inject the sidecar: a single-instance database is down for that restart, a replicated one switches over. `immediate: true` takes the first base backup at once, so the WAL archive is restorable from the first day.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A
kubectl cnpg status -n <namespace> <cluster-name>
```

`Cluster in healthy state` is the phrase; ArgoCD's built-in health check reads the same field, which lets a sync wave wait for a database before the application in front of it. The plugin prints the primary, replication lag, WAL position and last failover.

```bash
kubectl get backups.postgresql.cnpg.io -A           # Phase completed, one per night
kubectl get clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io -A \
  -o custom-columns='NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ARCHIVING:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="ContinuousArchiving")].status'
kubectl get objectstores.barmancloud.cnpg.io -A -o yaml | grep -A3 serverRecoveryWindow
```

`ContinuousArchiving` `True` means the last WAL segment reached the object store; `False` means WAL is [piling up](<#pitfalls>). The recovery window lives on the `ObjectStore`, per server name: the `Cluster`'s own backup fields and the `cnpg_collector_*_backup_timestamp` metrics stay empty with a plugin, which upstream documents as deprecated under CNPG-I. `prometheusrule.yaml` therefore reads the `ObjectStore` and `Backup` objects through kube-state-metrics' [custom resource metrics](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#scrape-targets>): `CNPGBackupStale` when a server's last successful base backup is older than the rule's threshold, `CNPGBackupFailed` when a recent Backup ended in `failed`. WAL archiving is read from the instances' own exporter, whose `pg_stat_archiver` and `archive_status` figures stay accurate under the plugin: `CNPGWALArchivingFailing` when the last attempt failed and none succeeded since, `CNPGWALArchiveBacklog` when segments queue without a failure, a stuck archiver. All four are warnings on the daily mail.

## Pitfalls

- **A stuck archive fills the volume.** PostgreSQL keeps every WAL segment the sidecar has not archived; a broken bucket or policy shows as `ContinuousArchiving` `False` long before the PVC is full. Fix the cause, never delete `pg_wal`.
- **A new database is refused until the next policy run.** Its `<namespace>.db` user gets write access to `offsite` only when the `offsite-policy` CronJob next runs ([Backup writers](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>)); until then archiving fails with `AccessDenied` and PostgreSQL retries, losing nothing.
- **An idle database archives nothing.** A segment is shipped only once it holds WAL, so an empty prefix is not proof the archiver works. Force one, without touching a table: `kubectl -n <namespace> exec <primary-pod> -c postgres -- psql -c "select pg_logical_emit_message(false,'probe','x')" -c "select pg_switch_wal()"`.
- **A dead replica fills the primary.** Its replication slot holds WAL until the replica catches up, so every multi-instance `Cluster` caps it with `max_slot_wal_keep_size` at a quarter of the volume; past that the slot is invalidated and the replica restores from the WAL archive or must be recreated with `kubectl cnpg destroy <cluster> <instance>`.
- **A full volume is not resized by the operator.** An instance stopped with `no free disk space for WALs` keeps its PVC size although `storage.size` grew; patch that PVC to the new size by hand, as [upstream documents](<https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/instance_manager/>) under "Disk full failure".
- **The operator cannot create host-access pods.** The `controller-pod-limits` [admission policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) refuses any pod it creates with host networking, PID, IPC, a `hostPath` or privilege.
- **A restore is a new `Cluster`.** Recovery bootstraps a fresh cluster from the archive; it never rewinds a running one. Give the new cluster its own `ObjectStore` destination, or its archive would mix with the one it was restored from.

## Recovery

### Point-in-time restore

1. Pick the target time (UTC) and check it lies inside the window:

```bash
kubectl -n <namespace> get objectstore <db> -o jsonpath='{.status.serverRecoveryWindow}{"\n"}'
```

1. In the workloads repository, add a second `Cluster` named `<db>-restore` beside the original, which stays untouched: every Application prunes, so a renamed `Cluster` is a deleted one. It bootstraps from the old store, keeping the old name as `serverName`:

```yaml
  bootstrap:
    recovery:
      source: origin
      recoveryTarget:
        targetTime: "2026-10-21 12:00:00+00"
  externalClusters:
    - name: origin
      plugin:
        name: barman-cloud.cloudnative-pg.io
        parameters:
          barmanObjectName: <db>
          serverName: <db>
```

Its own `plugins` entry keeps the same `barmanObjectName` with `serverName: <db>-restore`, so the new archive lands beside the old one.

1. Merge and wait for `Cluster in healthy state`; both databases run, and the application reads the original.
2. In a second PR, point the application at `<db>-restore-app`, rename the `ScheduledBackup` and its `cluster.name` to `<db>-restore`, and delete the original `Cluster`; the sync prunes it.

# Descheduler

The scheduler places a pod once and never looks at it again. After [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) drains a node, everything that lived there restarts on the others and stays there when the node comes back, so a cluster that has rebooted through an update ends up with one idle node and the rest loaded. The [descheduler](<https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler>) runs on a schedule, evicts a few pods from the loaded nodes, and lets the scheduler place them where there is room.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `descheduler` |
| Depends on | [metrics-server](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/metrics-server/index.md>) for the node usage `LowNodeUtilization` compares |
| If it is down | Nothing visible: pods stay where the last drain left them |
| Health check | `kubectl -n descheduler get jobs` → the last run `Complete` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/descheduler/application.yaml`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/blob/main/payload/platform/descheduler/application.yaml>) |

## Configuration

The reasoning behind the values in `application.yaml`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `kind: CronJob` with a `schedule` | A Deployment would poll continuously for a cluster that changes shape once per Flatcar update. A pass every few hours drifts a rebooted cluster back into balance the same day |
| `nodeFit: true` | A pod is only evicted when another node has room for it, so an eviction never turns into a Pending pod |
| `podProtections.extraEnabled: PodsWithPVC` | Ceph volumes would follow an evicted pod, but the pods that own them run alone: a moved [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>) primary is a failover and a cold restart of its application, a moved Loki a detach and reattach. Their PDBs are off so that Kured can drain, so this is the only guard. `emptyDir` pods stay protected at the default because their data goes with them |
| System-critical pods at the default | `evictSystemCriticalPods` stays off, so nothing with `priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical` is ever moved. Those components hold their own placement rule instead — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#replica-placement>) |
| `maxNoOfPodsToEvictPerNode` and `evictionLimits.node` | A few pods per node per pass: one Kured reboot already moved everything on a node once, a second mass move is what this component is meant to avoid |
| `LowNodeUtilization` with `metricsUtilization.source: KubernetesMetrics` | Usage comes from metrics-server, not from requests. Requests here are still being tuned and many are far below what the pod uses, so a requests-based view would call a loaded node idle |
| `thresholds` and `targetThresholds` | A node under the low mark is a candidate to receive, one over the high mark a candidate to lose pods; nodes in between are left alone |
| `RemoveDuplicates` and `RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint` for both `DoNotSchedule` and `ScheduleAnyway` | After a drain, replicas of one workload sit on the same node; both plugins put them back on separate ones. Soft constraints count too, because the scheduler honoured them only until the drain |
| `RemovePodsHavingTooManyRestarts` | A pod in a restart loop for hours is more likely stuck on its node than broken; a move is cheap and the restart count resets |
| Metrics off | A CronJob pod exists for seconds; a `ServiceMonitor` would scrape an empty Service |

## Usage

Nothing to operate. To run a pass now:

```bash
kubectl -n descheduler create job --from=cronjob/descheduler manual-$(date +%s)
```

Every eviction is an event on the pod, so `kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=Descheduled` shows what moved and why.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n descheduler get cronjob,jobs
kubectl -n descheduler logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=descheduler --tail=100 | grep -i "evict\|error"
kubectl top nodes    # what LowNodeUtilization sees
```

## Pitfalls

- **It only evicts, never schedules.** Where a pod lands is the scheduler's decision; the descheduler assumes the scheduler will do better the second time, which holds after a drain and not much else.
- **It honours PodDisruptionBudgets.** An eviction that would violate a PDB is refused. The single-instance [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>) clusters carry none, so that Kured can drain; `PodsWithPVC` is what keeps the descheduler off them.
- **A capped number of evictions per node per pass**, the limits in [Configuration](<#configuration>). A badly skewed cluster takes several passes, which is the point of running it on a schedule rather than once.
- **A move is a restart.** Anything without a second replica is briefly down when it is evicted; `nodeFit` guarantees a place to go, not zero downtime.

# external-dns

[external-dns](<https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/external-dns/>) creates the Route53 records for this cluster's hostnames from the `HTTPRoute`, `TLSRoute` and `GRPCRoute` objects that already declare them. Without it every hostname is a record made by hand in the AWS console, a step that lives nowhere in the repository and leaves a record pointing at nothing when the workload goes.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `external-dns` |
| Depends on | [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) for its Route53 credential, [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md>) for the HTTPRoutes it reads |
| If it is down | New hostnames get no DNS record. Existing records are left alone |
| Health check | `kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns --tail=50` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/external-dns/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/external-dns>) |

## Configuration

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Sources `gateway-httproute` and `gateway-grpcroute` | Every HTTP and gRPC hostname here is a route; the address comes from the route's parent `Gateway`, so nothing is written down twice. The `GRPCRoute` is Argo CD's, see [CLI access](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#cli-access>) |
| `target` annotation on `apps-gateway` | The cluster sits behind NAT, so the Gateway's own address is a LAN one nobody outside can reach. external-dns reads the public address off the Gateway, not the routes, so every `*.k8s.wlkr.ch` record gets it once. `infra-gateway` has none: those names stay LAN-only on purpose |
| Source `gateway-tlsroute` | The agents' SSH hostnames are `TLSRoute`s, one per session. This version reads `TLSRoute` `v1`, the version installed, so each session's record appears with its route and no wildcard record exists to maintain; see [SSH listener](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#ssh-listener>) |
| `domainFilters`, one entry per subtree a Gateway serves | Nothing outside them is touched. A zone or subtree missing from the list has its routes ignored rather than refused, which reads as external-dns being down, so a new domain adds it here |
| TXT registry with an owner id | A companion `_externaldns.*` TXT record stamps every record it creates, and it only modifies or deletes records carrying that stamp. Hand-made records in the same zone are invisible to it |
| Policy `sync` | Deleting an HTTPRoute removes its record. Safe only because of the registry; without it `sync` would happily delete your MX records |
| `--aws-zone-match-parent` | The records live in the `wlkr.ch` zone, not a zone of their own |
| Credentials as a file (`AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`), not environment variables | The environment puts a key that can repoint every hostname into `kubectl describe pod`, crash dumps and every child process. The `ExternalSecret` templates an INI `credentials` key, the only key mounted; the original keys stay in the Secret so nothing still reading them breaks |

The credential is a separate IAM user and OpenBao path from cert-manager's — see [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kv-layout>) for why. Its policy needs `route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets` on the hosted zone, plus `route53:ListHostedZones` and `route53:ListResourceRecordSets`.

## Usage

Nothing beyond the `HTTPRoute` you were already writing — see [Gateway API](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#usage>). The credential is stored once, by `make bao-secrets` or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/external-dns/route53 \
  access-key-id="AKIA..." \
  secret-access-key="..."
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n external-dns logs deploy/external-dns --tail=50
dig +short argo.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch
kubectl -n external-dns port-forward deploy/external-dns 7979:7979
curl -s localhost:7979/metrics | grep endpoints_total
```

`external_dns_source_endpoints_total` counts the hostnames it sees and `external_dns_registry_endpoints_total` the records it owns; with the TXT registry, zero owned records while sources are non-zero means it writes nothing.

`All records are already up to date, there are no changes for the matching hosted zones` means it found no zone to change: sources fine, provider not, which on Route53 is usually zone matching.

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A record that will not update is one external-dns does not own**
>
> Check for the matching `_externaldns.` TXT record in Route53. To adopt a hand-made record, create that TXT entry or delete the record and let external-dns recreate it.

# External Secrets Operator

[External Secrets Operator (ESO)](<https://external-secrets.io/>) bridges [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) to native Kubernetes `Secret` objects. Workloads consume secrets the standard way — `envFrom`, `volumeMounts`, `imagePullSecrets` — with no sidecar and no code that knows what a Vault token is.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `external-secrets` |
| Depends on | [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) at runtime, though not to be installed |
| If it is down | Secrets already materialised keep working. Nothing rotates, and nothing new resolves |
| Health check | `kubectl get clustersecretstore` → `Valid` on both |
| Files | [`payload/platform/external-secrets/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/external-secrets>); the stores in [`payload/platform/openbao/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/openbao>) `cluster-secret-store.yaml` |

## Configuration

```
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Workload
    participant ES as ExternalSecret
    participant ESO as ESO Controller
    participant Bao as OpenBao
    participant K as K8s Secret

    ESO->>Bao: login (k8s SA JWT)
    Bao-->>ESO: vault token
    ESO->>Bao: read kv/path
    Bao-->>ESO: secret data
    ESO->>K: create/update Secret
    App->>K: mount / envFrom
```

ESO mints a short-lived token for an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount through the TokenRequest API, granted only by `cluster-secret-store.yaml`'s ClusterRole for that one name. OpenBao validates it through TokenReview and issues its own, bound to that store's policy. Platform namespaces use the `openbao` store and the ServiceAccount in `external-secrets`; a workload uses `openbao-apps` and its own, which confines it to `kv/<namespace>/` — see [Kubernetes auth](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kubernetes-auth>). No long-lived credential exists.

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Chart's token grant off | It covers every ServiceAccount; a new `serviceAccountRef` needs its own grant |
| `SecretStore`, `ClusterExternalSecret`, `ClusterPushSecret` not reconciled | Unused; no workload brings its own store, and the controller cannot write namespaces |
| No `ClusterSecretStore` here | A store only validates against a running, unsealed OpenBao, so it ships with `openbao`, whose readiness it reports — see [Bootstrap convergence](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-convergence>) |
| Webhook ServiceAccount token stays mounted | The webhook has no RoleBinding but builds an in-cluster client and exits without the token (`unable to load in-cluster config`) |
| More than one webhook replica, a PodDisruptionBudget and a hostname spread | The webhook's `failurePolicy` is `Fail`, so while a lone replica reschedules through a drain every `ExternalSecret`, `PushSecret` and store apply fails — see [Replica placement](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#replica-placement>) |

## Usage

### Adding a secret

1. Store the value in OpenBao, following the [KV layout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kv-layout>). A random value is not typed in at all: a `Password` generator and a `PushSecret` write it, see [Generated secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generated-secrets>).

   ```bash
   bao kv put kv/<workload>/<purpose> key1="value1" key2="value2"
   ```
2. Declare an `ExternalSecret` alongside the workload's other manifests; the parent Application picks it up. A workload names `openbao-apps` and ships the ServiceAccount that store logs in as, and its namespace goes on the `openbao-apps` list in `cluster-secret-store.yaml` here, then `make bao-policies`; a platform component names `openbao`, lists its namespace there and needs no ServiceAccount:

   ```yaml
   ---
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: ServiceAccount
   metadata:
     name: external-secrets-vault
     namespace: my-app
     annotations:
       argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-2"
   automountServiceAccountToken: false
   ---
   apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
   kind: ExternalSecret
   metadata:
     name: my-app-credentials
     namespace: my-app
     annotations:
       # ESO's CRDs arrive with the external-secrets Application; this
       # covers a sync before they have landed.
       argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
   spec:
     refreshInterval: 1h
     secretStoreRef:
       name: openbao-apps
       kind: ClusterSecretStore
     target:
       name: my-app-credentials   # name of the resulting K8s Secret
       creationPolicy: Owner
     data:
       - secretKey: key1           # key in the K8s Secret
         remoteRef:
           key: my-app/<purpose>   # the namespace is the prefix
           property: key1          # key inside the KV entry
   ```

   To pull every key without listing them, use `dataFrom` instead of `data`:

   ```yaml
   spec:
     dataFrom:
       - extract:
           key: <workload>/<purpose>
   ```
3. Consume the Secret:

   ```yaml
   spec:
     containers:
       - name: my-app
         envFrom:
           - secretRef:
               name: my-app-credentials
   ```

`refreshInterval` polls OpenBao; `0` re-syncs only on resource changes. To sync now:

```bash
kubectl annotate externalsecret -n <namespace> <name> \
  force-sync=$(date +%s) --overwrite
```

## Health check

Start with the store; if it is not Ready, nothing downstream is. `openbao-apps` reports `Valid` without logging in, so its auth failures show on the `ExternalSecret`:

```bash
kubectl get clustersecretstore openbao -o jsonpath='{.status}' | jq
```

| Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| OpenBao is sealed | [Unseal it](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#unsealing-after-a-restart>) |
| Kubernetes auth role missing | `make bao-policies` writes all three roles; it needs a [root token](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generating-a-root-token>) |
| Wrong `serviceAccountRef` | `external-secrets-vault`, in `external-secrets` for `openbao` and without a namespace for `openbao-apps` |

Then the individual object:

```bash
kubectl describe externalsecret -n <namespace> <name>
```

| Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| The KV path does not exist (`bao kv get kv/<path>` returns 404) | Store the secret first |
| `property:` matches no key in the KV entry | `bao kv get kv/<path>` lists them |
| `permission denied` from `openbao-apps` | The path is outside `kv/<namespace>/`, or the namespace has no `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount |
| `using cluster store ... is not allowed from namespace` | The store's `conditions` do not list the namespace: a workload on `openbao`, a platform namespace on `openbao-apps`, or a new workload not yet added |

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Rotation does not restart anything**
>
> A rotated value reaches the `Secret` within `refreshInterval`, but a pod that read it into an environment variable keeps the old one until something restarts it. A rollout, or Reloader-style tooling, is the other half of rotation.

# Gateway API

The [Kubernetes Gateway API](<https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/>), implemented by Cilium for load balancing and TLS termination, is [used instead of Ingress](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#gateway-api-not-ingress>) for its split in ownership: the cluster owns the `Gateway` — addresses, certificates, ports — and each app its `HTTPRoute`.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system`, where Cilium runs |
| Depends on | [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) to implement it, [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for the wildcard certificates |
| If it is down | Nothing reaches any hostname. Running pods keep running |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kube-system get gateway` → both `PROGRAMMED=True` with an address |
| Files | [`payload/platform/gateway-api/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/gateway-api>), [`payload/platform/gateway-api-crds/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/gateway-api-crds>) |

## Configuration

Two Gateways in `kube-system`, defined in `gateways.yaml`, each with an address from its own Cilium pool, announced over L2 and BGP ([Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>)). `apps-gateway` serves user-facing workloads under the router's public address; `infra-gateway` serves the platform UIs, LAN only. A route names a listener by `sectionName`:

| Gateway | Listener | Hostnames | Certificate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `apps-gateway` | `https` | `*.k8s.wlkr.ch` | `apps-gateway-tls` |
| `apps-gateway` | `https-wollbi` | `*.wollbi.ch`, the neighbourhood sites | `wollbi-gateway-tls` |
| `apps-gateway` | `ssh` | `*.ssh.wlkr.ch`, passthrough; see [SSH listener](<#ssh-listener>) | None here |
| `infra-gateway` | `https` | `*.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` | `infra-gateway-tls` |

A listener pins one hostname pattern and a wildcard certificate covers one zone, so a new domain is three files, never a name added to an existing listener:

1. A `Certificate` in `payload/platform/certificates/certificates.yaml`.
2. An HTTPS listener in `gateways.yaml` referencing it.
3. The zone in external-dns's `domainFilters`; see [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md#configuration>).

The HTTPS listeners terminate TLS with cert-manager's wildcard certificates, so a new hostname needs no certificate of its own and nothing to renew. Each HTTPS listener pins its hostname pattern, so a route can only claim a name inside its Gateway's tree. Port 80 and `infra-gateway` admit named namespaces only; port 80 exists for the rule in `http-redirect.yaml`. `apps-gateway` carries the annotation that makes [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md#configuration>) publish the router's public address instead of the Gateway's LAN one; the router forwards ports 80 and 443 to that LAN address.

`payload/platform/cilium/rbac-gateway-fix.yaml` grants the operator read access to Ingresses and IngressClasses: its Gateway API controller lists them too, and the chart grants that only with the Ingress controller enabled. Retry removing it on a chart major.

### Backend protocol

Envoy speaks HTTP/1.1 to every backend unless the Service port says otherwise: Cilium's `gatewayAPI.enableAppProtocol` makes it honour `appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c` and open HTTP/2 cleartext instead. A `GRPCRoute` needs that, because the Gateway translates gRPC-web into native gRPC, which only an HTTP/2 backend answers; Argo CD's `http2` port is the one user, see [Argo CD → CLI access](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#cli-access>).

The CRDs arrive twice from one tag: `make install-cilium` applies the release bundle `standard-install.yaml` before ArgoCD exists, and the `gateway-api-crds` Application applies `config/crd/standard`, the directory that bundle is generated from. The Makefile reads the tag out of the Application, so the two cannot drift apart.

### SSH listener

The in-cluster Claude Code agents are reached over SSH tunnelled in TLS on port 443, the only port the router forwards to `apps-gateway`. Each agent's chart ships a `TLSRoute` for `<session>.ssh.wlkr.ch` pointing at its SSH Service.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `mode: Passthrough` | Cilium rejects a `TLS` listener in `Terminate` mode: the listener goes `Accepted=False` with "Using TLSRoute with TLS.mode Terminate is unsupported", and no route attaches. The Gateway forwards the stream by SNI and the agent pod ends the TLS with its own certificate |
| No `Certificate` here | A Secret cannot be referenced across namespaces, and a passthrough listener has no use for one. The chart requests one per session from `letsencrypt-prod` in the agent's namespace |
| `allowedRoutes.kinds: TLSRoute` | The listener serves nothing else, and `HTTPRoute`s cannot attach to it by accident |
| `TLSRoute` `v1` | Installed in the standard channel of the Gateway API CRDs; `v1alpha2` is no longer served. After the CRDs change, restart `cilium-operator` ([why](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#pitfalls>)) |

DNS needs no record by hand: [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md#configuration>) reads the `TLSRoute` hostnames and publishes the router's public address, as for an `HTTPRoute`. A client connects with a TLS tunnel as its `ProxyCommand`, for example `openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h`.

Envoy checks its egress against the backend like any Gateway traffic, so the agents' namespace must admit the `ingress` entity on the SSH port; see [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#network-policies>).

## Usage

Where the chart renders an `HTTPRoute` (Argo CD, OpenBao, Grafana), enable it in the values; a route only becomes a file of its own when it targets something the chart does not own, such as the Authentik outpost. Otherwise create an `HTTPRoute` in the app's namespace referencing the right Gateway; [external-dns](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-dns/index.md>) creates the record and the wildcard covers the name:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: apps-gateway
      namespace: kube-system
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - "my-app.k8s.wlkr.ch"
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: my-app-svc
          port: 80
```

A platform route uses `infra-gateway` and always carries the security headers as a `ResponseHeaderModifier` filter; copy it from `payload/platform/cilium/httproute.yaml`.

### Route hostnames

`apps-gateway` admits every namespace; the `route-hostnames-reserved` [policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) reserves names:

| Name | Only from |
| --- | --- |
| `*.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, wildcards | The namespaces `infra-gateway` admits; a new platform UI extends both lists |
| `<session>.ssh.wlkr.ch` | `claude-<session>` |
| `auth.k8s.wlkr.ch`, `advent.wollbi.ch`, `fest.wollbi.ch` | `authentik`, `advent-wollbi`, `fest-wollbi`; a new owned name extends the policy's `owners` map |
| No hostname | `kube-system` |

## Health check

Check that each Gateway's HTTP listener carries only the redirect — `http` should show exactly `1` on both:

```bash
for gw in apps-gateway infra-gateway; do
  kubectl get gateway "$gw" -n kube-system \
    -o jsonpath='{.metadata.name}: {range .status.listeners[*]}{.name}={.attachedRoutes} {end}{"\n"}'
done
```

## Pitfalls

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Always set `sectionName`**
>
> Port 80 admits only `kube-system`, so a route that names no listener fails to attach there; on `apps-gateway` it still attaches to every HTTPS listener it matches.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Two apps can claim the same hostname**
>
> `apps-gateway` admits routes from every namespace, so a stray `HTTPRoute` can claim any name the policy above does not reserve — see [Security Posture](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md>).

# GitHub runners

Linux jobs of a private repository run here instead of on GitHub's hosted runners, whose minutes a free organisation pays for. The [Actions Runner Controller](<https://github.com/actions/actions-runner-controller>) is two components: `arc-controller` runs the controller and its CRDs, `arc-runners` one scale set per repository. A job gets a fresh runner pod that exits when the job ends. macOS jobs cannot run here and stay on GitHub.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Scale sets | `homelab` and `homelab-wait` (`AutoscalingRunnerSet`), Helm releases `shotapp` and `shotapp-wait` |
| Workflow label | `runs-on: homelab` |
| Depends on | [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) for the GitHub App in `kv/arc-runners/github-app` |
| If it is down | Jobs on `runs-on: homelab` queue on GitHub until a runner registers; nothing else notices |
| Health check | `kubectl -n arc-systems get pods` → the controller and one listener per scale set Running |
| Namespaces | `arc-systems` for the controller and the listeners, `arc-runners` for the runner pods, `arc-jobs` for the job pods the container hook starts |
| Files | [`payload/platform/arc-controller/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/arc-controller>), [`payload/platform/arc-runners/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/arc-runners>), and the three namespaces' files under `payload/platform/security/` |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Controller and scale set chart on the same `targetRevision` | The controller deletes an `AutoscalingRunnerSet` whose chart version differs from its own, and Argo CD recreates it, in a loop; Renovate moves both in one PR |
| `githubConfigUrl` on the repository, not the organisation | No other repository in the organisation can schedule code onto the cluster |
| `githubConfigSecret: github-app` | A GitHub App rather than a PAT: no expiry and a token scoped to the installed repository — see [GitHub App](<#github-app>) |
| `controllerServiceAccount` spelled out | The chart finds the controller with Helm `lookup`, which Argo CD does not run |
| `minRunners` and `maxRunners` | No idle pods between pushes; the ceiling lets several pull requests run their parallel Linux jobs at once without queueing, while the requests stay a fraction of the workers' memory |
| `containerMode: kubernetes-novolume` | A job with `services:` or `container:` gets its own pod, started by the container hook through the API server. No privileged Docker daemon and no PVC per job. Where that pod runs, and with which token: [Job pods](<#job-pods>) |
| `ACTIONS_RUNNER_REQUIRE_JOB_CONTAINER: "false"` | A job without `container:` runs in the runner pod itself, as on a hosted runner |
| `arc-runners` and `arc-jobs` enforce `baseline` | The runner image uses `sudo`, and a service container such as PostgreSQL starts as root; neither passes `restricted` |
| `arc-jobs` is exempt from the user-namespace kill | buildah builds the images as root without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, which `baseline` forbids, so it re-executes itself in a user namespace; [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md#enforcement>) records those instead of killing them, and its [alerts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md#policies>) leave out buildah's and `go`'s expected events |
| The runner image as a full reference with a digest | Renovate tracks it; the chart passes the same image to the hook for the job pod's init container |
| `resources` | Unmeasured; the request fits a test suite beside a database, the limit stops a runaway build before it starves the node |
| A second scale set, `homelab-wait`, for `ci-ok` alone | The wait holds its runner until every other check finishes; on the shared set, `maxRunners` open pull requests fill it with waits and their checks never start. It builds nothing: no container mode, a small request |

### Job pods

The chart's own ServiceAccount for `kubernetes-novolume` may read every Secret in `arc-runners`, where the GitHub App key and each runner's JIT config live, and a step without `container:` runs in the runner pod with that token. The `homelab` set therefore runs its hook one namespace over.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `serviceAccountName: homelab-runner` | The chart then renders no Role of its own; `job-pods-rbac.yaml` grants the ServiceAccount rights in `arc-jobs` only |
| `ACTIONS_RUNNER_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE: arc-jobs` | The hook creates the job pod and its environment Secret there, so the Secret verbs it needs reach nothing else |
| The Role is the hook's `requiredPermissions`, Secret `get` and `list` included | The hook checks every verb before each command and fails the job if one is missing; a step can read the environment of a concurrent job from the same repository |
| `default` ServiceAccount in `arc-jobs` without a token | A job pod never calls the API server |
| Hook template `job-pod-template.yaml` | The kubelet's `RuntimeDefault` refuses buildah its user namespace and `baseline` forbids `Unconfined`, so the job container runs the [`arc-jobs` profile](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-profiles-operator/index.md#seccomp>) |

All jobs share `arc-jobs` and one Role, so a job can reach the pods and Secrets of any job running beside it. That is accepted because no repository with other contributors will use these runners; if that changes, it takes one scale set and namespace per trust level, each with its own Role.

### Controller

The `arc-controller` values:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `flags.watchSingleNamespace: arc-runners` | The controller gets a Role in this namespace instead of a ClusterRole over every namespace |
| `logLevel: info`, `logFormat: json` | The chart's default is `debug`, which logs every reconcile; JSON is what Loki parses |
| Restricted security context on the controller and the listener | Both are distroless and run as non-root; the namespace enforces `baseline` and audits `restricted` |

### Metrics

`metrics` in the controller values turns on `/metrics` on the metrics port of the controller and of every listener it starts. The listener's are the scale set's view from GitHub (assigned jobs, desired, idle and registered runners, job start-up and run times), the controller's the runner pods it manages. Both PodMonitors in `payload/platform/arc-controller/podmonitors.yaml` set `honorLabels`, so the metrics keep their own `namespace`, the runners' namespace, instead of the pod's `arc-systems`.

The **GitHub Actions Runners** dashboard in `payload/platform/arc-controller/grafana-dashboards.yaml` reads them. The job metrics carry no scale set label, so its job panels take the scale set from the listener pod's name. Upstream's sample dashboard is not vendored: it filters on a scale set label this version does not export.

### Network policy

Every rule in `arc-runners.yaml` and `arc-jobs.yaml` under `payload/platform/security/network-policies/`. Unlike the other namespaces, egress is every public address rather than a list of names.

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Ingress from the namespace and the node only | Runners and job pods serve nothing; the listener in `arc-systems` reaches GitHub, not the runners, and a runner reaches its job pod through the API server |
| Egress to the API server, `homelab` runner pods only | The container hook creates the job pod and execs each step into it; the `homelab-wait` runners run no hook, and job pods carry no token |
| Egress to `0.0.0.0/0` on the HTTP and HTTPS ports, minus the private, carrier-grade and link-local ranges | A job downloads whatever its workflow names (actions, toolchains, packages), which no name list keeps up with. Cutting the private ranges keeps the LAN, the nodes and every in-cluster service out of reach |

The controller's and listeners' egress, GitHub's API and the Actions service only, and Prometheus' scrape of their metrics port, are in `payload/platform/security/network-policies/arc-systems.yaml`.

### GitHub App

One app per organisation, installed on each repository that has a scale set.

1. Create the app under the organisation's **Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App**: any name and homepage URL, **Webhook → Active** unticked, **Repository permissions → Administration: Read and write**, **Metadata: Read-only**, installable on this account only.
2. On the app's page, note the **App ID** and **Generate a private key**; the `.pem` file downloads.
3. **Install App** → **Only select repositories** → the repository. The installation ID is the number at the end of the installation's URL.
4. Store all three:

```bash
make bao-secrets    # answers the arc-runners/github-app prompts
```

1. Push the secret through and wait for the listener:

```bash
kubectl -n arc-runners annotate externalsecret github-app force-sync="$(date +%s)" --overwrite
kubectl -n arc-systems get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/component=runner-scale-set-listener
```

The scale set then appears under the repository's **Settings → Actions → Runners**.

## Usage

A job opts in with its label:

```yaml
runs-on: homelab
```

| Job shape | What runs where |
| --- | --- |
| Steps only | In the runner pod, on the runner image |
| `container:` | A job pod from that image; steps exec into it |
| `services:` | Needs a `container:` too; the services join the job pod and answer on `localhost` |

The runner image is GitHub's minimal [`actions-runner`](<https://github.com/actions/runner/blob/main/images/Dockerfile>), not the hosted `ubuntu-latest`: `git`, `curl`, `jq`, `unzip` and `sudo`, and no language toolchains. A job installs what it needs, pinned, or uses a `setup-*` action.

### Adding a scale set

1. Install the [GitHub App](<#github-app>) on the repository.
2. In `payload/platform/arc-runners/application.yaml`, copy a chart source with its own `helm.releaseName`, `githubConfigUrl` and `runnerScaleSetName`; a set that runs job pods keeps `containerMode`, `serviceAccountName` and `ACTIONS_RUNNER_KUBERNETES_NAMESPACE`.
3. In `job-pods-rbac.yaml`, a ServiceAccount, Role and binding for the set's hook, or `homelab-runner` again when the jobs share its trust level, see [Job pods](<#job-pods>).
4. In `payload/platform/security/network-policies/arc-runners.yaml`, the `container-hook` policy selects `actions.github.com/scale-set-name` `homelab` only; a set that runs a hook needs the same rule for its name.
5. A repository that runs `ci-ok` needs a `-wait` twin of the set, like `homelab-wait`, for the reason in [Configuration](<#configuration>).
6. Workflows opt in with `runs-on: <runnerScaleSetName>`.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n arc-runners get autoscalingrunnerset,ephemeralrunner
kubectl -n arc-systems get pods
kubectl -n arc-systems logs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=runner-scale-set-listener --tail=50
```

A job waiting on `runs-on: homelab` with no runner pod in `arc-runners` means the listener is not getting it; its log and the controller's say why.

## Pitfalls

- **`Job Container is required.`** A job with `services:` and no `container:`. The hook runs services only beside a job container.
- **No Docker daemon.** The image carries the `docker` CLI, but nothing answers it: `docker build` and `docker run` steps fail.
- **No listener until the app is in OpenBao.** An empty `kv/arc-runners/github-app` syncs cleanly; the controller then fails to register the scale set with GitHub and says so in its log.
- **Removing a scale set takes the controller.** Its Roles carry the `actions.github.com/cleanup-protection` finalizer, which only the controller removes; take the scale set out first and let it go before touching `arc-controller`.

# Kured

[Kured](<https://kured.dev/>) applies the updates the nodes have staged. It watches every node for a sentinel file and, when it finds one, takes a cluster-wide lock, cordons and drains the node, reboots it and uncordons it when it is back. Flatcar's own `locksmithd` is masked because it reboots without draining, on a cluster where every node is a storage node.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kured` |
| Depends on | [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the alerts it gates on |
| If it is down | Nothing visible: staged OS and sysext updates never get applied |
| Health check | `kubectl -n kured logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kured --tail=50` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/kured/application.yaml`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/blob/main/payload/platform/kured/application.yaml>); [`payload/platform/security/network-policies/kured.yaml`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/blob/main/payload/platform/security/network-policies/kured.yaml>) for the Prometheus egress the alert gate needs |

## Configuration

An update stages on disk and signals it by touching `/run/reboot-required`, Kured's default sentinel, on tmpfs so a reboot clears it.

| Mechanism | Stages | Signals by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flatcar OS (update-engine) | New image on the passive A/B partition | `flatcar-reboot-sentinel.timer` |
| Kubernetes sysext | New `.raw` under `/opt/extensions/kubernetes` | `systemd-sysupdate` drop-in |

```
flowchart TD
    OS["update-engine<br/>OS image on the passive partition"] --> SEN
    KUBE["systemd-sysupdate<br/>kubernetes sysext"] --> SEN

    SEN["/run/reboot-required<br/>sentinel, on tmpfs"] --> TICK{"Kured checks<br/>every period"}

    TICK -->|"no sentinel"| SLEEP["Nothing to do until<br/>an update stages one"]
    TICK -->|"sentinel present"| ALERT{"Blocking alert firing?<br/>Ceph, etcd, node, API, Velero"}
    ALERT -->|"yes"| HELD["Reboot deferred while<br/>the cluster is unhealthy"]
    ALERT -->|"no"| LOCK{"Cluster lock free?"}
    LOCK -->|"another node<br/>is rebooting"| TAINT["Taint PreferNoSchedule,<br/>wait for the lock"]
    LOCK -->|"acquired"| DRAIN["Cordon and drain"]
    DRAIN -->|"drain fails"| GIVEUP["No reboot: uncordon,<br/>release the lock, retry"]
    DRAIN -->|"drained"| BOOT["systemctl reboot;<br/>new partition and<br/>sysexts take effect"]
    BOOT --> UP["Node comes back,<br/>sentinel gone with tmpfs"]
    UP --> DONE["Uncordon, drop the annotation,<br/>release the lock after a delay"]

    style SEN stroke-width:3px
```

The reasoning behind the values in `application.yaml`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No reboot window | Kured acts as soon as it sees a sentinel; the guards below make that safe, not the clock |
| `concurrency` and `lockReleaseDelay` | One node down at a time. The rebooted node is uncordoned as soon as Kured's pod is back; the delay only holds the *next* node, long enough for the OSD to rejoin and the few minutes of backfill a reboot leaves, and as long as `CephOSDDown`'s `for`, so an OSD that did not come back is a firing alert before the next drain |
| `period` | How often each node checks its sentinel and retries a blocked reboot. Every wait before a drain is a multiple of it, and the lock is handed on only at the next check after the hold, so it sets most of a rollout's length; a check is one file test and one Prometheus query per node |
| `drainTimeout` | Above the slowest successful drain, which is `drainGracePeriod` plus a CloudNativePG switchover; a drain that runs longer is blocked by a PodDisruptionBudget, usually Ceph's while another OSD is down, and is retried at the next check instead of holding the lock |
| `forceReboot: false` | A node that will not drain is a node worth looking at |
| `preferNoScheduleTaint` | A node pending reboot stops attracting pods about to be evicted again |
| `annotateNodes: true` | `kubectl get node -o yaml` shows why a node is cordoned |
| `VeleroBackupInProgress` on the alert list | Velero marks any backup it finds running at startup as Failed, and draining its node restarts it. The rule in `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml` compares attempts with outcomes per live Velero pod over a window longer than Velero's default limit on asynchronous operations; a backup that hangs drops out of the window, so it holds reboots for that long at most. A backup that starts in a Velero pod's first scrape interval has no zero sample to increase from and does not hold the gate. It routes to the `null` receiver because it fires every night |
| `alertFilterRegexp` with `alertFilterMatchOnly: true` | Kured asks Prometheus before taking a node down and refuses while any Ceph, etcd, node, API or OpenBao alert on the list fires.
