OpenBao unseals by hand, so a rollout waits for `make bao-unseal` after each node that held a pod; a second sealed pod loses the Raft quorum. This is why [Rebooting a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebooting-a-node>) has no Ceph check of its own: a second reboot during a backfill can take a placement group below its minimum replica count. Kured matches the alert name only, so Prometheus loads rules from [platform namespaces only](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#scrape-targets>) |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The regex means the opposite of what it looks like**
>
> `alertFilterRegexp` normally lists alerts to **ignore**. With `alertFilterMatchOnly: true` these become the only alerts that block, because something is almost always firing in a homelab and blocking on any alert would mean never rebooting. An alert not on the list does not stop a reboot; read the flag twice before widening it. A name that no `PrometheusRule` defines blocks nothing and fails silently. Check every entry against the rules that exist, with the last command under [Health check](<#health-check>).

## Usage

To stop Kured rebooting anything without uninstalling it, take its cluster lock by hand; it holds until the annotation is removed. Clearing the sentinel does not work, because `flatcar-reboot-sentinel.timer` in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` re-touches it while an update is staged, and a DaemonSet cannot be scaled.

```bash
kubectl -n kured annotate ds kured weave.works/kured-node-lock='{"nodeID":"manual"}'
kubectl -n kured annotate ds kured weave.works/kured-node-lock-    # release it
```

To reboot nodes on Kured's next pass:

```bash
make reboot-all LIMIT=<node>         # no LIMIT: all nodes
```

`NodeRebootPending` in `payload/platform/monitoring/node-update-rules.yaml` fires when the sentinel outlasts the rule's `for`: a marker that old is a node blocked by the alert gate, not a queued one.

## Health check

```bash
# Which nodes want a reboot: kured_reboot_required is the sentinel's presence, per node
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus 9090:9090 &
curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=kured_reboot_required == 1' \
  | jq -r '.data.result[].metric.node'

# Which node is being rebooted right now
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["weave.works/kured-reboot-in-progress"]) | .metadata.name'

# Whether a node has staged anything
ssh core@<node> 'ls -l /run/reboot-required; update_engine_client -status'

kubectl -n kured logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kured --tail=50

# The alert names the gate may use: every entry in alertFilterRegexp must be here
kubectl get prometheusrule -A -o json | jq -r '.items[].spec.groups[].rules[] | select(.alert) | .alert' | sort -u | grep -E 'Ceph|etcd|KubeNode|KubeAPI|OpenBao(Sealed|NoActiveNode)|VeleroBackupInProgress'
```

# Logging

[Loki](<https://grafana.com/oss/loki/>) stores logs; [Grafana Alloy](<https://grafana.com/docs/alloy/latest/>) collects them. Both are queried from the existing Grafana at [monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch>). Without them a crashed pod's logs are gone with the container, and on Flatcar the `kubelet`, `containerd`, `systemd-sysupdate` and `update-engine` logs live in journald and are reachable only over SSH to the node that is misbehaving.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `logging` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) object storage for chunks, [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the Grafana that queries it |
| If it is down | Logs stop being collected and are not backfilled. The [audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) loses its durable copy, and the [log alerts](<#alerting>) stop |
| Health check | `kubectl -n logging get pods`, then a `{job="kubernetes-audit"}` query in Grafana |
| Metrics | Loki and Alloy, each through its chart's `ServiceMonitor`; both sets of dashboards are listed under [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#dashboards>) |
| Files | [`payload/platform/loki/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/loki>) and [`payload/platform/alloy/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/alloy>), one chart Application each (`loki`, `alloy`); [`payload/platform/logging/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/logging>), the `logging` Application: the bucket claim in `bucket.yaml`, `loki-rules.yaml`, the Grafana datasource and the Alloy dashboards |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Not Promtail, and not the `grafana/loki` chart**
>
> Promtail is end of life; Alloy is its supported replacement. Loki comes from `grafana-community/loki`, where the OSS chart is maintained now ([grafana-community/helm-charts](<https://github.com/grafana-community/helm-charts>)); `grafana/loki` serves Grafana Enterprise Logs customers and lags behind.

## Configuration

### Sources

| Source | Path | Labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container logs | `/var/log/pods/<ns>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/*.log` | `namespace`, `pod`, `container`, `node`, `app` |
| Node journal | `/var/log/journal` | `unit`, `node`, `job="systemd-journal"` |
| API server audit log | `/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log` | `verb`, `audit_level`, `node`, `job="kubernetes-audit"` |
| Hubble policy verdicts | `/var/run/cilium/hubble/events.log` | `verdict`, `node`, `job="hubble"` |

The first three are on the root filesystem, so one `varlog: true` mount covers them; the Hubble export is a separate read-only hostPath — see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>). The audit log exists only on the control-plane nodes; Alloy runs everywhere and `local.file_match` finds nothing on the workers. Audit events keep only `verb` and `audit_level` as labels — small closed sets — while user and resource stay in the line where `| json` can reach them. See [Audit logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) for what is recorded.

### Alloy pipeline

| Stage | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `discovery.kubernetes` with a `spec.nodeName` field selector | Each agent discovers only its own node's pods; without it every agent watches every pod and discards all but its own |
| `stage.cri {}` on container logs | containerd writes `<timestamp> <stream> <flags> <message>`; without it the timestamp lands inside the line and Loki stamps everything at ingest time |
| `discovery.relabel "journal"` sets `job` | `loki.source.journal` overwrites `job` with its component ID after applying `labels`; only relabel rules run after that |
| `stage.drop` on the journal | A [logging seccomp profile](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-profiles-operator/index.md#seccomp>) records every `clone3`, refused by design |
| `stage.json`, `stage.labels`, `stage.timestamp` on audit events | Stamps each event with its `requestReceivedTimestamp` rather than when Alloy read the file |

| Setting in `alloy/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Control-plane toleration | Without it Alloy runs on the workers alone and neither the audit log nor the control-plane kubelets' journals reach Loki |
| `enableReporting: false` | Alloy otherwise sends usage statistics to `stats.grafana.org`; telemetry is off in every component here |
| `runAsUser: 0` | The log files are root-owned; a non-root Alloy does not fail, it silently collects nothing. Read-only root, no capabilities and the [logging seccomp profile](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-profiles-operator/index.md#seccomp>) lock the rest down |
| `emptyDir` at `/tmp` | The chart's `storagePath` defaults to `/tmp/alloy`, unwritable on a read-only root; it holds tailing positions |
| `rbac.rules` without `secrets` and `configmaps` | The chart's ClusterRole reads every Secret and ConfigMap for `remote.kubernetes.*`, which nothing here uses; [`KubernetesAuditSecretReadByUser`](<#alerting>) shows Secret reads, but an unused grant is better not made |

### Storage

Loki runs as a single binary (`deploymentMode: Monolithic`) and keeps chunks in the [Ceph object store](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#object-storage>); a local PVC on `rook-ceph-block` holds the WAL and the index being built. The bucket is the `ObjectBucketClaim` in `logging/bucket.yaml`, with a fixed `bucketName`: a generated name carries a random suffix that would have to be read back at runtime, a fixed one keeps Loki's config static and identical after a rebuild.

| Setting in `loki/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `singleBinary.extraArgs` `-config.expand-env=true` and `singleBinary.extraEnvFrom` | Rook writes the bucket credentials to a Secret, Loki reads them as `${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}` — nothing in Git |
| `loki.analytics.reporting_enabled: false` | Loki otherwise sends usage statistics to `stats.grafana.org` a few times a day; same reason as Alloy's switch above |
| `chunksCache` and `resultsCache` off | Four memcached pods in front of a Loki this size |
| `loki.podSecurityContext` | Adds `RuntimeDefault` seccomp at pod level, covering the rules sidecar too |
| Retention with the compactor enabled | Old chunks are actually deleted |
| `rulerConfig` | The ruler evaluates LogQL alerts and posts them to Alertmanager; without it the audit log and the journal are query-only. Rules come from local files the chart's sidecar copies out of `loki_rule` ConfigMaps, so `storage.type` is `local` rather than the bucket the chart would pick; `rule_path` is the ruler's scratch directory and must not be the rules directory |
| `rbac.namespaced: true` and `sidecar.rules.resource: configmap` | The rules are ConfigMaps in `logging`, so a Role there replaces the chart's cluster-wide ClusterRole, for the same reason as Alloy's `rbac.rules` above; the chart's binding could not be repointed because a `roleRef` is immutable. `resource: configmap` keeps the sidecar from listing Secrets |
| `retention_stream` for the `findings-history` container | The daily [Trivy summary](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/trivy-operator/index.md#history>) is a few lines and the only long-range record of findings, so that one stream outlives the general `retention_period` by far |

### Alerting

Alerts over logs live in `logging/loki-rules.yaml`, a ConfigMap labelled `loki_rule` in the same format as a `PrometheusRule` group with LogQL expressions. The `k8s-sidecar-target-directory: fake` annotation puts the file under the tenant directory the ruler reads (`fake` is the tenant when `auth_enabled` is off). Prometheus-side rules stay with their components; these are the events only a log carries. Loki's own health alerts (request errors, latency, panics, the compactor) are the chart's `monitoring.alerts`, the mixin Grafana maintains, not rules written here.

| Alert | Fires on | Why it is a log alert |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `KubernetesAuditExecIntoPod` | A successful `exec` or `attach` | Only the [audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) records who ran what in which pod |
| `KubernetesAuditSecretReadByUser` | A Secret read by a person, or by a ServiceAccount outside its own namespace that is not on the allowlist of platform controllers | A stolen token reads across namespaces; the allowlist is the ServiceAccounts RBAC grants Secrets to cluster-wide, plus the runner's in `arc-jobs` only, where its [container hook](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md#job-pods>) keeps each job's environment, and a ServiceAccount reading its own namespace is what its Role is for |
| `KubernetesAuditRbacBindingChanged` | A ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding written by anything but the ArgoCD controller or a `kube-system` controller | Argo CD is the only intended writer; namespaced RoleBindings are left out because CloudNativePG reconciles one per database continuously |
| `KubernetesAuditForbiddenBurst` | More than ten 403s from one identity in ten minutes | What RBAC probing from a compromised pod looks like |
| `KubernetesAuditAnonymousRequest` | A successful anonymous request, except the read of `kube-public/cluster-info` | The health endpoints and kubeadm's bootstrap discovery ConfigMap are the only legitimate anonymous paths; the audit policy drops the first, the rule skips the second |
| `KubernetesAuditEsoTokenMinted` | A successful `serviceaccounts/token` create for an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount by anyone but ESO's controller, a kubelet starting a pod under that ServiceAccount included | OpenBao records the same role and ServiceAccount whoever minted the token, so only the audit log names the minter. A stolen controller token or a legacy token Secret does not trip it: neither shows a different user on this request |
| `OpenBaoSecretReadOutsideEso` | A `kv/data/` read from OpenBao by any token whose display name is not `kubernetes-<namespace>-external-secrets-vault`, ESO's login for one of its [stores](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kubernetes-auth>) | [OpenBao's audit device](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#audit-devices>) writes to stdout; ESO is the only day-to-day reader, every Kubernetes role is bound to that ServiceAccount name, and a token created by hand is prefixed `token-`, so it cannot borrow the name |
| `TetragonSudoInContainer` | `sudo` executed in a container, except the `smartctl` and `nvme` calls `ceph-osd` makes once a day for its device health report | Only the exec event carries the binary and its parent |
| `TetragonPrivilegedExec` | A setuid, setgid or file-capability binary raised privileges on exec, with the same `ceph-osd` exception | The `binary_properties` field exists only in the exec event |
| `TetragonFilelessExec` | A binary executed from memory, via `memfd_create` or an anonymous descriptor, except runc's sealed self-copy on every `exec` | Same |
| `TetragonDeletedBinaryExec` | A binary executed after its last link was removed | Same; see [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md#policies>) |
| `TetragonUnsignedKernelModule` | A kernel module loaded without a valid signature, on a node or from a container | The `add_taint` kprobe event, not a metric label |
| `HubblePolicyDrops` | More than three `POLICY_DENIED` packets in ten minutes for one source workload, destination and port, each counted once although Hubble also reports it as a policy verdict; replies, ICMP errors (a pod's port-unreachable answer to a DNS reply that came too late), pods still in the `init` identity, pod and service addresses Cilium had no pod for at that moment (the world or a local CIDR identity, as during an agent restart or a pod start) and the wanted drops below are left out. The `namespace` label is the policy that refused, so the mail names the file to edit | A connection's retransmits pass the threshold and a name rule's single early `SYN` does not; the metric counts per namespace pair only and misses the first burst of a new pair |
| `HostFirewallDrops` | More than three `POLICY_DENIED` packets in ten minutes from one source to one node's own address, which only the [host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) refuses; `HubblePolicyDrops` leaves these out | Grouped by node and source without the port, so a port scan of one `SYN` per port alerts as well as a refused connection's retransmits |
| `NodeSshLogin` | An accepted SSH login on a node | Nothing routine logs in after provisioning |
| `NodeSshAuthFailures` | More than five failed SSH attempts on a node in ten minutes | Password authentication is off; repeats are a scan or a retried key |

`HubblePolicyDrops` leaves out a drop that is wanted but cannot be switched off, one filter stage each, so every other drop from the same workload still mails:

| Source namespace | Destination | Why it cannot be switched off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `authentik` | `*.gravatar.com` | Avatars are a database setting no blueprint reaches; see [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#chart-values>) |
| `dependency-track` | `repo.packagist.org`, `packages.atlassian.com` | Built-in metadata repositories are database rows and the policy leaves these two out. Turning them off under **Administration → Repositories** ends the lookups too |

A drop belongs here only when no config switch exists; telemetry with a switch is turned off instead.

To confirm the ruler loaded a rule:

```bash
kubectl -n logging port-forward svc/loki 3100:3100
curl -s localhost:3100/loki/api/v1/rules
```

### Dashboards

`grafana-dashboards.yaml` carries three dashboards from the Alloy mixin (`operations/alloy-mixin/rendered/dashboards/`), unmodified; the chart renders none and Renovate does not see the copy, so re-copy them when Alloy moves a minor version. The mixin's other dashboards cover features this Alloy does not use. The Loki datasource in `grafana-datasource.yaml` declares its namespace as `monitoring`, the only namespace the Grafana sidecar watches for `grafana_datasource` ConfigMaps.

## Usage

Choose **Loki** as the datasource in Grafana and query by label:

```text
{namespace="rook-ceph"} |= "error"
{unit="kubelet.service", node="odin"}
{namespace="openbao"} |= "sealed"
{job="kubernetes-audit"} | json | objectRef_resource="secrets"
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n logging get pods
```

Then run a `{job="kubernetes-audit"}` query in Grafana; an empty result with healthy pods means the control-plane agents are not reading the file.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Loki settings belong on `singleBinary`, not `global`**
>
> `global.extraArgs` and `global.extraEnvFrom` look right, but the single-binary StatefulSet reads only `singleBinary.extraArgs` and `singleBinary.extraEnvFrom`. Set globally, the config is full of unexpanded `${...}` and Loki cannot authenticate to RGW, with an error pointing nowhere near the cause. Likewise `singleBinary.podSecurityContext` does not exist and is silently inert.

# metrics-server

[metrics-server](<https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server>) serves the `metrics.k8s.io` API that `kubectl top`, every `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` and the [descheduler](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/descheduler/index.md>) read; the scheduler does not, it places on requests. Without it `kubectl top` errors and an HPA sits at `<unknown>/<target>` with no logs, events or clue. Prometheus is not a substitute: it answers PromQL from its own store, while the resource metrics API is an aggregated Kubernetes API that core controllers read directly.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system`; kubelet-csr-approver in `kubelet-csr-approver` |
| Depends on | kubelet-csr-approver, or the kubelet certificates it verifies are never issued; [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>) for its own serving certificate |
| If it is down | `kubectl top`, every HPA and the [descheduler](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/descheduler/index.md>)'s node usage. Nothing else notices |
| Health check | `kubectl top nodes` → a row per node |
| Files | [`payload/platform/metrics-server/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/metrics-server>), [`payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver>) |

## Configuration

### Verifying the kubelet instead of trusting it

A kubelet serves a self-signed certificate by default, so the usual shortcut is `--kubelet-insecure-tls`, which makes the metrics path spoofable by anything that can occupy a kubelet's address. Kubernetes does not auto-approve `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` CSRs, since a compromised node could request a certificate for any name, so doing it properly takes three pieces:

| Piece | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `serverTLSBootstrap: true` | `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2` | The kubelet requests a serving certificate from the cluster CA |
| [kubelet-csr-approver](<https://github.com/postfinance/kubelet-csr-approver>) | `payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/application.yaml` | Approves those CSRs, constrained by `providerRegex` (only the inventory's node names; anything else is **denied**), `providerIpPrefixes` (the nodes' subnet), a short `maxExpirationSeconds`, and `bypassDnsResolution` because node names come from the Ansible inventory, not a resolver |
| `--kubelet-certificate-authority` | `payload/platform/metrics-server/application.yaml` | metrics-server verifies against the cluster CA |

| Setting in `metrics-server/application.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Flags via `defaultArgs`, not `args` | The default list already sets `--kubelet-preferred-address-types`, and a flag passed twice leaves the winner to parsing order. It is `InternalIP` because node hostnames do not resolve here |
| `replicas` above one and a PodDisruptionBudget | A node reboot does not take the resource metrics API down |
| `tls.type: cert-manager` with `apiService.insecureSkipTLSVerify: false` | The other half of the path: the chart's self-signed `Issuer` signs the serving certificate and the cainjector copies its CA into the `APIService`, so kube-apiserver verifies metrics-server instead of trusting whatever answers at the Service |

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get csr | grep kubelet-serving   # should be Approved,Issued
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   # Available True, caBundle filled
kubectl top nodes
```

`Pending` CSRs mean kubelet-csr-approver is not running or a node name does not match the regex. `Denied` means the regex or the IP prefix is wrong — check the controller's logs before widening either.

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Adding a node means editing the regex**
>
> A node missing from `providerRegex` has its CSR denied, keeps its self-signed certificate, and silently goes missing from `kubectl top`. Add it to the regex when you add it to the inventory.

# Monitoring

[kube-prometheus-stack](<https://github.com/prometheus-community/helm-charts/tree/main/charts/kube-prometheus-stack>): Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, node-exporter and kube-state-metrics. Prometheus evaluates the rules, Alertmanager mails what fires to one mailbox, and [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) reads the same alerts as its reboot gate; what that one mailbox leaves uncovered is in [Known limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>). The chart's default rules are good; its default routing swallows every alert.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `monitoring` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana volumes, [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md>) for Grafana login |
| If it is down | No alerts and no metrics — and [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) loses the alert gate it checks before rebooting a node |
| Health check | `kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus,alertmanager`; the `Watchdog` alert should always be firing |
| UI | `monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` (Grafana), `prometheus.` and `alertmanager.` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/monitoring/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/monitoring>), [`payload/platform/prometheus-operator-crds/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/prometheus-operator-crds>) |

## Configuration

### CRDs

The `monitoring.coreos.com` CRDs are a separate `prometheus-operator-crds` Application, from the prometheus-community chart of that name, and this chart runs with `crds.enabled: false`. Other components render ServiceMonitors or PrometheusRules, and a missing kind fails their sync until the CRDs exist — see [Bootstrap convergence](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-convergence>). The Application has no resources finalizer, so deleting it leaves the CRDs, and every ServiceMonitor, Prometheus and Alertmanager with them, in place.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Two versions that have to agree**
>
> `prometheus-operator-crds` must carry the same operator version as kube-prometheus-stack; an operator newer than its CRDs can depend on fields they do not define. Renovate bumps them separately: merge the CRD bump first, or both together — see [Maintenance](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/maintenance/index.md>).

### Alerting

Alertmanager routes to email. The chart's `config` is off (`alertmanagerSpec.useExistingSecret`) and `alertmanager-config.yaml` renders the whole `alertmanager.yaml` through ESO into `alertmanagerSpec.configSecret`, because only the password has a file form (`smtp_auth_password_file`) and the login and recipient are e-mail addresses that do not belong in Git.

| Setting in `alertmanager-config.yaml` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `smtp_smarthost` on the implicit-TLS port | Alertmanager selects TLS from the port; `smtp_require_tls` stays on so a move to the STARTTLS port cannot fall to plaintext |
| `smtp_from` equals the login | mailbox.org refuses a sender the login does not own |
| Grouping by `namespace`, with `group_interval` and `repeat_interval` in hours and a shorter pair for `critical`; resolved notifications sent | mailbox.org caps what an account may send, and a namespace's alerts usually share a cause, so one mail lists them together |
| `Watchdog` routed to `null` | It fires continuously as proof the pipeline is alive; mailing it would train the recipient to filter it |
| `VeleroBackupInProgress` routed to `null` | It fires for every nightly backup as [Kured's gate](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md#configuration>), not as a problem |
| `KubeJobFailed` disabled in the chart (`defaultRules.disabled`) and redefined in `job-rules.yaml`, bound to Jobs started in the last day | The chart's rule fires for as long as a failed Job object exists, so one old failure reads as an outage for weeks. Failed Jobs carry no failure time, so the bound counts from the start |
| Inhibit rules repeated from the chart defaults | A supplied config replaces the whole document, so nothing is inherited |
| Every templated value through `toJson` | A password containing `:`, `#` or a quote cannot break the rendered file |
| `externalUrl` on both `prometheusSpec` and `alertmanagerSpec` in `application.yaml` | The "Source" and Alertmanager links in a mail are built from these; unset, they point at the in-cluster Service, which nothing outside can open |

Rules written here, beside the chart's; the thresholds are in each file:

| Alert | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `CertificateNotReady`, `CertificateExpiringSoon` | A Certificate is not Ready, or is close to expiry |
| `ArgoCDApplicationUnhealthy`, `ArgoCDApplicationOutOfSync` | An Application stays Degraded, Missing or OutOfSync longer than the [retries](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#sync-policy>) run |
| `ExternalSecretNotReady`, `PushSecretNotReady` | One is not Ready; after an OpenBao restart every one fires until it is unsealed |
| `NodeRebootPending`, `NodeOsVersionDrift`, `NodeKubeletVersionDrift`, `ControlPlaneVersionLag` | A staged update waits for its reboot, or nodes or API server disagree on versions — see [OS updates](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md#os-updates>) |
| `KubeClientCertificateExpiringSoon` | The control-plane client certificates come due — see [Control-plane certificates](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md#control-plane-certificates>) |

The three values come from `kv/monitoring/smtp` (`username`, `password`, `to`); `make bao-secrets` prompts for them, or by hand:

```bash
bao kv put kv/monitoring/smtp username=... password=... to=...
```

For another provider, change `smtp_smarthost` in the template and the three values in OpenBao.

### Scrape targets

Every `ServiceMonitor` and `PodMonitor` in every namespace, through the five `*SelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false` settings: the chart treats an empty selector as unset and renders `release: kube-prometheus-stack` in its place, which limits Prometheus to its own targets. `ScrapeConfig` and `Probe` load from `monitoring` only, as a workload could aim them anywhere Prometheus reaches. `enforcedNamespaceLabel` stays off: several monitors rely on `honorLabels`.

`PrometheusRule`s load only from the namespaces the `apps` project cannot deploy to, matched on the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label the API server sets. [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md#configuration>) gates reboots on alert names, so a workload's rule named `CephHealthError` would otherwise stop OS updates cluster-wide. A new platform namespace's rules load only once it is listed in `ruleNamespaceSelector`.

| Target | Made scrapable by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| node-exporter | Its own `node-exporter` namespace, running as `spc_t` | Only that namespace is admitted at `privileged` ([Pod Security Admission](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#pod-security-admission>)); SELinux refuses `container_t` the host's `/proc` |
| kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager | A per-node `bind-address` patch in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` (kubeadm binds them to `127.0.0.1`) | HTTPS with a self-signed certificate, hence `insecureSkipVerify`; the control-plane monitors read the pod's projected token (`controlPlaneScrapeClass`), so no long-lived token Secret exists |
| etcd | A per-node `listen-metrics-urls` patch in the same template (kubeadm listens on `127.0.0.1` only) | Plain HTTP, serving only `/metrics` and `/health`, so its `plain-http` scrape class sends no token; client and peer APIs stay on mTLS |
| Ceph | `monitoring.enabled` on the `CephCluster` — see [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#monitoring>) |  |
| kube-proxy | Not scraped (`kubeProxy.enabled: false`) | Cilium replaces it; the default would keep `KubeProxyDown` firing forever |
| CRD status fields: CloudNativePG's ObjectStores and Backups | kube-state-metrics' `customResourceState` config in the chart values, one `rbac.extraRules` entry per kind | A `StateSet` per enum field and a `Gauge` per timestamp; the rule that reads a kind sits with its component, in a namespace on the rule list above |
| Pod labels: OpenBao's `openbao-sealed` | kube-state-metrics' `metricLabelsAllowlist` in the chart values | Exported as `label_<name>` on `kube_pod_labels`; only listed labels, since every one adds a series per pod |

### Grafana

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `disable_login_form` and `oauth_auto_login` | The URL bounces straight to Authentik; `role_attribute_path` with `role_attribute_strict` maps the three Grafana groups and refuses everyone else, see [Groups and roles](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#groups-and-roles>) |
| `cookie_secure` and `content_security_policy` | HTTPS-only: the session cookie never travels in clear; the shipped CSP limits what pages load |
| `analytics.*` off and `disable_gravatar` | Usage reports, update checks and Gravatar are switched off in config, not permitted by network policy, as in every component here |
| `grafana-oidc.yaml` | The OIDC client is generated into OpenBao and read by both sides — see [Authentik](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#client-secrets>) |
| `grafana.route.main` | The chart renders Grafana's `HTTPRoute`. Prometheus and Alertmanager stay in `httproute.yaml`: their routes point at Authentik's outpost, which no chart template can express |
| `grafana.admin.existingSecret`, from `grafana-admin.yaml` | Unset, the chart regenerates the password on every render and Grafana restarts on every sync. The admin account is the [break-glass path](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/authentik/index.md#when-authentik-is-down>); never set `grafana.adminPassword` in Git |
| `grafana.rbac.create: false` with `grafana-sidecar-rbac.yaml`, and `sidecar.*.resource: configmap` | Dashboards and datasources are ConfigMaps, so a ClusterRole bound by a RoleBinding in each `searchNamespace` namespace grants those alone, not the chart's cluster-wide ConfigMaps-and-Secrets pair; the chart's binding is dropped rather than repointed because a `roleRef` is immutable |
| `Recreate` strategy | The dashboard PVC is RWO; under `RollingUpdate` the new pod waits for a volume the old pod releases only once the new one is Ready |
| Prometheus and Grafana memory limits well above their requests | Both grow with series count and dashboard load; the limit, sized by the [2.5x-peak rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>), is a ceiling for a runaway |
| Prometheus's memory request at its measured median working set | A request below real use lets a drain move it onto a small worker that swaps until the kubelet goes `NotReady`. 2.5x its peak exceeds every node, so the limit stays under the largest node's allocatable |
| Prometheus `retention` and `retentionSize` | Whichever is hit first wins; the size cap drops the oldest blocks instead of filling the disk and crashlooping Prometheus |
| Alertmanager `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, on the ServiceAccount and in `alertmanagerSpec` | Nothing binds a role to it — the operator talks to the API — so the token would only be a credential in a pod reachable from the Gateway. The operator sets the pod field itself, so the account's setting alone does nothing |

### Dashboards

Where a chart can render a dashboard, it does; only charts without one get a vendored copy, which Renovate does not update — the header of each file names its upstream tag.

| Component | Dashboards | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) | Cilium Metrics, Cilium Operator, four Hubble dashboards | Chart: `dashboards`, `operator.dashboards`, `hubble.metrics.dashboards` |
| [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) | OpenBao | Chart: `serverTelemetry.grafanaDashboard` |
| [External Secrets](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>) | External Secrets Operator | Chart: `grafanaDashboard` |
| [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md>) | CloudNativePG | Chart: `monitoring.grafanaDashboard` |
| [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) | Ceph Cluster, Ceph - OSD (Single), Ceph - Pools | Vendored: `rook-ceph/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) | Alloy / Controller, Alloy / Loki Components, Alloy / Resources | Vendored: `logging/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) | The Loki mixin | Chart: `monitoring.dashboards`, with `monitoring.rules` for the recording rules they read |
| ArgoCD | ArgoCD | Vendored: `argocd-config/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Tetragon](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md>) | Tetragon | Written for this cluster: `tetragon/grafana-dashboards.yaml`; upstream ships none |
| [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>) | GitHub Actions Runners | Written for this cluster: `arc-controller/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |
| [Trivy Operator](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/trivy-operator/index.md>) | Trivy Operator | Written for this cluster: `trivy-operator/grafana-dashboards.yaml` |

## Usage

### Adding a dashboard

Add a ConfigMap labelled `grafana_dashboard: "1"` next to the component it describes, in a file named `grafana-dashboards.yaml` and a ConfigMap named `<component>-grafana-dashboards`; a Secret carrying the label is not read. The sidecar watches only the platform namespaces listed in `sidecar.dashboards.searchNamespace`, so a workload cannot replace a dashboard; a component in a new namespace adds it there and a RoleBinding in `grafana-sidecar-rbac.yaml`, and the `apps` project must not be able to deploy to it. A dashboard built in the UI lives only on the PVC: not in Git, not on a rebuilt cluster.

### Growing the Prometheus volume

Kubernetes cannot expand a StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplate`, so raising the request in `application.yaml` does not resize the existing claim. The operator rebuilds the StatefulSet orphaned so the pod survives, logging `recreating StatefulSet because the update operation wasn't possible`.

1. Merge the size bump and wait for the Application to sync.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n argocd get app kube-prometheus-stack -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}'
   ```
2. Patch the claim to the same size. This is the one step nothing automates.

   ```bash
   SIZE=$(awk '/prometheusSpec:/{f=1} f&&/storage: /{print $2; exit}' \
     payload/platform/monitoring/application.yaml)
   kubectl -n monitoring patch pvc \
     prometheus-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus-db-prometheus-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus-0 \
     --patch "{\"spec\": {\"resources\": {\"requests\": {\"storage\": \"$SIZE\"}}}}"
   ```
3. The claim parks on `FileSystemResizePending` and the filesystem grows at the next mount, so the pod restarts and replays its WAL: a scrape gap of about a minute. Wait for the claim to report the new capacity.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n monitoring get pvc -w \
     -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CAP:.status.capacity.storage
   ```

If the operator has not rebuilt the StatefulSet within a sync interval, delete it with `--cascade=orphan`, which keeps the pod and the claim.

```bash
kubectl -n monitoring delete statefulset \
  -l operator.prometheus.io/name=kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus --cascade=orphan
```

Alertmanager and Grafana take the same two steps, with their own claim names.

### Resetting the Grafana admin password

Grafana reads the password only when it creates its database, so changing `kv/monitoring/grafana-admin` later does not change what it checks. Reset it to the value in OpenBao, not a new one: `grafana-admin.yaml` pushes the password with `updatePolicy: IfNotExists`, so OpenBao keeps the first value and a rebuilt Grafana starts from it.

```bash
PASSWORD=$(kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- \
  bao kv get -mount=kv -field=password monitoring/grafana-admin)
kubectl -n monitoring exec deploy/kube-prometheus-stack-grafana -c grafana -- \
  grafana cli admin reset-admin-password "$PASSWORD"
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus,alertmanager
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceMonitorSelector}'   # should print {}
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-stack-alertmanager 9093:9093
# then open http://localhost:9093 and check Status -> Config
```

`Watchdog` proves the pipeline only as far as Alertmanager; SMTP auth and an expired password are unmonitored. With the port-forward above, send a test alert; it takes the default `email` route and arrives after `group_wait`:

```bash
curl -s -XPOST http://localhost:9093/api/v2/alerts -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '[{"labels":{"alertname":"TestAlert","namespace":"monitoring","severity":"warning"}}]'
```

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Prometheus is a single replica, Alertmanager is not**
>
> Alertmanager runs two replicas spread over the workers with a PDB that lets one go, so a [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) drain keeps alerting up. A second Prometheus would double the memory limit and the volume in `application.yaml`, which the [2.5x-peak rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>) leaves no room for on a worker, so it stays single: its node's drain loses metrics for the restart, and Kured's alert gate fails closed until it is back.

# OpenBao

[OpenBao](<https://openbao.org/>) is the cluster's secret store, an open-source fork of HashiCorp Vault, [chosen over sealed-secrets and SOPS](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#openbao-not-sealed-secrets-or-sops>). It holds every secret the cluster consumes, surfaced as native `Secret` objects by the [External Secrets Operator](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md>).

```
flowchart LR
    Operator([Operator]) -->|bao CLI| Bao[(OpenBao<br/>KV v2)]
    ESO[External Secrets<br/>Operator] -->|read, write once| Store[ClusterSecretStore<br/>openbao / openbao-apps]
    Store -->|Kubernetes auth<br/>kv/namespace/| Bao
    ESO -->|create/update| KSecret[K8s Secret]
    App[App Pod] -->|env / volume| KSecret

    style Bao fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#0288d1
```

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `openbao` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for its Raft volumes. A fresh bootstrap [pauses here](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#bootstrap-pauses-at-openbao>) until OpenBao is initialised and unsealed |
| Seal | Shamir, unsealed by hand; the share count and threshold are set in `scripts/bao-init.sh` |
| If it is down — or merely sealed | No `ExternalSecret` resolves, so cert-manager cannot renew and pods that mount a materialised Secret will not start |
| Health check | `bao status` on every pod → `Sealed: false`; see [Health check](<#health-check>) |
| UI | `vault.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` — the one platform UI *not* behind Authentik, deliberately |
| Files | [`payload/platform/openbao/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/openbao>) |

## Configuration

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Mode | HA, integrated Raft on a Ceph PVC per replica; the replica count is in `application.yaml` |
| Audit storage | Separate PVC on `rook-ceph-block`, written by the `file` audit device — see [Audit devices](<#audit-devices>) |
| TLS | Terminates at the Gateway; plain HTTP at `http://openbao.openbao.svc.cluster.local:8200` |
| Chart | Upstream [`openbao/openbao-helm`](<https://github.com/openbao/openbao-helm>), pinned in `application.yaml` |

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Pod security context restated in full | The chart's `securityContext.pod` and `.container` replace rather than merge, so a block that names only what differs loses the rest. The image's `USER` is a name, so without the numeric IDs the kubelet refuses the container as unprovably non-root. The full block lets the namespace enforce `restricted` ([security policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#pod-security-admission>)) |
| `unauthenticated_metrics_access` | `/v1/sys/metrics` otherwise wants a token the ServiceMonitor lacks. |
| `retry_join` stanzas | `bao operator init` initialises one Raft cluster on one pod; these make the other replicas join it. `service_registration "kubernetes"` only labels pods `active` and `standby` |
| `serverTelemetry.grafanaDashboard` | Renders OpenBao's upstream dashboard (grafana.com 23725) |
| `server.gateway.httpRoute` | The chart renders the UI's `HTTPRoute`, to the `active` Service so the browser never lands on a standby; the chart's warning about terminating TLS concerns certificate authentication, which nothing here uses |

### Audit devices

Two, declared as `audit` stanzas in the server config in `application.yaml` (this OpenBao refuses `bao audit enable` over the API): a `file` device on the audit PVC, and a second `file` device on `stdout`, which [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) ships to Loki with the rest of the container's output. Without one, who read which secret is recorded nowhere; with only one, a full PVC would make OpenBao refuse every request, because a request no enabled device can log is refused. Values are HMACed in both; paths and identities are not. The config is read at start-up and the StatefulSet updates `OnDelete`, so a change lands at each pod's next restart — see [Unsealing after a restart](<#unsealing-after-a-restart>).

`OpenBaoSecretReadOutsideEso` in [`loki-rules.yaml`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>) fires on a `kv/data/` read by anything but the External Secrets Operator's roles: the operator, a root token, or a token that should not exist. A standby audits a request before it resolves the token, so its `please forward to the active node` rejections carry no identity; the rule drops them, and every `ClusterSecretStore` targets `openbao-active`.

```text
{namespace="openbao", container="openbao"} |= `"type":"response"` |= `kv/data/` | json | __error__=""
```

### KV layout

One KV v2 engine at `kv/`; every leaf is `<workload>/<purpose>`, where a workload's prefix is its namespace, the only one [its store](<#kubernetes-auth>) reaches. ExternalSecrets reference `cert-manager/route53` without the `data/` prefix ESO adds itself. A path is written by exactly one of two things: a `PushSecret` beside the `ExternalSecret` that reads it, when every value is random — see [Generated secrets](<#generated-secrets>) — or `make bao-secrets` (an agent session's PAT: `make claude-session-pat`), when a value belongs to an account outside the cluster. A path never mixes the two, because a `bao kv put` replaces the whole path.

| Path | Keys | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `authentik/config` (generated) | `secret-key`, `bootstrap-password`, the ArgoCD and Grafana client id/secret pairs | Authentik, ArgoCD and Grafana — generating the OIDC credentials up front keeps both sides of each integration declarative |
| `cert-manager/route53` | `access-key-id`, `secret-access-key` | The `certificates` Application |
| `external-dns/route53` | `access-key-id`, `secret-access-key` | external-dns |
| `monitoring/grafana-admin` (generated) | `password` | Grafana |
| `cilium/bgp` | `password` | The BGP session's TCP MD5 password, also on the router — [BGP session password](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#bgp-session-password>) |
| `monitoring/smtp` | `username`, `password`, `to` | Alertmanager |
| `kneadtime/config` | `vapid-private-key` | The Knead Time reminder service — a P-256 key in PEM that signs every push; rotating it retires every subscription taken with the old one |
| `claude-homelab/argocd` | `token` | The homelab session's Argo CD API token — [Agent account](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#agent-account>); empty until generated |
| `shot-bridge/accounts` | `lm-username`, `lm-password`, `apns-key-id`, `apns-key-p8` | The Shot Timer bridge's La Marzocco login and APNs key — [Shot Timer bridge](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/shot-bridge/#secrets>); the APNs keys are empty until the key is created |
| `arc-runners/github-app` | `app-id`, `installation-id`, `private-key` | The GitHub App the Actions runners register with — [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md#github-app>); empty until the app is created |
| `claude-<session>/github` | `token` | One agent session's GitHub PAT, for any session name: `make claude-session-pat SESSION=<session>` stores it, adding `DELETE=1` removes the path. Not part of `make bao-secrets`; write it before the session's first sync. Empty until typed in |
| `velero/repository` (generated) | `password` | Velero, as the kopia password of every backup repository — [Repository password](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/index.md#repository-password>); changing it orphans every volume backup |
| `<app>/oidc`, `<app>/config` (generated) | The workload's OIDC client id or secret, beside its own keys | The workload, and Authentik's blueprint through `secrets-<app>.yaml` in `payload/platform/authentik/`; the workload's `PushSecret` writes it |
| `dependency-track/sbom-upload` | `api-key` | The SBOM upload job, [Dependency-Track](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/dependency-track/#secrets>); written even when empty, so the job fails on its own rather than stalling the sync |

The two `route53` leaves are separate IAM users on purpose: cert-manager's [policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md#configuration>) allows only `_acme-challenge` TXT records, while a stolen external-dns key can repoint hostnames.

### Generated secrets

Every random value — session keys, break-glass admin passwords, OIDC client pairs — comes from an ESO `Password` generator, written into OpenBao by a `PushSecret` in the same file as the `ExternalSecret` that reads it back: `payload/platform/authentik/secrets.yaml` here, `<app>/secrets.yaml` in the workloads repository. A fresh cluster needs no prompt for them, and a workload that adds a path needs no change to this repository.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `updatePolicy: IfNotExists` | ESO checks each property before writing it and skips one that exists, so a value is written once and the next reconcile's freshly generated one is discarded |
| `deletionPolicy: None` | Deleting the `PushSecret`, or its Application, leaves the value in OpenBao; the policy grants no `delete` either |
| `symbols: 0`, `allowRepeat: true` | Alphanumeric only, so a value survives a URL, a `.env` line and a shell unquoted; repeats allowed because without them the generator cannot produce more than ten digits |
| `encoding` or a `template` where the reader wants a format | Umami's keys are hex, Dependency-Track's KEK is base64 of 32 bytes |
| One `Password` per path, its `secretKeys` the property names | A generator produces one map per call; one key per property keeps every value independent |
| Sync wave `-2` in the workloads repository | Its `ExternalSecret`s sit at `-1`, and ArgoCD waits for a wave to be healthy before the next |

ESO refuses to write into a path it did not create (`secret not managed by external-secrets`), which keeps it away from everything `make bao-secrets` wrote. Reading a generated value, such as the `akadmin` password, after [Authenticating locally](<#authenticating-locally>):

```bash
bao kv get -mount=kv -field=bootstrap-password authentik/config
```

### Operator credential

No root token outlives the command that needs it. `make bao-init` ends by creating a userpass login for the scripts and revoking the root token; the password lands in `output/credentials/openbao-operator.json` (mode `0600`). The policy and login are written by `bao_create_operator` in `scripts/lib/bao.sh`, which also strips `root_token` from the key file. No target writes a `.bak`; one beside it is a stale hand copy, so delete it.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| The `operator` policy: `kv/` read, write and delete, `sys/storage/raft/snapshot` read | Everything `make bao-secrets`, `make claude-session-pat`, [rotation](<#rotating-a-credential>) and a [snapshot](<#backups>) need; policies, auth methods and snapshot restores still need root |
| `sys/generate-root-token/*` and `sys/decode-token` in the same policy | Since OpenBao 2.6 `bao operator generate-root` needs a token, so without these a revoked root could not be regenerated; the unseal shares still decide |
| `token_ttl` and `token_max_ttl`, short | The scripts cache the token in the pod; one a dropped connection leaves behind expires on its own, and the exit trap revokes it sooner |
| Userpass, not OIDC | Authentik reads its own database password from OpenBao, so an Authentik login would be a loop |
| The scripts fall back to the root token in `openbao-init.json` | A cluster initialised before this keeps working, with a warning, until `make bao-rotate-root` creates the login and revokes the root token |

### Kubernetes auth

ESO authenticates with a short-lived ServiceAccount JWT, which OpenBao validates against the TokenReview API (`rbac.yaml` binds `system:auth-delegator` to the `openbao` ServiceAccount) and answers with a token bound to one policy. Two `ClusterSecretStore`s in `cluster-secret-store.yaml` log in with their own roles, so what a namespace can reach follows from the store it is allowed to use:

| Store | Who may use it | Logs in as | Reaches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `openbao` | The platform namespaces | `external-secrets-vault` in `external-secrets` | The platform's own prefixes and every `kv/<app>/oidc` and `kv/<app>/config`; writes only `authentik/`, `monitoring/` and `velero/`, where its `PushSecret`s are |
| `openbao-apps` | The workload and agent-session namespaces the store lists | `external-secrets-vault` in the `ExternalSecret`'s own namespace | `kv/<namespace>/`, with create, read and update |

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `openbao-apps` names no ServiceAccount namespace | ESO then requests the token in the namespace of the `ExternalSecret` or `PushSecret`, and the `external-secrets-apps` policy templates that namespace, as OpenBao read it from the token, into its paths. One role serves every workload |
| Both stores list their namespaces by name, and `bao-policies.sh` binds the `external-secrets-apps` role to the `openbao-apps` list | A label would not do: a workload may ship its own `Namespace` with any label. A role bound to every namespace would let any new `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount log in. A platform namespace that reads a secret adds itself to `openbao`, a workload to `openbao-apps` ([steps](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md#adding-a-secret>)) |
| An agent session is a `claude-<session>` namespace, declared in `pod-security.yaml` and listed on `openbao-apps` | Its token at `kv/claude-<session>/github` sits in the one prefix its namespace reaches. `namespace-name-guard` keeps `apps` from creating it, so a session is a platform change, then `make bao-policies`, then the workloads repository |
| Each workload ships an `external-secrets-vault` ServiceAccount | The role is bound to that name; `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, because only ESO needs a token for it |
| Referent stores report `Valid` without logging in | ESO cannot know the namespace until an `ExternalSecret` names the store, so a missing role or ServiceAccount shows on the `ExternalSecret`, not the store |

One more role, `openbao-snapshot`, belongs to no store: it is bound to the `openbao-snapshot` ServiceAccount in `backup` and reads the Raft snapshot and nothing else, for the nightly [snapshot CronJob](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#openbao>).

The ServiceAccount the platform store uses lives in `cluster-secret-store.yaml` too, because the stores only validate against a running, unsealed OpenBao. `make bao-init` writes the policies and roles on a fresh cluster by running `scripts/bao-policies.sh`; after a change to that script or to the `openbao-apps` list, `make bao-policies` rewrites them on a live one. The operator login cannot write policies, so it asks for a [generated root token](<#generating-a-root-token>) and revokes it afterwards.

## Usage

### Bootstrap

1. Initialise, unseal and configure the engine and ESO's auth. Safe to re-run: each configuration step is skipped if already in place, and an initialised cluster is left alone.

   ```bash
   make bao-init
   ```

   > **Move the unseal keys before you do anything else**
   >
   > `make bao-init` writes the unseal keys to `output/credentials/openbao-init.json` and the [operator login](<#operator-credential>) to `openbao-operator.json` beside it (mode `0600`, gitignored) — a plaintext copy of the keys to every secret the cluster holds, next to the [etcd encryption key](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md>). Copy both into a password manager that does not need this cluster to be running, then delete the key file. Losing the keys means the data is unrecoverable: no support line, no recovery flow.
2. Write the values that belong to outside accounts — the prompts follow [Quickstart step 11](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>). The generated paths need nothing: their `PushSecret`s write them once the store validates.

   ```bash
   make bao-secrets
   ```
3. Confirm the stores validate:

   ```bash
   kubectl get clustersecretstore
   ```

### Authenticating locally

```bash
kubectl -n openbao port-forward svc/openbao-active 8200:8200 &   # a standby rejects requests
export BAO_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200
bao login -method=userpass username=operator   # password from openbao-operator.json
```

### Storing and reading a secret

```bash
bao kv put kv/cert-manager/route53 access-key-id='AKIA...' secret-access-key='...'
printf '%s' '{"access-key-id":"AKIA...","secret-access-key":"..."}' \
  | bao kv put -mount=kv cert-manager/route53 -     # what make bao-secrets does: JSON on stdin
bao kv get kv/cert-manager/route53
```

### Rotating a credential

A typed value is rotated with `make bao-secrets`, which asks per existing path whether to overwrite it; a generated one by deleting its path, after which the `PushSecret` writes a whole new set within its `refreshInterval`.

1. Rotate the path. For a typed value, answer `y` for that path; the others are left alone. `FORCE=1 make bao-secrets` overwrites every ordinary path without asking; `kneadtime/config` still wants a typed `OVERWRITE`, and without a terminal every existing path is left alone.

   ```bash
   make bao-secrets
   ```

   For a generated path, delete it, [authenticated locally](<#authenticating-locally>). Every key in it changes, with the consequences the reading component's page lists — for `authentik/config` that is every session, token and platform OIDC client at once:

   ```bash
   bao kv metadata delete -mount=kv <path>
   ```
2. Push the new value into the `Secret` now rather than at the next `refreshInterval`: [force a sync](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md#usage>) of each `ExternalSecret` that reads it.
3. Restart whatever read the old value into an environment variable; a rotated `Secret` reaches a running pod only through a rollout.

## Health check

```bash
for pod in $(kubectl -n openbao get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=openbao -o name); do
  kubectl -n openbao exec "$pod" -- bao status
done
kubectl get clustersecretstore
kubectl get externalsecret -A
```

`bao status` should show `Initialized: true`, `Sealed: false`, and `HA Mode: active` on one pod with `standby` on the others; it exits `0` unsealed, `2` sealed and `1` unreachable. Every `ClusterSecretStore` should report `Ready=True`.

`prometheusrule.yaml` mails `OpenBaoSealed` per pod sealed past the rule's `for`, read from the `openbao-sealed` pod label, as a sealed pod reports Ready, and `OpenBaoNoActiveNode` when no unsealed active pod is scraped. Both [hold Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md#configuration>).

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Sealed after every restart, and Ready does not mean unsealed**
>
> OpenBao seals itself on every pod restart — node reboot, chart bump, Kured — and no auto-unseal is configured, so it stays shut until someone with the key shares unseals it. The readiness and liveness probes answer healthy while sealed (`sealedcode=204`), deliberately, so a rollout does not stop at the first pod waiting for keys; the cost is that only `bao status`, not `kubectl get pods`, can tell you OpenBao is usable. While sealed no `ExternalSecret` resolves, so cert-manager loses its Route53 credentials and nothing breaks until a certificate expires up to sixty days later, with no obvious link to the reboot. See [Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A `PushSecret` cannot add a key to a path `make bao-secrets` wrote**
>
> A path written before its `PushSecret` existed carries no `managed-by` metadata, so a new key on it fails with `secret not managed by external-secrets` and the `PushSecret` goes Degraded. The existing keys are unaffected. Mark the path as ESO's once, and the next reconcile adds the key: `bao kv metadata put -mount=kv -custom-metadata=managed-by=external-secrets <path>`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`#` and `!` on a command line**
>
> Inside double quotes an interactive bash expands `!` from history before the quotes are considered, and an unquoted `#` truncates the line. Both are silent and store a credential that does not work. Use single quotes, or write the secret as JSON and pass `@file` — a missing file then fails loudly.

## Recovery

### Unsealing after a restart

```bash
make bao-unseal
```

It feeds a threshold of shares from `output/credentials/openbao-init.json` to each sealed replica, waits for one that has not joined Raft yet, and is idempotent. With the key file deleted, which is the correct end state, unseal by hand:

```bash
for pod in $(kubectl -n openbao get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=openbao -o name); do
  kubectl -n openbao exec "$pod" -- bao status >/dev/null 2>&1
  case $? in
    0) echo "$pod: already unsealed" ;;
    2) for i in 1 2 3; do
         kubectl -n openbao exec -it "$pod" -- bao operator unseal
       done ;;
    *) echo "$pod: OpenBao did not answer, check the pod" ;;
  esac
done
```

A replica that says `Vault is not initialized` has not joined the Raft cluster — one that predates the `retry_join` stanzas or started before `openbao-0` was initialised. Point it at the leader once; it takes unseal keys afterwards:

```bash
kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-1 -- \
  bao operator raft join http://openbao-0.openbao-internal:8200
```

### Rolling out a new revision

`OnDelete` leaves a chart or config change's new `updateRevision` unapplied, and `KubeStatefulSetUpdateNotRolledOut` fires, until every pod restarts. Standbys first, the active replica last, so leadership moves once:

1. For a version bump, take a [snapshot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#openbao>) first; downgrading does not undo a data-store change.
2. Find the active replica and confirm all three are unsealed.

   ```bash
   for p in openbao-0 openbao-1 openbao-2; do echo "$p: $(kubectl -n openbao exec $p -c openbao -- bao status | grep -E '^(Sealed|HA Mode)' | tr -s ' ' | paste -sd ' ' -)"; done
   ```
3. Each standby in turn: delete the pod, wait for Ready, unseal it with `make bao-unseal`, and check it rejoined as a standby.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao delete pod openbao-0 && kubectl -n openbao wait --for=condition=Ready pod/openbao-0 --timeout=5m
   ```
4. The active replica last, the same way; a standby takes over.
5. Confirm the rollout.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao get sts openbao -o jsonpath='{.status.currentRevision} {.status.updateRevision}{"\n"}'
   ```

### Generating a root token

For what the operator policy does not cover — a policy, an auth method, a snapshot restore, or the operator login itself broken. Needs the operator login and a threshold of unseal shares; each step runs in the pod.

1. Log in as the operator; it prompts for the password from `openbao-operator.json`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- bao login -method=userpass username=operator
   ```
2. Generate a one-time password and start the attempt with it; note both the OTP and the nonce.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -generate-otp
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -init -otp=<otp>
   ```
3. Enter one share per run until the threshold is met; the last prints `Encoded Token`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -nonce=<nonce>
   ```
4. Decode it into the root token.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao operator generate-root -decode=<encoded-token> -otp=<otp>
   ```
5. Do the one job with it, then revoke it and clear the pod's token cache.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -i openbao-0 -- bao login -     # paste the root token, then Ctrl-D
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao token revoke -self
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- sh -c 'rm -f "$HOME/.bao-token"'
   ```

With the operator login gone too, no token can start an attempt: set `disable_unauthed_generate_root_endpoints = false` in the listener stanza in `application.yaml`, restart and unseal the pods, and drive the deprecated `sys/generate-root/*` API with the shares; revert the setting afterwards.

To recreate the operator login with that root token, put it as `root_token` into a copy of `openbao-init.json`, move `openbao-operator.json` aside, and run `make bao-rotate-root`, which writes a new password and revokes the token.

### Backups

A CronJob saves a Raft snapshot nightly; it, the snapshot by hand and the restore are in [Backups & Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#openbao>). A snapshot is encrypted with a key that exists only in the unseal shares, so it is exactly as recoverable as your key custody.

# Rook-Ceph

Distributed block storage using [Rook](<https://rook.io/>) as the Kubernetes operator for [Ceph](<https://ceph.io/>), the component that still has your data after a node dies; [why Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#rook-ceph-not-longhorn-or-local-volumes>). Never ignore a `WARN`.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `rook-ceph` |
| Depends on | A raw `rook-osd` partition on every worker, written at install time |
| If it is down | Every pod with a volume — `openbao` first, which turns a storage problem into a cluster problem |
| Health check | `make storage-check` — it binds a real PVC, which `ceph status` alone does not prove |
| UI | `rook.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/rook-ceph-operator/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/rook-ceph-operator>): the operator's `rook-ceph` chart, in `kustomization.yaml`. [`payload/platform/rook-ceph-cluster/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/rook-ceph-cluster>): the `rook-ceph-cluster` chart, whose `valuesObject` holds the `CephCluster`, the object store and the storage classes. [`payload/platform/rook-ceph/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/rook-ceph>): the CSI driver and its RBAC, the dashboards and the UI route |

## Configuration

### Disks

Each worker has a raw partition labelled `rook-osd`, created by Ignition as the **last** partition with whatever the root leaves, which Rook adds as an OSD; block data is replicated across them. `placement.all` leaves the control-plane taint untolerated, so no Ceph daemon runs beside etcd: their fsyncs on one disk stall each other. Its contents are wherever Ceph last wrote them, so inserting a partition ahead of it shifts its offset and takes the OSD data with it: changing the partition table is a [reinstall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md>), not an edit.

Ignition declares it with `format: none` and `wipe_filesystem: true`, because `ceph-volume` reads the BlueStore *signature*, not the partition table, and a reinstalled node would present an OSD from a cluster that no longer exists. Ceph declines any device that already carries a filesystem; see [No OSDs after reprovisioning](<#no-osds-after-reprovisioning>).

### Storage classes

| StorageClass | Provides | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rook-ceph-block` | RBD block volumes, cluster default | `ReadWriteOnce` only; `ReadWriteMany` needs CephFS, which is not enabled. Block PVs are deleted with their claim, and every Application prunes, so removing a PVC from Git removes the volume — see [Backups](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>) |
| `ceph-bucket` | S3 buckets from the object store | Reclaim `Retain`, so deleting a claim cannot delete the bucket |

### Object storage

A `CephObjectStore` provides an S3 endpoint at `http://rook-ceph-rgw-object-store.rook-ceph.svc`, so backups and log chunks live somewhere other than the block pool they protect. The infra Gateway publishes the same endpoint as `https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` for [Velero](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/index.md#configuration>), whose S3 client only signs cleanly over TLS. More than one RGW instance (`gateway.instances`) keeps a node reboot from stalling a backup, which only holds on separate nodes: `gateway.placement` carries the spread constraint, because `placement.all` belongs to the `CephCluster` and never reaches this CR. It is a hard one: every gateway is daemon `a`, so on one node Prometheus drops their counters, and the descheduler never evicts a `system-cluster-critical` pod to fix that. The data pool is erasure coded (`dataChunks` and `codingChunks`): less overhead than three replicas, safe at `failureDomain: host` only with more workers than chunks.

### Off-cluster reader

TrueNAS pulls the [off-cluster copy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#off-cluster-copy>) as one S3 user, `offsite-reader`, which owns the `offsite` bucket every backup writes into, so TrueNAS sees that bucket in its list.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `CephObjectStoreUser` in `rook-ceph/offsite-reader.yaml` | One key pair for the pull, in the Secret `rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-offsite-reader` and, through `bucketOwner`, in the `offsite-bucket` claim's Secret |
| `bucketOwner: offsite-reader` on `backup/offsite-bucket` | S3 lists only the buckets a user owns, and TrueNAS's Cloud Sync form picks the bucket from that list. A bucket has exactly one owner |
| Full `opMask` | Rook creates an owned bucket and sets its policy with the owner's own keys |
| `obcAllowAdditionalConfigFields` in `rook-ceph-operator/kustomization.yaml` | Rook ignores `bucketPolicy` and `bucketOwner` unless listed. `bucketOwner` hands a claim the keys of the user it names, so the `obc-bucket-owner` [admission policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) allows it on that one claim only |

### Backup writers

Each backup writes into the `offsite` bucket as its own S3 user, declared as a `CephObjectStoreUser` next to the job or database it belongs to, under the prefix `offsite/<user>/`. Adding a user is all it takes; nothing lists the writers by hand.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `allowUsersInNamespaces: ["*"]` on the store in `rook-ceph-cluster/application.yaml` | A user may live in any namespace, with `spec.clusterNamespace: rook-ceph`; Rook writes its keys to the Secret `rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-<user>` beside it (`AccessKey`, `SecretKey`, `Endpoint`) |
| Named `<namespace>.<purpose>` | The S3 user ID is the CR's name, one ID space for the whole cluster, and Rook hands a CR the keys of an existing user with that ID. A namespace name cannot contain a dot, so the prefix before it names exactly one namespace; the `object-store-user-scope` [admission policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) enforces it outside `rook-ceph` |
| `offsite-policy` CronJob in `backup/offsite-policy.yaml` | Every few minutes, writes the `offsite` claim's `bucketPolicy` from the users that exist: each may list the bucket and do anything under its own prefix. Ceph's bucket policies have no `${aws:username}` variable, so the policy is generated. Argo CD ignores the field, see `backup/application.yaml` |
| Listing is not per prefix | The S3 clients check the bucket before they touch their prefix, so every writer can list the object names of the others; it can read or change none of them |
| `offsite-reader` may get every object | An object belongs to the user that wrote it, not to the bucket's owner |

### Monitoring

In `rook-ceph-cluster/application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `monitoring.enabled` | Turns on the mgr `prometheus` module and lets the operator maintain a `ServiceMonitor`. Without it a degraded pool, a down OSD or a near-full cluster is invisible to Prometheus, and a full Ceph cluster stops accepting writes |
| `monitoring.createPrometheusRules` | Ships Ceph's own alerting rules as a `PrometheusRule`. Its CRD comes from the `prometheus-operator-crds` Application; a sync before it lands fails and is retried — see [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#crds>) |
| `monitoring.prometheusRuleOverrides` | `CephOSDDownHigh` gets a `for:` because upstream fires it, as critical, on the first evaluation with one OSD of a small cluster down, which a Rook upgrade's rolling OSD restart always is; an OSD that stays down still pages after it. `CephNodeDiskspaceWarning` and, under `cephConfig`, `mon_data_avail_warn` are lowered to the kubelet's image garbage-collection threshold: the mon store shares the root filesystem with the images, which the kubelet only prunes there |
| `cephClusterSpec.dashboard.prometheusEndpoint` | The dashboard's Prometheus link. The operator owns `mgr/dashboard/PROMETHEUS_API_HOST` and writes it from this field whenever it restarts the dashboard module, so the same key under `cephConfig` is blanked at the next operator restart |
| `cephClusterSpec.cephConfig` `mgr/dashboard/GRAFANA_*` | The Grafana link, through the mon config store, which the operator reapplies on every reconcile, rather than a one-off `ceph dashboard set-*` Job; the operator has no field for it |
| `mon_cluster_log_level: info` | The mons copy the cluster log to stderr, and at the `debug` default Rook's probes and the mgr's pgmap ticks flood [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>). Warnings and errors are unaffected |

Rook's Grafana dashboards are vendored in `grafana-dashboards.yaml` — see [Monitoring → Dashboards](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#dashboards>).

### CSI driver

The operator chart's ceph-csi-operator subchart deploys the RBD driver only once an `OperatorConfig` and a `Driver` CR tell it what to run; without them every PVC stays `Pending` on `ExternalProvisioning`. Rook's `ceph-csi-drivers` chart ships them, but its nodeplugin ClusterRole cannot drop the grants step 4 below cuts, so they live in `csi-driver.yaml`.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `csi-driver.yaml` in `rook-ceph`, with `SkipDryRunOnMissingResource` | The CRs need the ceph-csi-operator's CRDs, which arrive with the operator chart |
| `OperatorConfig` pointing at the chart's image-set `ConfigMap` | A chart bump moves every sidecar and the cephcsi image together |
| Driver name `rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com` | Derived from the namespace and must match the StorageClasses' `provisioner`. RBD is the only driver; CephFS is not enabled |
| More than one controller plugin replica, `RollingUpdate` without surge, a PodDisruptionBudget | A drain of the provisioner's node otherwise stalls every provision, attach, resize and snapshot until the pod reschedules. The operator already keeps the replicas on distinct nodes with required anti-affinity and runs every sidecar with leader election, so the `Driver` CR carries no spread constraint, and no field for one |
| `csi-rbac.yaml` | The ceph-csi-operator creates no ServiceAccounts, and `CSI_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_PREFIX` fixes their names. Without them the Deployment and DaemonSet create no pods |
| `$patch: delete` in `rook-ceph-operator/kustomization.yaml` | The subchart's `NetworkPolicy` allows every egress, and no value turns it off ([why that matters](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#network-policies>)); the one the operator creates for the controller plugin stays |

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`csi` values on the operator chart do nothing**
>
> Helm accepts values a chart no longer reads. Driver settings go in `csi-driver.yaml`.

`csi-rbac.yaml` is the RBD half of the ceph-csi-operator's `deploy/multifile/csi-rbac.yaml` at the version the rook-ceph chart pulls in; Renovate does not see it. To refresh it:

1. Fetch and rename:

   ```bash
   curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ceph/ceph-csi-operator/vX.Y.Z/deploy/multifile/csi-rbac.yaml \
     | sed -e 's/ceph-csi-operator-system/rook-ceph/' -e 's/ceph-csi-operator-//'
   ```
2. Keep only the rbd documents (CephFS, NFS and NVMe-oF are not enabled).
3. Re-indent the sequences for yamllint and prefix the cluster-scoped names.
4. Cut the nodeplugin ClusterRole back: drop `secrets`, `serviceaccounts` and `serviceaccounts/token`, and keep `get` on the `rook-csi-rbd-node` and `rook-csi-rbd-provisioner` Secrets in the `rbd-nodeplugin-r` Role. Its token sits on every node; upstream's grants serve only the encryption KMS providers, which nothing here uses, and minting any ServiceAccount's token is cluster-admin.

### cephx keys stay on aes

Ceph 20 warns about the legacy `aes` cipher, and every key here is deliberately on it: the kernel client krbd does not implement `aes256k`, so CSI keys moved to it make every `rbd map` fail with `map failed: (22) Invalid argument` while Ceph reports the rotation a success. Two ciphers in one cluster trigger `AUTH_EMERGENCY_CIPHERS_SET` and buy no security. In `rook-ceph-cluster/application.yaml`'s `valuesObject`:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `keyType: aes` | krbd cannot use anything else |
| `mon_auth_allow_insecure_key: "true"` | Its default differs between mons; one that says `false` refuses an OSD's start-up key fetch, and an OSD whose on-disk key predates a rotation then fails with `Permission denied` |
| `keyRotationPolicy: KeyGeneration` | Changing `keyType` alone never rotates existing keys while the policy is `Disabled` |
| `keyGeneration` | Rotation only triggers on an increase, so a generation can never be lowered to undo one |
| `healthCheck.muteHealthWarning` | The `AUTH_*` warnings would otherwise keep the Application `Degraded` while the data is healthy. Temporary: remove once RBD moves to the userspace `rbd-nbd` mounter and the keys can leave `aes` |

### SELinux

`hostpathRequiresPrivileged` in `rook-ceph-operator/kustomization.yaml` runs every Ceph daemon privileged: `container_t` may not write their hostPath data or use another pod's admin socket. The cost is in [Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>).

## Usage

### Requesting a volume

Any workload can claim the default class:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: my-app-data
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
```

Add `storageClassName: rook-ceph-block` to say so explicitly. A Deployment with two replicas sharing one RWO PVC schedules one pod and leaves the other in `ContainerCreating` with a multi-attach error.

### Requesting a bucket

Ask for an `ObjectBucketClaim`; Rook creates the bucket and writes a `ConfigMap` (`BUCKET_NAME`, `BUCKET_HOST`, `BUCKET_PORT`) and a `Secret` (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) sharing the claim's name:

```yaml
apiVersion: objectbucket.io/v1alpha1
kind: ObjectBucketClaim
metadata:
  name: my-app-bucket
  namespace: my-app
spec:
  generateBucketName: my-app
  storageClassName: ceph-bucket
```

No claim is copied off the cluster, so the `obc-backup-exempt` [admission policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) refuses one without the annotation `homelab.wlkr.ch/backup-exempt` and its reason, as Loki's carries. A backup does not get a bucket: it is a [backup writer](<#backup-writers>) in `offsite`.

### Quotas

A full object store stops every writer, so the `object-store-quota` [policy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) asks a new user outside `rook-ceph` for `spec.quotas.maxSize` and a new claim for `maxSize` in `additionalConfig`. It only warns until every object carries one.

### Dashboard login

The dashboard sits behind Authentik for `infra-users`, then asks for its own login. The only user is `admin`, and its password is the `rook-ceph-dashboard-password` Secret, which the operator writes back to Ceph whenever it restarts, undoing a password changed in the dashboard. For a password of your own, add a second user rather than changing `admin`.

```bash
kubectl -n rook-ceph get secret rook-ceph-dashboard-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
```

## Health check

### Is storage ready?

