```bash
make storage-check
```

Run it after the GitOps handover: a `CephCluster` reports `Ready` with no OSDs. It stops at the first missing link:

| Check | What its absence means |
| --- | --- |
| `CephCluster` is `Ready` | the cluster Application has not synced yet |
| an OSD pod is `Running` | Rook took no disk — see [No OSDs after reprovisioning](<#no-osds-after-reprovisioning>) |
| `ceph health` is not `HEALTH_ERR` | Ceph itself is unwell; `HEALTH_WARN` is allowed through |
| the CSI driver is registered | no `Driver` CR, so the ceph-csi-operator deployed nothing |
| node plugin and provisioner are up | usually a ServiceAccount the DaemonSet cannot find |
| a 1 GiB PVC binds and is cleaned up | the only check that proves the other five |

The PVC check waits `TIMEOUT` seconds (default in `scripts/storage-check.sh`); `NAMESPACE` and `CLASS` override where and what it asks for.

Ceph's own view, from the script's toolbox: `HEALTH_OK`, every OSD `up` and `in`:

```bash
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- ceph status
```

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Ceph warnings show as Degraded**
>
> ArgoCD maps `HEALTH_WARN` to Degraded, so `rook-ceph-cluster` reports Degraded for the whole of a warning; nothing else waits on it — see [GitOps](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md>).

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Rook skips tainted nodes**
>
> The operator neither creates nor updates an OSD on a node with a taint `placement.all` does not tolerate, `PreferNoSchedule` included, and logs `placement settings do not match`. [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) taints every node waiting for its reboot lock, so that taint is tolerated.

## Recovery

### No OSDs after reprovisioning

A node whose `rook-osd` partition still carries a previous cluster's BlueStore signature gets no OSD: the `CephCluster` reports `Ready` with `HEALTH_WARN`, `kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods -l app=rook-ceph-osd` is empty, and the first PVC — `data-openbao-0` on a fresh bootstrap — stays `Pending`.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **The old cluster's data is already gone**
>
> Once the mons that held the cluster map left with the old control plane, those OSDs cannot be re-adopted by anything. Take a backup off the disks *before* a rebuild if you need one.

1. Confirm the cause:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n rook-ceph logs job/rook-ceph-osd-prepare-<node> | tail -3
   # skipping device "nvme0n1p10" because it contains a filesystem "ceph_bluestore"
   # skipping osd.3: "..." belonging to a different ceph cluster "..."
   ```
2. Rebuild the node, steps 3 to 7 of [Rebuilding or repartitioning a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>): `make reinstall` only arms the PXE menu, and the [installer](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md>) wipes the disk when the node network-boots.
3. If the node cannot be rebuilt now, wipe the partition by hand over SSH. `wipefs` removes the signature Rook skips on; the `dd` removes the BlueStore label behind it. Address it by label, as Ignition does, rather than by the device name in the log:

   ```bash
   sudo wipefs -a /dev/disk/by-partlabel/rook-osd
   sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/disk/by-partlabel/rook-osd bs=1M count=200
   ```
4. Restart the operator so it recreates the `osd-prepare` jobs:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout restart deploy/rook-ceph-operator
   ```
5. Confirm an OSD per node and a binding PVC:

   ```bash
   make storage-check
   ```

# Security Policies

Five cluster-wide controls: Pod Security Admission, default-deny network policy in both directions, a host firewall on the nodes, no API token on the `default` ServiceAccount, and admission policies. The pattern is the same for all: measure first, enforce second. All five are enforced; [Rollout](<#rollout>) is how a batch of new network policies gets there.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` for the Application; it owns Namespace objects across the cluster |
| Depends on | [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md>) to enforce the network policies |
| If it is down | Nothing at the time; the labels and policies stay applied and only stop being corrected |
| Health check | See [Health check](<#health-check>) |
| Pruning | Enabled, except for the Namespaces: each carries `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false`, because pruning a Namespace deletes everything inside it, PVCs included. Pruning the rest keeps the Application from sitting OutOfSync on leftovers |
| Files | [`payload/platform/security/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/security>), the network policies one file per namespace under `network-policies/`, plus the CoreDNS PodDisruptionBudget — see [Components](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>) |

## Configuration

### Pod Security Admission

A namespace without labels gets the cluster default from `ansible/templates/admission.yaml.j2`: `enforce` at `baseline`, `audit` and `warn` at `restricted`. It reaches a control-plane node only at provisioning; see [Node hardening](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md#node-hardening>). It exempts only `kube-system`, which Cilium needs before Argo CD can label anything; an exemption skips `audit` and `warn` as well. Each namespace in `pod-security.yaml` carries three labels:

| Label | Set to | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enforce` | The level the namespace demonstrably needs | Rejects pods that violate it |
| `audit` | Stricter | Records violations in the [API server audit log](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/audit-logging/index.md>) |
| `warn` | Stricter | Warns whoever applies the manifest |

The level per namespace is in `pod-security.yaml`; the rule behind it:

| Enforce | Which namespaces | Why not stricter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `privileged` | Those with a component on the host: the CNI and control plane, Ceph's OSDs, node-exporter, Trivy's node-collector, the etcd jobs and Velero's node-agent, Alloy, Kured, `selinuxd` | Host networking, the host PID namespace, raw block devices, privileged containers or a hostPath under the kubelet, etcd, log or SELinux directories, all of which `baseline` forbids. node-exporter has its own namespace so the monitoring stack need not follow it |
| `baseline` | Those with a container that starts as root or escalates: Grafana's `init-chown-data`, the runners and their job pods, and the operators not yet checked against `restricted` | Reduced when the chart offers a non-root path, one namespace at a time |
| `restricted` | Everything else, and the namespaces that run no pods | — |

`privileged` here means "not yet reduced", not "unexamined": `audit` and `warn` are still `baseline` or `restricted` on all of them. Namespace objects are owned by this Application so the labels stay declarative rather than drifting after `CreateNamespace=true`. `cilium-secrets` is the exception: the Cilium chart creates it, so its labels are `secretsNamespaceLabels` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml`, and a second owner would fight the first. Workload namespaces label themselves in the workloads repository, and `namespace-privileged-allowed` keeps them off `privileged`.

### Network policies

One file per namespace in `network-policies/`, holding that namespace's `CiliumNetworkPolicy` objects. A namespace gets two whole-namespace policies, `default-ingress` and `default-egress`, so every pod in it is default-deny in both directions, plus one policy per workload that needs more than the rest of the namespace does. Each policy's `description` is the record of who may connect and why; the rules are not repeated here. `cluster-wide.yaml` holds the `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` objects: the rules every pod gets, so a namespace file is the record of what its namespace may do *beyond* those.

#### Why CiliumNetworkPolicy and not NetworkPolicy

Two kinds of traffic have no pod identity a standard `NetworkPolicy` can name: Gateway traffic, which reaches a backend from the per-node Envoy, and kubelet health probes, which come from the node. A plain default-deny therefore kills ingress *and* probes, and the pods restart forever. Cilium's `fromEntities` names them: `ingress` for Envoy-proxied traffic, `host` and `remote-node` for the kubelet.

#### Cluster-wide rules

A rule that is word-for-word the same in every namespace file is lifted into `cluster-wide.yaml`, selecting every endpoint that has a namespace, not `{}`, which also takes the Gateway's `reserved:ingress` and health endpoints. `enableDefaultDeny` is off in both directions, since a cluster-wide egress rule would otherwise close every pod of a namespace without policies. DNS is the only rule lifted; the intra-namespace and node-probe rules stay in the namespace files.

The second policy there, `init`, is for the seconds before the agent has resolved a new pod's labels: the pod carries the reserved `init` identity, which no namespace policy selects. It admits the node, DNS out and DNS in, nothing else.

The third, `cnpg-backups`, selects every CloudNativePG pod by its `cnpg.io/cluster` label and admits only the object store, by the same two rules Velero's namespace has. Every database's backup sidecar needs exactly that, wherever the database runs, so one policy replaces a rule per workload.

The fourth, `default-deny`, closes every pod outside `kube-system` in both directions except the node and DNS, so a namespace that ships no `default-*` policies is closed until it allows what it needs; namespaces with them are unchanged.

#### What every policy contains

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Ingress from within the namespace | Replicas, sidecars and a workload's own database talk to each other on ports that change with the chart |
| Ingress from `host` and `remote-node` | Kubelet probes come from the node, and so do the API server's webhook calls, the aggregation layer and `kubectl port-forward`; all of them carry the node's identity, on a control-plane node with the `kube-apiserver` label as well |
| Ingress from `ingress` | Only where an HTTPRoute sends the Gateway's Envoy straight at the namespace; a namespace behind the Authentik outpost admits `authentik` instead. Kept at L4: the HTTPRoute is already the L7 filter for that traffic |
| Ingress from `monitoring` on the scraped port, `GET /metrics` | The one port a ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor names, at L7, so the scraper can open nothing else |
| Egress within the namespace, and to `kube-apiserver` where there is a Kubernetes client | The `kube-apiserver` entity is the endpoints behind `kubernetes.default`; no pod uses the kube-vip address. DNS is not repeated: the cluster-wide rule above sends every lookup through the proxy, which is what makes `toFQDNs` work and every lookup visible in Hubble |
| Egress to external names as `toFQDNs` | A name reads as the dependency it is; an address does not. The Gateway's own addresses count as external: a pod calling `auth.k8s.wlkr.ch` is classified `world`, not `ingress` |
| Egress to the backend pod as well, when the name is one the Gateway serves | The Gateway's Envoy checks the caller's egress policy a second time, against the backend pod it picked and that pod's port, and answers `403 Access denied` itself when no rule matches; audit mode never sees it. The OIDC clients of Authentik carry both rules |
| HTTP rules on plaintext ports, ingress side only | A request crossing a namespace boundary is proxied once, by the receiving node. TLS and gRPC ports stay at L4; the proxy cannot read them. A machine caller gets the methods and paths Hubble recorded; a browser UI behind the Authentik outpost stays at `http: [{}]`. The path is matched with its query string: a rule anchored with `$` names the query as well, as OpenBao's `/v1/sys/metrics\?format=prometheus$` does |

Host-networked pods (Cilium, kube-vip, the control plane, node-exporter, Tetragon, the CSI node plugins) have no endpoint of their own and cannot be selected; to everything else they are `host` or `remote-node`. `kube-system` therefore covers only its pod-networked workloads, each selected by label.

A chart's own `NetworkPolicy` objects are switched off in its values (`argocd`), or deleted after rendering where no value does (`rook-ceph-operator`): Cilium unions them, so a chart rule allowing everything overrides the default-deny.

### Host firewall

Pod policies cannot select a host-networked port. A `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` with a `nodeSelector` can, and Cilium's [host firewall](<https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/host-firewall/>) enforces it on the native device and `cilium_host`. What each port is for is the policy's `description`; [Host Firewall Inventory 2026-10-30](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/host-firewall-inventory-2026-10-30/index.md>) is the evidence.

| Behaviour | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Only packets addressed to a node IP are checked | The kube-vip address counts on the node holding it; Gateway addresses and NodePorts are translated first, so their policy is the backend pod's |
| A node with no selecting policy is not denied anything on IPv4 | The switch can merge alone, and reverting the policy needs no second rollout |
| No rule in a direction leaves that direction unenforced | A host policy with `ingress` only never blocks a node's own connections, and their replies pass through conntrack |
| Host endpoint labels are filtered | `kubernetes.io/hostname` is not among them, so a node can only be chosen by a label such as `node-access` in the upstream example, or by the `control-plane` role label |
| A pod reaching another node's IP is masqueraded to its own node | The target sees `remote-node`, so the firewall can tell the LAN from the cluster but not Prometheus from any other pod; the source pod's egress policy decides that |
| A connection a node opened before its agent started has no conntrack entry | For about half a minute after a boot the firewall drops the replies to it, typically the kubelet's first connection to the control-plane address, which Cilium sees as `world`; the client reconnects and nothing else is lost |

`network-policies/host-firewall.yaml` selects every node without `host-firewall.wlkr.ch/exempt`, so a new node is filtered from its first boot and the label is the one switch that frees a node. It denies the LAN everything but SSH, the API server, DHCP and ping, and admits the whole cluster to every port, since a narrower cluster rule could not name Prometheus and could lock out a node. The LAN reaches etcd only from the control-plane addresses of the inventory, so a control plane at a new address needs its `/32` here before it joins. A refused source mails [`HostFirewallDrops`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>). The rollout is in [Host Firewall Rollout 2026-11-18](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/host-firewall-rollout-2026-11-18/index.md>).

### Default ServiceAccount tokens

A pod that names no `serviceAccountName` lands on `default` and gets an API token it has no use for, so `default-serviceaccounts.yaml` sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on it in every namespace with nothing to preserve, empty namespaces included. Left out: `kube-system`, where the control plane authenticates with client certificates. `authentik-server` runs on `default` by chart default and is covered: Authentik's Kubernetes calls are worker tasks, which run under the `authentik` account.

The same rule applies to a chart workload whose own ServiceAccount has no binding — Alertmanager, Cilium's Envoy and Argo CD's HAProxy switch the mount off in their values — unless the process needs the in-cluster config to start at all ([the External Secrets webhook](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/external-secrets/index.md#configuration>)) or the chart offers no switch (Rook's `rook-ceph-default` and `rook-ceph-rgw`).

### Agent RBAC

`claude-agent-rbac.yaml` gives the in-cluster Claude Code agents two ClusterRoles for the `claude-reader` and `claude-writer` ServiceAccounts of the `claude-homelab` namespace, the one session with cluster access. Cluster-scoped RBAC cannot come from the `apps` project.

| Role | Bound | Grants | Leaves out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-agent-read` | Cluster-wide, to both ServiceAccounts | `get`, `list`, `watch` on named core, workload and CRD kinds, `pods/log` included | Secrets, RBAC, webhooks, CRDs, `pods/exec`, Trivy's exposed-secret reports |
| `claude-agent-write` | Nowhere by the platform: the workloads repository adds a RoleBinding in each namespace a writer session may change | Create, update, patch and delete on pods, workloads, Services, ConfigMaps, jobs, autoscalers and disruption budgets | The above, plus PersistentVolumeClaims (deleting one deletes data), NetworkPolicies and routes (they change who may reach what, which is a pull request) |

- **Creating a pod reads every Secret in its namespace.** That is why the write role is bound per namespace, and the `apps` project cannot place a RoleBinding in the namespaces its [destinations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/argocd/index.md#projects>) exclude.
- **Each session is a `claude-<session>` namespace** declared in `pod-security.yaml`; `namespace-name-guard` keeps the `apps` project from creating one, so a new session is a platform pull request first. It reaches only its own [OpenBao prefix](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kubernetes-auth>), host name and certificate.
- **`claude-writer-pod-limits`** in `admission-policies.yaml` refuses any pod or pod template from a `claude-writer` ServiceAccount that uses the host's network, PID or IPC namespace, a `hostPath` volume, a privileged container, or a ServiceAccount other than `default` or the one the workload already runs as. A namespace without a Pod Security level allows all of those, and another ServiceAccount's token is that account's RBAC.
- **`pods/log` is cluster-wide**, so the reader sees whatever any component logs, platform namespaces included. Triage needs it, and a cluster-wide grant cannot leave out namespaces.

Kinds are listed, never wildcarded, so a new CRD is invisible to the agents until someone adds it.

### Admission policies

Trivy reports a bad image after it is running; `admission-policies.yaml` refuses or records it at admission with built-in `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy`, and one `MutatingAdmissionPolicy`, not a policy engine. The image policies match Pods, ephemeral containers and every controller producing them, so a bad Deployment fails at `kubectl apply`, not in its ReplicaSet. The others close what RBAC and the `apps` project cannot express.

| Policy | Action | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image-tag-pinned` | `Deny` | A tag other than `latest`, or a digest: an unpinned image is one Renovate can neither track nor roll back |
| `image-registry-allowed` | `Deny` | The registries the cluster pulls from; a reference with no registry counts as `docker.io` |
| `claude-writer-pod-limits` | `Deny` | Host access and borrowed ServiceAccounts from the agent writer, see [Agent RBAC](<#agent-rbac>) |
| `namespace-privileged-allowed` | `Deny` | A Namespace may carry `enforce: privileged` only if it is in the policy's list, the `privileged` rows above. The `apps` project creates its own Namespaces and their labels, so without it a workload could opt out of Pod Security |
| `authentik-foreign-objects` | `Deny` | In `authentik`, an object an Argo CD Application applied must come from `authentik` or `security`: blueprints run with full Authentik rights, and Argo CD cannot deny a project one namespace's kinds. Objects without a tracking annotation are not matched |
| `namespace-name-guard` | `Deny` | A platform namespace, `kube-*`, `velero` or `claude-<session>` may be applied only by a platform Application: `apps` creates Namespaces, so a workload could otherwise relabel a platform one or take a name [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kubernetes-auth>) reaches by prefix |
| `priority-class-scope` | `Deny` | Outside the platform namespaces a pod takes `batch` or no [priority class](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#priority-classes>), so a workload cannot have the platform evicted first |
| `obc-bucket-owner` | `Deny` | Only `backup/offsite-bucket` may set `bucketOwner` on an `ObjectBucketClaim`, and only to `offsite-reader`. Rook hands a claim the keys of the user it names, so any other claim could take over any S3 user, Rook's internal ones included — see [Off-cluster reader](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#off-cluster-reader>) |
| `object-store-user-scope` | `Deny` | Outside `rook-ceph`, a `CephObjectStoreUser` is named `<namespace>.<purpose>` and carries no admin `capabilities`. Its name is its S3 user ID, so a free choice would hand one namespace another's keys — see [Backup writers](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>) |
| `cnpg-cluster-backed-up` | `Deny` | A CloudNativePG `Cluster` names the Barman Cloud plugin as its WAL archiver |
| `cnpg-objectstore-offsite` | `Deny` | A Barman Cloud `ObjectStore` writes to `s3://offsite/<namespace>.<purpose>/`, the prefix TrueNAS pulls |
| `obc-backup-exempt` | `Deny` | A new `ObjectBucketClaim` says why it needs no backup; nothing copies a bucket off the cluster |
| `object-store-quota` | `Audit` and `Warn` | A new object store user or `ObjectBucketClaim` sets a size limit, see [Quotas](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#quotas>) |
| `certificate-issuer-scope` | `Deny` | Who may use a ClusterIssuer, see [Issuer scope](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md#issuer-scope>) |
| `controller-pod-limits` | `Deny` | No pods from the cert-manager controller, no host access for CloudNativePG's, see [Pods from the controllers](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md#pods-from-the-controllers>) |
| `route-hostnames-reserved` | `Deny` | Who may claim the platform, `ssh` and wollbi names on a route, see [Route hostnames](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md#route-hostnames>) |
| `gateway-namespace-scope` | `Deny` | Only `kube-system` holds Gateways: external-dns publishes a route at its [Gateway's](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/gateway-api/index.md>) target |
| `selinuxd-memory-request` | Mutate | Lowers `selinuxd`'s fixed memory request, see [Security Profiles Operator](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-profiles-operator/index.md#configuration>) |

`cnpg-cluster-backed-up`, `cnpg-objectstore-offsite` and `obc-backup-exempt` [keep a backup from being forgotten](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#off-cluster-copy>): each yields to the annotation `homelab.wlkr.ch/backup-exempt` with the reason as its value, and none checks an object being deleted, so an operator's finalizer removal still goes through.

All but three carry `failurePolicy: Ignore`: an expression that errors lets the request through rather than stopping every pod. `claude-writer-pod-limits` and `controller-pod-limits` fail closed, since they match only named identities, and `selinuxd-memory-request` because a `selinuxd` pod at full request preempts others.

## Usage

### Adding a registry

A pod from a registry outside the list is refused. If the registry is intended, add it to the regular expression in `image-registry-allowed`.

### Tightening a namespace

1. See what running pods a stricter level would reject, without changing anything:

   ```bash
   kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns cert-manager \
     pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
   ```
2. Catch what is not running right now, such as a CronJob, from the `audit` label's records over the full Loki retention window, in Grafana:

   ```text
   {job="kubernetes-audit"} |= "pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-violations"
   ```
3. Raise `enforce` in `pod-security.yaml`.

### Rollout

A new policy is enforced on arrival: `policyAuditMode` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml` is off. Switched on, it makes every agent evaluate each verdict and log it with `AUDIT` instead of dropping, and those verdicts reach Loki the way drops do. The mode is cluster-wide, so while it is on the older policies are not enforced either, which is why a batch of new policies goes through it together.

1. Merge the values change; the agents roll on their own. `Enabled` on every node before anything else merges:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/cilium
   kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- cilium-dbg config get PolicyAuditMode
   ```
2. Merge the policies and let them run for a week. What enforcement would have refused, by namespace pair:

   ```promql
   sum by (source_namespace, destination_namespace) (increase(hubble_policy_verdicts_total{action="audit"}[7d]))
   ```

   and flow by flow, in Grafana:

   ```text
   {job="hubble", verdict="AUDIT"} | json | line_format "{{.flow_source_namespace}}/{{.flow_source_pod_name}} -> {{.flow_destination_namespace}}/{{.flow_destination_pod_name}} {{.flow_l4_TCP_destination_port}}{{.flow_l4_UDP_destination_port}}"
   ```
3. Add a rule for every audited flow that is legitimate. Layer 7 rules are never audited: a request an HTTP rule does not match is answered `403` on the spot, which is why a new policy carries `http: [{}]` — proxied and recorded, nothing refused — until the week's requests have been read:

   ```text
   {job="hubble"} | json | flow_l7_http_method != "" | line_format "{{.flow_source_namespace}} -> {{.flow_destination_namespace}}:{{.flow_l4_TCP_destination_port}} {{.flow_l7_http_method}} {{.flow_l7_http_url}}"
   ```
4. Tighten each `http: [{}]` to the methods and paths seen, set `policyAuditMode: false`, which rolls the agents again. The first week's reading is [Network Policy Audit 2026-09-27](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/network-policy-audit-2026-09-27/index.md>), the reading before the flip [Network Policy Audit 2026-10-16](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/network-policy-audit-2026-10-16/index.md>). From then on the verdict to watch is `DROPPED`, live or from Loki — see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#health-check>) — and the [`HubblePolicyDrops`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>) alert mails each refused connection.

If a single endpoint needs the same treatment later, audit mode can be set on it alone, until the agent restarts:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- \
  cilium-dbg endpoint config <endpoint-id> PolicyAuditMode=Enabled
```

### Changing the host firewall

A rule that might lock out a node is tried in audit mode first. Audit is a setting of the running agent, not of the policy, and an agent restart drops it, so set it per node and expect to set it again after any restart:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec <agent-on-node> -c cilium-agent -- \
  sh -c 'cilium-dbg endpoint config $(cilium-dbg endpoint get -l reserved:host -o "jsonpath={\$[0].id}") PolicyAuditMode=Enabled'
```

What enforcement would refuse: audit verdicts addressed to a host identity. Pods and nodes are admitted, so anything here came from the LAN.

```text
{job="hubble", verdict="AUDIT"} | json dst_id="flow.destination.identity", src="flow.IP.source", dst="flow.IP.destination", tcp="flow.l4.TCP.destination_port", udp="flow.l4.UDP.destination_port" | dst_id="1" | line_format "{{.src}} -> {{.dst}} {{.tcp}}{{.udp}}"
```

Then restart the agent to enforce again. `policyAuditMode` in the Cilium values is not the switch: it stops enforcing every pod policy too.

## Health check

```bash
kubectl get ns -L pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce
kubectl get cnp -A
kubectl get ccnp
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy,mutatingadmissionpolicy
```

## Pitfalls

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Audit mode stops at the proxy**
>
> `policyAuditMode` is a datapath setting. A request the Gateway's Envoy or an HTTP rule refuses is answered `403 Access denied` on the spot, and Hubble records it as a forwarded response, not an audited verdict. Look for it with `hubble observe --http-status 403`; in Loki the denied request is a `DROPPED` flow of type `REQUEST` whose source carries the caller's namespace and the `ingress` identity. A gRPC caller sees `server: envoy` and `grpc-message: Access denied`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **A name rule audits one SYN in twenty**
>
> A `toFQDNs` rule admits the addresses the DNS proxy has seen for the name, and the proxy releases the answer after at most 100ms whether or not every datapath has the new address. About one connection in twenty to a CDN name is recorded `AUDIT` with a `world` destination; under enforcement that `SYN` drops and the retransmit a second later goes through. A run of drops on one source port is different: the application connected to an address it cached past the DNS TTL.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The token change is not retroactive**
>
> The mount is decided at admission, so existing pods keep their token until recreated. That makes the change safe to roll out, and means a posture scan will not agree it is fixed until things restart.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **A reboot can isolate a node a host policy selects**
>
> [Upstream](<https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/48070>) reports a selected node on this same combination, tunnel, kube-proxy replacement and WireGuard, dropping everything after a cold boot or a runtime audit-off, until an out-of-band fix. It is open and has not reproduced here. A power cut would hit every node at once, and the [lockout runbook](<#host-firewall-lockout>) is the way back.

## Recovery

### Host firewall lockout

Work down until the node answers. An agent that cannot reach the API server hears neither a policy change nor a label removal, so step 1 alone does not free a node that is already cut off.

1. API server answering: take the node out of the policy. Argo CD does not own node labels, so nothing puts it back; remove the label once the cause is fixed. Use `--all` instead of a name for every node.

   ```bash
   kubectl label node <node> host-firewall.wlkr.ch/exempt=true
   ```
2. SSH answering: put the node in audit mode, which needs no API server and lasts until the agent restarts.

   ```bash
   ssh core@<node> sudo bash -s <<'EOF'
   id=$(crictl ps -q --label io.kubernetes.container.name=cilium-agent)
   crictl exec "$id" sh -c 'cilium-dbg endpoint config $(cilium-dbg endpoint get -l reserved:host -o "jsonpath={\$[0].id}") PolicyAuditMode=Enabled'
   EOF
   ```
3. Nothing answering, the API server up: nothing filters a node until its agent has started after boot, so stop the agent coming back. Run this from the workstation, then power-cycle the node, then do step 1 and start the kubelet again with `sudo systemctl unmask kubelet && sudo systemctl start kubelet`.

   ```bash
   until ssh -o ConnectTimeout=2 core@<node> sudo systemctl mask --now kubelet; do sleep 1; done
   ```
4. Every control plane cut off: the API server needs no CNI, so it comes up before the agent does. Power-cycle all three and exempt every node in that window.

   ```bash
   until kubectl label node --all host-firewall.wlkr.ch/exempt=true; do sleep 2; done
   ```
5. Still nothing: at the node's console, add `flatcar.autologin` to the boot entry in the GRUB menu, since `core` has no password, then run the inner command of step 2. Failing that, [rebuild the node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>).
6. Then [unseal OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#after-any-node-reboot-unseal-openbao>) and revert in Git: the policy first; the switch only if the firewall itself is the fault, since that revert rolls every agent again.

# Security Profiles Operator

The [Security Profiles Operator](<https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/security-profiles-operator>) (SPO) turns a `SelinuxProfile` object into a policy module on every node: a `spod` DaemonSet runs `selinuxd` beside the host's policy store, and a pod then uses `<profile>.process` as its `seLinuxOptions.type`. It carries the modules the nodes need to move from permissive to enforcing; their denials are in [Node hardening](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md#node-hardening>). It also installs a [seccomp profile](<#seccomp>); AppArmor and the log enricher are off.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `security-profiles-operator` |
| Depends on | [cert-manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cert-manager/index.md>): the operator creates a self-signed Issuer and the webhook certificate itself |
| If it is down | No profile is installed or changed; modules already loaded stay loaded |
| Health check | `kubectl -n security-profiles-operator get spod,pods` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/security-profiles-operator/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/security-profiles-operator>), [`payload/platform/security/network-policies/security-profiles-operator.yaml`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/blob/main/payload/platform/security/network-policies/security-profiles-operator.yaml>) |

## Configuration

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `selinuxd-memory-request` in `admission-policies.yaml` | `selinuxd`'s fixed memory request at node-critical priority preempts pods on a full node; the policy lowers it at pod creation |
| `customTemplatesConfigMap` | The bundled templates do not load on Flatcar; see [Templates](<#templates>) |
| `selinux.options.deniedTypes` | Upstream's recommended kernel-memory types: profiles come from denials, so a logged kernel-memory access must not become a rule |
| `daemonUpdateStrategy` | A daemon that fails on Flatcar, which [upstream does not test](<#pitfalls>), stops the rollout at its first node |
| `selinuxdImage.default` | The chart's `el9` image, its digest tracked by its own Renovate manager: Flatcar matches none of the operator's OS patterns, and the default's RHEL 8 tooling fails there |
| Enricher, AppArmor, BPF recorder left off | Recording needs `auditd` and a log file the nodes do not have; the denials are in Loki |
| `replicaCount` | A second replica keeps a drain from stopping reconciliation |
| `resources` | Chart defaults, unmeasured; re-measure against the [2.5x rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>) once `SelinuxProfile` objects exist, since the manager caches every profile and pod |
| `enforce: privileged` on the namespace | `selinuxd` is privileged and mounts the host's SELinux directories; see [Pod Security](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#pod-security-admission>) |
| Network policy | Operator, daemon and webhook only reach the API server; Prometheus scrapes the daemon's ServiceMonitor |

### Policy store

Flatcar's `/var/lib/selinux` is a symlink into the read-only `/usr`, where `selinuxd` cannot install anything. `selinux-policy-store.service` in `butane_node_config.yaml.j2` replaces it with a copy before the kubelet starts. After a Flatcar update it copies again but keeps the profiles' modules, at priorities Flatcar does not ship: `selinuxd`'s datastore survives the reboot and never reinstalls them. The `spod` init container rebuilds them against the new base.

### Templates

`selinuxd-templates.yaml` replaces the image's template set, which does not load on Flatcar: it names two Fedora attributes Flatcar lacks and a `proc_type` rule Flatcar's `neverallow` rules forbid. `base_container.cil` is generated from a node's own `container` module by the skill's `gen_base_template.py`, because Flatcar grants most of `container_t`'s rights to the type itself: a profile's type starts with all of them and adds its own. `flatcar_runtime.cil` lets the container runtime, which runs as `kernel_t` here, start an `spc_t` container that sets `no_new_privs`. The daemon reads the files once, so a change takes a new ConfigMap name. To test one, run the `el9` image's `semodule -n -i` against a copy of a node's `/var/lib/selinux` and `/etc/selinux`: `-n` builds without loading.

## Usage

A profile is one entry in `profiles.yaml`, written from the denials Loki holds by the `selinux-denials` skill, which also says when `spc_t` or a host-path label needs no profile.

1. Merge the profile and wait for `kubectl get selinuxprofile <name>` to show `Installed`.
2. Then set `seLinuxOptions.type: <name>.process` on the pod, in a second merge: a pod whose type a node does not know cannot start, and a container with its own type gets its own level and loses the pod's volumes.

### Seccomp

`runtime-default-log` in `seccomp-profiles.yaml` is the runtime's default profile with the log flag: the same refusals, each now a `SECCOMP` record in [Loki](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>). A pod opts in with `localhostProfile: operator/runtime-default-log.json`, merged after the profile shows `Installed`. Authentik's server and worker and [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) do.

- **Only for containers that drop every capability**: the runtime adds syscalls per capability, this copy has none.
- **It goes stale.** After a containerd update, regenerate it with the `selinux-denials` skill's `gen_seccomp_profile.py` from `.info.runtimeSpec.linux.seccomp` of such a container's `crictl inspect`.
- **A record names no pod**: match `subj`'s category pair with `ps -eZ`.
- **`clone3` is missing from Loki.** The profile refuses it so glibc falls back to `clone`, and [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) drops those records. Every record stays in the node's journal:

  ```bash
  ssh core@<node> sudo journalctl _AUDIT_TYPE=1326 --since -1h
  ```

## Health check

| Check | Healthy |
| --- | --- |
| `kubectl -n security-profiles-operator get spod spod` | `STATE` is `RUNNING` |
| `kubectl -n security-profiles-operator get ds spod` | one pod per node, including the control planes |
| `kubectl get selinuxprofile,seccompprofile` | every profile `Installed` |

## Pitfalls

- **Two policy files.** `selinuxd` writes `policy.33`, the kernel's version, beside the shipped `policy.35`; a `semodule -B` with the host's tools rewrites only the latter, and the node then boots the stale one.
- **Upstream does not test it.** Its Flatcar end-to-end job runs with `E2E_TEST_SELINUX=false`.
- **A fresh node has no profiles** until its `spod` pod runs; whatever a node needs to boot belongs in the node template.
- **`keycreate: invalid argument` at sandbox creation**: the node's store lost a profile `selinuxd` records as installed; a new `spod` pod there reinstalls them all.

# Tetragon

[Tetragon](<https://tetragon.io/>) watches processes at the kernel, with eBPF, on every node. Trivy says what an image *could* do; Tetragon records what a process *did*: every exec and exit in a pod, and, where a `TracingPolicy` says so, file opens and credential changes. It is the only thing here that sees a shell spawned in a running container.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `kube-system` |
| Depends on | Kernel BTF at `/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux`, which Flatcar ships; [Logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) for the events, [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the alerts |
| If it is down | No runtime record and no runtime alerts; nothing else notices |
| Health check | See [Health check](<#health-check>); `TetragonPolicyNotLoaded` and `TetragonEventsLost` otherwise |
| Dashboard | [Tetragon](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch/d/tetragon-overview>): agent health, event rates and the latest policy hits, shells and execs from Loki |
| Files | [`payload/platform/tetragon/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/tetragon>): the chart, the policies, `prometheusrule.yaml` and a dashboard written for this cluster, since upstream ships none |

## Configuration

Cilium's own chart, from `helm.cilium.io`; Tetragon does not depend on Cilium and runs privileged on the host network by the chart's default.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Export to stdout | The chart runs a sidecar that tails Tetragon's JSON file to stdout, so [Alloy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md>) collects it as any container log: `{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"}` |
| `exportDenyList` | Exec and exit events from the host and from the platform's own `kube-system` pods, selected by label, stay out of the export, being most of the volume. Any other pod in `kube-system` is exported, because a stolen write role lands its privileged pod there. Policy hits still pass, which is the point of the `event_set` field |
| `redactionFilters` | Passwords, private keys and URL credentials in exec arguments are replaced before the export, which puts every argument in Loki; Hubble's counterpart is [`hubble.redact`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>) |
| `seLinuxOptions.type: spc_t` | SELinux refuses `container_t` the agent's BPF loads, tracefs mount and other processes' `/proc` |
| `enableProcessCred` | Capabilities and `privileges_changed` on every exec, so a setuid or file-capability escalation is visible without a policy |
| Agent metrics port | Moved off the chart's default, which is the port kube-vip binds on the same host network; see [Control-plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md#the-handover>). The Prometheus egress rule in `monitoring.yaml` names it too |
| Two `ServiceMonitor`s | `tetragon_policy_events_total` is what the alert reads; `tetragon_tracingpolicy_loaded` and the ring-buffer counters are its health |
| `ServerSideDiff=true` annotation | The `TracingPolicy` CRD defaults fields no manifest sets, which a client-side diff reads as drift. It costs a dry-run apply per resource per reconcile: the `dryRun=All` patches in the audit log |
| Memory limit | 2.5x the measured working set of the busiest agent, per the [platform rule](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#components>); the dashboard's first row shows the current worst node against it |

### Policies

`tracingpolicies.yaml` carries the cluster-scoped `TracingPolicy` objects, adapted from the [upstream policy library](<https://tetragon.io/docs/policy-library/observability/>). All post at most one event per minute per selector, and most watch containers only, since the host has the node journal; `sensitive-file-access` and the taint hook of `kernel-module-load` record the host too. Every hook carries a `message` and an `observability.*` tag.

| Policy | Hook | Fires on | Alerted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sensitive-file-access` | `security_file_permission` | A read of control-plane, etcd or kubelet key material, an admin kubeconfig or the encryption config, matched by the end of the path so a hostPath mounted anywhere counts; a read of `/etc/shadow` on the host; any write to the account, sudoers, cron, `ld.so.preload` or root SSH files. What touches these by design is exempted per selector in `tracingpolicies.yaml`, the backup Jobs and build pods in the alert, so what remains is someone reading secrets | Yes: `TetragonSensitiveFileAccess` |
| `process-creds-changed` | `commit_creds` | A container process that moved into another mount, pid, network or user namespace after its exec, except `runc`; the alert leaves out the `cilium` DaemonSet in `kube-system` and all of `rook-ceph`, whose init containers and OSD prepare Jobs `nsenter` into the host by design, and `/proc/self/exe` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which is buildah re-executing itself into [its user namespace](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>). The hook runs on every execve and fork; the selector keeps the escape signal. Upstream's `matchCapabilityChanges` is not used: it matches a change in either direction, so every entrypoint that drops root fires it | Yes: `TetragonCredentialsEscalated` |
| `exec-from-writable-path` | `security_bprm_check` | A container executing a file under `/tmp/`, `/var/tmp/`, `/dev/shm/`, `/run/`, `/var/run/`, `/shared/`, `/controller/` or `/plugins/`, except the two binaries an init container copies there and the scripts s6-overlay writes under `/run/s6*` and `/run/service/` at start; the alert leaves out `go` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which runs the test binaries it builds under `/tmp` | Yes: `TetragonExecFromWritablePath` |
| `library-from-writable-path` | `security_mmap_file` | The same paths mapped with `PROT_EXEC`, which is how a dropped shared library loads, except the native libraries runtimes unpack under `/tmp` on every start: Alloy's Snowflake driver (`/tmp/gosnowflake-cgo*`) and zstd-jni in Dependency-Track (`/tmp/libzstd-jni-*`); the alert leaves out `go` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods | Yes: `TetragonLibraryFromWritablePath` |
| `privileges-raise`, `privileges-raise-gid`, `privileges-raise-gid-argocd` | The `__sys_set*uid` and `__sys_set*gid` family | Any setuid or setgid to root inside a container. A record: root re-asserting root is routine (`logrotate`), and a setuid binary that actually raises privileges is `TetragonPrivilegedExec`. `runc`, which sets the ids on every container start, is dropped in the kernel. The redis-ha busybox calls setgid on every applet, so the gid hooks leave out pods labelled `app: redis-ha` in `argocd` only; one `podSelector` cannot say "this label in that namespace", hence two gid policies | No |
| `bpf-program-load` | `bpf_check` | Any BPF program load from a container; the alert leaves out `cilium` and `kube-system` | Yes: `TetragonBpfProgramLoaded` |
| `kernel-module-load` | `security_kernel_module_request`, `security_kernel_read_file`, `add_taint` | A module requested by name or read from a container, minus the `net-pf-2-proto-262` and `net-pf-10-proto-262` requests Go binaries and haproxy make when they probe MPTCP at start and the `net-pf-31` one Home Assistant makes when it looks for a Bluetooth adapter; the alert leaves out `rook-ceph`, whose CSI plugin loads `rbd`. The third hook fires on the unsigned-module taint, host included, because `module_sig_check` returns success for an unsigned module when Flatcar does not enforce signatures (`CONFIG_MODULE_SIG` without `_FORCE`) | Yes: `TetragonKernelModuleLoaded`; `TetragonUnsignedKernelModule` from Loki |
| `dns-outside-cluster` | `ip_output` | A port 53 packet from a container to anything but the kube-dns ClusterIP or the pod range, which is a hard-coded resolver in an image, a tunnel or exfiltration. The pod range is left out because it holds each node's Cilium router address, the pod's default gateway, which Home Assistant's dhcp integration asks for PTR records at start. The hook sees TCP and UDP alike, so musl's unconnected sends count too; the alert leaves out `kube-system`, where CoreDNS forwards upstream, and `cert-manager`, whose DNS-01 propagation check asks the zone's authoritative servers | Yes: `TetragonDnsOutsideCluster` |
| `mount-in-container` | `security_sb_mount` | Any mount from a container except by `runc`, which mounts the rootfs, proc and sysfs on every start. Escapes start with a mount of the host's disk, cgroup or proc; the alert leaves out `rook-ceph`, `cilium` and `kube-system`, which mount by design, and `/proc/self/exe` in the `arc-jobs` workflow pods, which is buildah mounting in its user namespace | Yes: `TetragonMountInContainer` |
| `ptrace-in-container` | `security_ptrace_access_check` | An attach-mode access to another process from a container: ptrace, `process_vm_writev`, `/proc/<pid>/mem`. The read mode `ps` uses is left alone | Yes: `TetragonPtraceInContainer` |
| `kill-unprivileged-user-namespace` | `create_user_ns` | A user namespace created without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in a container, killed, except in `arc-jobs`. The only policy in `enforce` mode | Yes: `TetragonUserNamespaceCreated` |
| `unprivileged-user-namespace-arc-jobs` | `create_user_ns` | The same in `arc-jobs`, recorded: buildah builds the images there in a user namespace, see [GitHub runners](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/github-runners/index.md>) | No; every image build would fire it |
| `egress-outside-cluster` | `security_socket_connect` | An IPv4 `connect()`, TCP or UDP, from a container to anything outside the pod, service and site ranges | No; ACME, S3, the Trivy database and Home Assistant all do this routinely |

The first policy's allow list is what reads key material in steady state. Add a binary there only after confirming it in the export; a person running `cat` on a node is exactly what the policy is for. A binary path is only trusted together with the host network namespace: any image can ship `/usr/local/bin/etcd`, but only a privileged namespace can run it with `hostNetwork`. The exemption stays in the kernel because the `podSelector` pitfall below would miss a pod that reads a key at start; namespace and workload exemptions go in the alert.

The third policy is the runtime half of an image check: nothing in an image lives on those paths, so a binary executing from one was written after the container started. The policy names the mounts this cluster puts binaries into, since an emptyDir can be mounted anywhere; a `readOnlyRootFilesystem` pod leaves a new binary nowhere else to land. The offline half, every binary Tetragon saw executed diffed against the image's file list, needs no policy: query Loki by image and binary and resolve each path in `crane export <image> - | tar t`.

Four more detections from the same library need no policy, because the exec event already carries what they look for; they are [Loki alerts](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>).

### Enforcement

Every policy but one only records. `kill-unprivileged-user-namespace` carries `policy-mode: enforce` and a `Sigkill`, because nothing here creates user namespaces and most kernel escalation chains start with one. It stays scoped to containers: a sysctl would cover the host too, where systemd's `PrivateUsers=` needs them. The one exception is `arc-jobs`, where buildah needs one for every image build; its `podSelector` excludes that namespace, at the price of the first seconds of every container (see Pitfalls), and a monitor-only twin records the events there. The limits, checked on the nodes: `Override` and enforcers need `CONFIG_FUNCTION_ERROR_INJECTION`, which Flatcar's kernel does not set, and BPF LSM hooks need `bpf` in the `lsm=` boot argument, which Flatcar does not pass. That leaves `Sigkill`, which upstream warns does not stop an operation already in flight. A policy without `policy-mode` loads in monitor mode and its kill actions are elided, so an enforcing policy has to say so.

## Usage

The dashboard is the summary; the queries below are what its Loki panels run.

```text
# Everything a policy caught
{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"} | json | process_kprobe_policy_name!=""

# Every exec in one namespace, with arguments
{namespace="kube-system", container="export-stdout"} | json | process_exec_process_pod_namespace="home-assistant"
  | line_format "{{.process_exec_process_binary}} {{.process_exec_process_arguments}}"
```

The `tetra` CLI in the agent pod does the same live:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra getevents -o compact --namespaces home-assistant
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get ds tetragon
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra tracingpolicy list   # STATE: enabled
```

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A `podSelector` misses a pod's first seconds**
>
> The policy filter learns pods from the API and maps their cgroups; a process that runs the moment a container starts is not yet selected, so a filtered policy misses it. Put the hook an alert depends on in a policy without a `podSelector`, and do exclusions in PromQL.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A first hit is a new series, and `increase()` of one sample is zero**
>
> `tetragon_policy_events_total` has a pod label, so the first hit from a pod creates a counter series inside the alert window and `increase()` reports nothing until the second scrape moves it. Every policy alert therefore also matches a series absent one window earlier, with `unless ... offset`, and holds with `keep_firing_for`, because the agent drops a pod's series when the pod exits and a one-shot pod would otherwise flap. Copy that shape for a new alert and test it with a pod that fires once.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **An exclusion has to outlive the pod**
>
> `increase(...[10m])` still sees a pod's events for ten minutes after the agent dropped its series, while a bare selector on the right of `unless` matches nothing once the series is stale, so a left-out one-shot pod fires when it exits. Write every exclusion as `unless on (...) last_over_time(...[10m])`, the same window as the `increase()`.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **A policy that does not load is silent**
>
> A `TracingPolicy` naming a kernel function this kernel does not export sits in state `error` and watches nothing. `TetragonPolicyNotLoaded` fires after its `for`; check its `STATE` column after every Flatcar release that moves the kernel.

# Trivy Operator

Aqua Security's [Trivy Operator](<https://aquasecurity.github.io/trivy-operator/latest/>) scans everything the cluster runs and writes every result back as a Kubernetes object. Reading those objects is [Vulnerability Triage](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/vulnerabilities/index.md>); this page is the operator itself, chosen over Kubescape for the reasons in [Design Decisions](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/decisions/index.md#trivy-operator-not-kubescape>).

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `trivy-system` |
| Depends on | [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>) for the `ServiceMonitor` and the dashboard, [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for the vulnerability database volume |
| If it is down | Reports expire after `scannerReportTTL` and are not rebuilt; `TrivyContainerNotScanned` fires for every container |
| Health check | `kubectl -n trivy-system get pods,jobs`, then the reconciliation below |
| Dashboard | [Trivy Operator](<https://monitoring.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch/d/trivy-operator-overview>) |
| Files | [`payload/platform/trivy-operator/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/trivy-operator>): the chart, `prometheusrule.yaml`, the `findings-history` and `report-prune` CronJobs, the `sbom-readers.yaml` grant and a dashboard written for this cluster. The namespace labels and the default-deny policy are in [Security Policies](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md>) |

| Scanner | Produces | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vulnerability | `VulnerabilityReport` | Which CVEs are in the images we run |
| Exposed secret | `ExposedSecretReport` | Which images have credentials baked in |
| Config audit | `ConfigAuditReport` | Which workloads are misconfigured |
| RBAC assessment | `RbacAssessmentReport` | Which roles grant too much |
| Infra assessment | `InfraAssessmentReport` | Whether the nodes pass CIS |
| Compliance | `ClusterComplianceReport` | CIS 1.23, NSA/CISA 1.0, PSS baseline and restricted |

The `eks-` and `rke2-` compliance specs are for other distributions and are left out rather than reported as failing.

## Configuration

The values in `application.yaml` that are not defaults:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `scannerReportTTL`, `vulnerabilityScannerScanOnlyCurrentRevisions`, `configAuditScannerScanOnlyCurrentRevisions`, `scanJobTTL` | Reports live in etcd. A stale report is rebuilt, superseded ReplicaSets are not scanned, and finished jobs do not accumulate |
| `builtInTrivyServer: true` | `ClientServer` mode: one `trivy-server` holds the vulnerability database on the PVC. Standalone mode downloads it in every scan job, which meets registry rate limits, and a rate-limited scan reports zero findings rather than an error |
| `ignoreUnfixed: false`, every severity | A finding with no fix is usually the signal that the base image is wrong, and a finding the scanner could not grade is worth reading |
| `ignorePolicy.authentik` | The image carries thousands of unfixed Debian findings and its reports exceed the etcd request limit. The Rego (v0 syntax, `object.get` because `FixedVersion` is absent when there is no fix) drops only findings that have no fix *and* are below HIGH |
| `skipFiles` | Debian's placeholder key in every CloudNativePG image, which serves TLS from certificates of its own, would otherwise sit in every Postgres report. Trivy's Rego input for a secret has no path, so an ignore policy could only drop the `private-key` rule and every real key with it; this skips one exact path |
| `additionalVulnerabilityReportFields` without `Description` and `Links` | A report is one API write, capped at 2 MiB, and `Links` is most of it. An oversized report is rejected with nothing but an operator log line |
| `operator.scanJobTimeout` and `trivy.timeout`, kept equal | The first is the Job's `activeDeadlineSeconds` and kills the pod whatever Trivy is doing; the second is Trivy's own flag and only fires if it is the shorter. Raising one alone does nothing |
| `accessGlobalSecretsAndServiceAccount: false` | The default grants the operator read on every Secret in the cluster so scan jobs can borrow a workload's `imagePullSecrets`, and every image here is public. A private image would fail its scan and raise `TrivyContainerNotScanned`. The flag also drops `nodes/proxy`, which node-collector needs for the kubelet CIS checks, so `node-collector-rbac.yaml` grants it back. The Job runs as the operator's ServiceAccount, the chart has no other, so it cannot be narrower |
| `clusterSbomCacheEnabled: false` | With the cache, every workload after the first to use an image gets an `SbomReport` from the cached SBOM and no `VulnerabilityReport`. Upstream: [trivy-operator\#1668](<https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy-operator/issues/1668>) |
| `configFile` with `scan.skip-version-check` and `scan.disable-telemetry` | The operator mounts it into every scan job as `trivy.yaml`. Trivy's version check and its usage telemetry share one request to `check.trivy.dev`, so switching off one still sends it; the server never makes the call, only the scan jobs |
| `metricsVulnIdEnabled: false` | One series per CVE per container is a six-figure cardinality, and every label is already in the report |
| `compliance.reportType: summary` | The collector skips reports in `all` format, so `trivy_compliance_info` disappears and the dashboard's failing-controls table empties. The `status` label is title-cased: `Fail`, `Pass` |
| Control-plane tolerations on `nodeCollector` and `scanJobTolerations` | Without them the CIS infra assessment covers only the workers and reports a clean control plane it never looked at |
| `enforce: privileged`, `audit`/`warn: restricted` on the namespace, in `payload/platform/security/pod-security.yaml` | node-collector hostPath-mounts `/var/lib/etcd`, `/var/lib/kubelet`, `/etc/kubernetes` and `/etc/cni/net.d`, which `baseline` forbids. Scan jobs themselves drop all capabilities and run read-only |
| `resources` on the operator | Its cache holds every report in the cluster, and the `SbomReport`s are most of that. At the limit it is OOM-killed mid-write, which shows as reports that never appear rather than as an error |
| `logDevMode: false` | Its `V(1)` lines are the only way to see decisions the operator makes silently, but it switches logging to console encoding |

### Alerting

The rules in `prometheusrule.yaml`. Reports expire and are rebuilt every `scannerReportTTL`, so a "new" finding is one absent from the reports an `offset` earlier rather than from the previous scrape, and every rule waits longer than a rebuild.

| Alert | Fires when | Why this shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TrivyContainerNotScanned` | A running container has no `VulnerabilityReport` | A rejected report is never written, so it looks identical to a clean one; only reconciling against what runs finds it |
| `TrivyExposedSecretNew` | A secret finding, by rule and path, was in no report an `offset` earlier, whichever container carried it | An accepted finding never clears, so an absolute rule would fire forever; and the same finding in a new pod is not new |
| `TrivyRbacCriticalNew` | A Role or ClusterRole gains a critical finding it did not have an `offset` earlier | Every critical ClusterRole is a chart's operator role or Kubernetes' own, see [Vulnerability Triage](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/vulnerabilities/index.md#what-is-load-bearing>); what matters is a new one |
| `TrivyConfigAuditCritical` | Any workload fails a critical config-audit check | A critical misconfiguration is fixed, not accepted, so the rule is absolute |
| `TrivyComplianceRegression` | A framework has more failing controls than an `offset` earlier | Compliance is recomputed on `compliance.cron`; a `for` spanning two runs makes it drift, not a rebuild |

The two "new" rules also require the operator to have been reporting at that offset, so a fresh cluster does not page on every existing finding.

`TrivyContainerNotScanned` compares every running container against the containers that have a `VulnerabilityReport` and names the difference:

```promql
count by (namespace, container) (
  kube_pod_container_info
  * on (namespace, pod) group_left ()
  (max by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1))
)
unless on (namespace, container)
count by (namespace, container) (
  label_replace(trivy_image_info, "container", "$1", "container_name", "(.+)")
)
```

- **Keyed on `(namespace, container)`, not the digest**: containerd's platform digest and the registry's tag digest differ permanently for mirrored images.
- **Restricted to `Running` pods**, or every completed Job counts as unscanned.
- **A `for` of several full sweeps**, so the TTL churn does not page.

The dashboard's stat and by-severity panels take `max by (image_digest)` before summing, and workload panels join ReplicaSets against `kube_replicaset_spec_replicas > 0`, so a finding counts once per image and a superseded revision drops out. The "Worst workloads" table stays per container on purpose: it answers where a finding runs.

### History

Reports live for `scannerReportTTL` and Prometheus for its `retention`, so neither can answer whether a count went up over a quarter. The `findings-history` CronJob in `findings-history.yaml` lists every report kind on its schedule and prints one JSON line per namespace, and per compliance framework, to stdout; Alloy ships it like any container log and Loki keeps that one stream far longer than the rest (`retention_stream` in `loki/application.yaml`). The dashboard's last row reads it. Images are counted once per digest per namespace, the same rule the dashboard applies.

```text
{namespace="trivy-system", container="findings-history"} | json | kind="vulnerabilities" | namespace="argocd"
```

### SBOM export

`sbomGenerationEnabled` makes the operator write one CycloneDX `SbomReport` per container next to the `VulnerabilityReport`. Nothing here reads them; [Dependency-Track](<https://homelab-apps.wlkr.ch/dependency-track/>) in the workloads repository uploads every one of them nightly and keeps the history Trivy's expiring reports cannot. `sbom-readers.yaml` is the `ClusterRole` and binding that let its upload job list them, and the ReplicaSets and Jobs, so it can skip the reports of superseded revisions and finished Jobs: the `apps` project may not create cluster-scoped RBAC, and which workload reads the operator's findings is decided here.

### Report pruning

`SbomReport`s and `ExposedSecretReport`s carry no TTL, unlike the `VulnerabilityReport`s: they live as long as the scanned ReplicaSet, and Deployments keep ten superseded revisions scaled to zero. The reports are most of etcd's bytes, and each API server holds them decoded in its watch cache. The `report-prune` CronJob in `report-prune.yaml` deletes the two kinds on its schedule for every ReplicaSet scaled to zero; the Dependency-Track upload skips those anyway, and the two `ScanOnlyCurrentRevisions` settings keep the operator from writing them again. It also deletes ownerless reports, which garbage collection never reaches, the leftovers of the disabled cluster SBOM cache, and every report of a Job: `targetWorkloads` leaves `job` out, because the operator rescans a finished Job daily and the workload sharing its image is scanned. CronJobs stay.

## Usage

The dashboard is a summary; the objects have the detail.

```bash
# What has been scanned, worst first
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A --sort-by='.report.summary.criticalCount'

# The findings themselves, for one workload
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -n <ns> <name> -o json \
  | jq '.report.vulnerabilities[]
        | select(.severity=="CRITICAL")
        | {id: .vulnerabilityID, pkg: .resource,
           installed: .installedVersion, fixed: .fixedVersion}'

# Misconfiguration, RBAC and node checks
kubectl get configauditreports -A
kubectl get rbacassessmentreports,clusterrbacassessmentreports -A
kubectl get infraassessmentreports -A

# Which compliance controls are failing
kubectl get clustercompliancereports k8s-cis-1.23 -o json \
  | jq '.status.summary, (.status.summaryReport.controlCheck[]
        | select(.totalFail > 0))'
```

## Health check

Reconcile running containers against scanned ones, keyed on `(namespace, container)` like the alert; the output is every running container with no `VulnerabilityReport`, and healthy is an empty output:

```bash
comm -23 \
  <(kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase=Running -o json \
      | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .spec.containers[] | "\($ns) \(.name)"' | sort -u) \
  <(kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A -o json \
      | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.metadata.labels["trivy-operator.container.name"])"' | sort -u)
```

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Zero is not the same as clean**
>
> A report that reads zero may be a clean image or a scan that failed: a rate-limited pull, a timeout, an image the operator could not resolve. Check the object exists and carries a real digest before believing a zero, and look at `kubectl -n trivy-system get jobs` when one never appears. This is where the `vulnerability-triage` skill in `.claude/skills/` starts.

## Pitfalls

Four ways a workload ends up with no `VulnerabilityReport`, all silent from the outside:

| Symptom | Cause | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No report, no `SbomReport`, operator logs `ResourceExhausted ... larger than max` or `etcdserver: request is too large` | The report exceeds the API write ceiling | Operator log. Fix: the fields and ignore policies above |
| No report, Job events show `DeadlineExceeded` | `scanJobTimeout` elapsed on a large image | `kubectl -n trivy-system get events --field-selector reason=DeadlineExceeded`, before `scanJobTTL` deletes the Job |
| Some containers of a multi-container workload missing; job succeeded; log has `failed to analyze layer ... unexpected EOF` | A scan container died reading the image and the operator keeps only containers that exited 0. Hits workloads with several containers on one image (Rook, Cilium) | Scan job pod logs |
| Reports missing at random, operator restart count climbing, last state `OOMKilled` | The report cache outgrew the memory limit | `kubectl -n trivy-system get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=trivy-operator -o jsonpath='{..lastState}'`. Fix: `resources` in `application.yaml` |
| `SbomReport` exists, no `VulnerabilityReport` | SBOM cache reuse path ran `trivy sbom` and produced nothing | Confirm `clusterSbomCacheEnabled` is off |

A completed scan job counts against `concurrentScanJobsLimit` until `scanJobTTL` deletes it, so a backlog drains in batches of the limit, the chart's default, once per TTL; that is the expected shape, not a stall.

# Velero

[Velero](<https://velero.io/>) backs up Kubernetes objects and, through CSI snapshots and its data mover, every PVC, nightly into its prefix of the `offsite` bucket. Coverage and restore runbooks are in [Backups & Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>); this page is the chart tuning.

## At a glance

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Namespace | `backup` |
| Depends on | [Rook-Ceph](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>) for its S3 user and RBD snapshots |
| If it is down | Nightly backups stop; `VeleroBackupTooOld` fires once the last success is older than the rule's threshold |
| Health check | `kubectl -n backup get backupstoragelocation` reads `Available` |
| Files | [`payload/platform/velero/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/velero>), [`payload/platform/backup/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/backup>), [`payload/platform/snapshot-controller/`](<https://github.com/JanWelker/homelab/tree/main/payload/platform/snapshot-controller>) |

## Configuration

In `application.yaml`'s `valuesObject` unless a file is named:

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `checksumAlgorithm: ""` on the `BackupStorageLocation` | The AWS plugin's SDK sends a trailing checksum Ceph RGW rejects (`XAmzContentSHA256Mismatch`) |
| `s3Url: https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, not the RGW Service | kopia signs plain-HTTP uploads with streaming SigV4, which Ceph RGW rejects since [CVE-2026-54330](<https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/security/CVE-2026-54330/>); over TLS it sends `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD` and RGW accepts it. The infra Gateway's Let's Encrypt wildcard means no CA has to reach Velero or the movers |
| `velero-plugin-for-aws` init container | The plugin minor must match the chart's Velero appVersion |
| `credentials.useSecret: false` with `extraEnvVars` | Keys come from the environment, fed by the `Secret` Rook writes for the `backup.velero` [backup writer](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>); nothing is rendered into a file or Git |
| `bucket: offsite`, `prefix: backup.velero` | The only place the writer's keys may write |
| `defaultSnapshotMoveData`, `deployNodeAgent`, `uploaderType: kopia` | A CSI snapshot lives in the same cluster; the data mover streams it into the bucket and deletes it |
| `volumeSnapshotLocation: []` | The chart's placeholder renders a `VolumeSnapshotLocation` the CRD rejects, failing every sync; Helm replaces lists, so the empty list removes it |
| `VolumeSnapshotClass` in `payload/platform/backup/volumesnapshotclass.yaml` | The `velero.io/csi-volumesnapshot-class` label is how Velero finds the class; without it volumes are skipped silently. `deletionPolicy: Delete`, because the durable copy is the data mover's. A `PartiallyFailed` backup with no volume data means the label is missing |
| `snapshot-controller` Application | Neither kubeadm nor Rook installs the CSI snapshot controller or its CRDs, which the `VolumeSnapshotClass` needs. It applies the two kustomize directories of [kubernetes-csi/external-snapshotter](<https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshotter>) at each tag in `backup`, patched with the hardening, a liveness probe restarting a leader that cannot renew its lease, and the tag's image, since upstream's Deployment names the previous image; Renovate moves the two together, see [Maintenance](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/development/maintenance/index.md#automerge-policy>). `pdb.yaml` adds the PDB upstream lacks |
| `rbac.clusterAdministrator` at the chart default | A restore re-creates arbitrary kinds, RBAC included, and the API server refuses a binding granting rights the caller lacks |
| `schedules.daily` | Excludes what rebuilds from Git or a rescan, listed in [Backups](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#velero>). Its `ttl` is the window [CloudNativePG](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md#backups>)'s `retentionPolicy` mirrors |
| Node agent `containerSecurityContext` | Root and capabilities stay because kopia reads every pod volume; escalation is off and seccomp is on |
| `configMaps.node-agent-config`, `--node-agent-configmap` | Data mover pods ignore `nodeAgent.priorityClassName`; this puts them in the backup [tier](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/index.md#priority-classes>) |
| `prometheusRule` | Four rules: `VeleroBackupFailures` (critical) and `VeleroBackupPartialFailures` (warning) on a schedule's outcome, `VeleroBackupTooOld` (critical), which alone catches a backup hanging `InProgress`, and `VeleroBackupInProgress` (info), which is [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md#configuration>)'s reboot gate rather than a problem to mail |

### Repository password

Kopia encrypts the volume data in every repository with one password, read from the Secret `velero-repo-credentials` (key `repository-password`) in Velero's namespace. When it is missing Velero creates it with a compiled-in default, which protects nothing, so `payload/platform/backup/velero-repo-credentials.yaml` supplies it.

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A `Password` generator and `PushSecret` writing `velero/repository` | A [generated secret](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generated-secrets>): random, written once, and in the OpenBao snapshot that a restore on a fresh cluster needs anyway |
| `creationPolicy: Owner` on the `ExternalSecret` | ESO takes over the Secret Velero created at start-up and overwrites the default |
| `velero.io/exclude-from-backup` on the Secret | The resource backup lands in the same bucket as the repositories the password unlocks |
| Secrets stay in the resource backup | The tarball under `backups/` is not encrypted, so every backed-up `Secret` sits in the bucket as JSON. Excluding them would break a namespace restore: CloudNativePG, the bucket claims, cert-manager and Argo CD generate Secrets that exist nowhere else. Velero's prefix and every key that reads it are as sensitive as an unencrypted etcd |

A repository keeps the password it was initialised with, and all repositories share one, so a changed value makes every existing repository unreachable; see [Re-initialising the repositories](<#re-initialising-the-repositories>).

## Usage

```bash
velero -n backup backup create manual-$(date +%s) --include-namespaces my-app
```

## Health check

```bash
kubectl -n backup get backupstoragelocation       # Available
kubectl -n backup get backups.velero.io           # Completed, not PartiallyFailed
kubectl -n backup get volumesnapshotclass rook-ceph-block
kubectl -n backup get backuprepositories.velero.io  # Ready
kubectl -n backup get externalsecret velero-repo-credentials   # SecretSynced
```

## Pitfalls

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every `BackupRepository` NotReady, `Access Denied` on `kopia.blobcfg`**
>
> Objects upload, volume data does not: RGW logs `PUT /offsite/backup.velero/kopia/...` from `minio-go` with no authenticated user while the AWS SDK's PUTs succeed. The S3 URL is plain HTTP again; see the `s3Url` row above.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every `BackupRepository` NotReady, `invalid repository password`**
>
> The password changed under existing repositories: OpenBao was rebuilt without its snapshot, `velero/repository` was deleted, or a backup ran on a fresh cluster before OpenBao was unsealed and initialised them with Velero's default. Volume data stops and backups end `PartiallyFailed`. Restore the old value into OpenBao if it exists anywhere; otherwise re-initialise as below.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`repository not initialized in the provided storage` after a bucket or prefix change**
>
> Velero re-establishes only some `BackupRepository` objects when the backup location moves; the rest stay `Ready` against a prefix that holds no repository, and their volumes fail. Delete them all with `kubectl -n backup delete backuprepositories.velero.io --all`; the next backup re-creates each under the new prefix.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Every `BackupRepository` without a phase, `failed to wait BackupRepository`**
>
> The repository controller waits for each maintenance job to finish, one at a time. A job whose pod cannot start, typically `CreateContainerConfigError` after the credentials Secret was renamed, blocks every other repository behind it; `KubeContainerWaiting` fires on the job's pod. Delete it, then restart `deploy/velero`.

## Recovery

### Re-initialising the repositories

Discards every Velero backup, resource backups included: a `Backup` with unreachable snapshots never finishes deleting, so the prefix is emptied whole.

1. Confirm the Secret carries the value from OpenBao, not Velero's default.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup get externalsecret velero-repo-credentials   # SecretSynced
   ```
2. Delete the repository objects.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup delete backuprepositories.velero.io --all
   ```
3. Empty Velero's prefix with its own keys, from a machine that reaches the infra Gateway.

   ```bash
   export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(kubectl -n backup get secret rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-backup.velero -o jsonpath='{.data.AccessKey}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(kubectl -n backup get secret rook-ceph-object-user-object-store-backup.velero -o jsonpath='{.data.SecretKey}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$(mktemp)    # path-style addressing, without touching ~/.aws
   printf '[default]\ns3 =\n    addressing_style = path\n' > "$AWS_CONFIG_FILE"
   aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 rm s3://offsite/backup.velero --recursive
   ```
4. Restart Velero and the node agents, so no cached repository connection survives.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup rollout restart deployment/velero daemonset/node-agent
   ```
5. Take a backup now and confirm it.

   ```bash
   velero -n backup backup create --from-schedule velero-daily
   kubectl -n backup get backups.velero.io               # Completed
   kubectl -n backup get backuprepositories.velero.io    # Ready
   ```

### Removing a deleted workload

A removed namespace leaves its `BackupRepository` and its Kopia data in the bucket, which Velero never prunes.

1. Delete the repository object and its finished maintenance Jobs.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup delete backuprepositories.velero.io <namespace>-default-kopia
   kubectl -n backup delete jobs -l velero.io/repo-name=<namespace>-default-kopia
   ```
2. List, then remove, its Kopia data, with the exports from step 3 of [Re-initialising the repositories](<#re-initialising-the-repositories>).

   ```bash
   aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 ls s3://offsite/backup.velero/kopia/<namespace>/ --recursive
   aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 rm s3://offsite/backup.velero/kopia/<namespace>/ --recursive
   ```
