## Routine health check

| Command | Healthy looks like |
| --- | --- |
| `kubectl get nodes` | Every node `Ready` |
| `kubectl -n argocd get applications` | Every Application `Synced` *and* `Healthy` |
| `kubectl get certificate -A` | Every certificate `READY=True` |
| `ssh core@<control plane> sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration` | More than thirty days left on every line; less and the [yearly renewal](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md#control-plane-certificates>) is due |
| `kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- ceph status` | `HEALTH_OK`, and an OSD count matching your node count |
| `bao status` on [every OpenBao pod](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#health-check>), each seals on its own | `Sealed: false`; the one failure that looks like health, so run it after anything restarted |

The Rook toolbox pod is enabled, so `ceph status`, `ceph osd tree` and `ceph health detail` need nothing installed. Ceph metrics are scraped and Ceph's own alerting rules are loaded, so a degraded pool reaches Prometheus without anyone running `ceph status`; run it anyway, because it is the fastest way to see *why* — see [Rook-Ceph → Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#monitoring>).

# Backups & Recovery

## Current state

| Data | Backed up | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kubernetes objects | Nightly | [Velero](<#velero>) to the Ceph object store |
| Ceph RBD volumes (PVCs) | Nightly | Velero CSI snapshot, moved into the object store |
| PostgreSQL databases | Continuous WAL, nightly base backup | [CloudNativePG's Barman Cloud plugin](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md#backups>), each database to its own prefix; restores to a point in time |
| Grafana dashboards | Nightly | Its PVC is covered by the above |
| etcd (raw) | Nightly | [CronJob](<#etcd>) to the object store |
| OpenBao secrets | Nightly | [Raft snapshot CronJob](<#openbao>) to the object store |
| OpenBao unseal keys | Manual, off-cluster | Written once to `output/credentials/openbao-init.json` by `make bao-init` |
| Prometheus metrics | **No** | Its PVC carries `velero.io/exclude-from-backup`; metrics live for the `retention` in `payload/platform/monitoring/application.yaml`, then are gone |
| Trivy reports and vulnerability database | **No** | `trivy-system` is excluded; the operator rescans and the server downloads the database again |
| Everything in `payload/` | Yes | It is in Git |

## Backup chain

Each backup writes straight into its own prefix of one bucket, `offsite`, and TrueNAS pulls that bucket and snapshots it. Each step runs after the one before has finished, so nothing is pulled while it is being written.

```
flowchart LR
    subgraph cluster["Cluster, Ceph object store"]
        offsite[("offsite")]
        etcd["etcd-backup<br/>CronJob"] -->|"backup.etcd/"| offsite
        bao["openbao-snapshot<br/>CronJob"] -->|"backup.openbao/"| offsite
        velero["Velero<br/>schedule"] -->|"backup.velero/"| offsite
        cnpg["CloudNativePG<br/>WAL + base backup"] -->|"&lt;namespace&gt;.db/"| offsite
    end
    subgraph nas["TrueNAS"]
        pull["Cloud Sync<br/>PULL, SYNC"] --> dataset[("encrypted<br/>dataset")]
        dataset --> snaps["periodic<br/>ZFS snapshots"]
    end
    offsite -->|"offsite-reader keys"| pull
```

| Step | Scheduled in | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| etcd, OpenBao, Velero, databases | Their CronJobs, `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml` and each `ScheduledBackup`, in UTC | Through the night, never overlapping |
| TrueNAS Cloud Sync task | The NAS | 07:00 local time, after the last of the above |
| TrueNAS periodic snapshot task | The NAS | 09:00 local time, after the pull |

The TrueNAS times are not in Git, so this table is their only record: change them here when they change on the NAS.

## What is not covered

**Every automated backup lands in the same cluster's Ceph first.** That protects against operator error (a deleted PVC, a bad `prune`, a corrupted database) and not against losing the cluster, so TrueNAS pulls a [copy](<#off-cluster-copy>) nightly. The NAS sits on the same LAN, so a fire or theft that takes the cluster can take the copy too; nothing leaves the house yet.

Nothing backs up the deployment host's `output/` either:

| File | Holds | If lost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kubeconfig` | Admin credential | `make kubeconfig` |
| `credentials/openbao-init.json` | Unseal key shares | Gone, hence the [password manager](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#bootstrap>) |
| `credentials/openbao-operator.json` | OpenBao operator login | Recreate with a [root token](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generating-a-root-token>) |
| `credentials/encryption_key` | etcd's Secret encryption key | Base64-encoded in every control plane's `/etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml`; restore it before `make config` renders a new one, or [rotate](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/encryption-key-rotation/index.md>) |
| `credentials/kubeadm_token_*`, `credentials/certificate_key` | Join credentials | `make config` generates and installs new ones |
| `credentials/ssh_host_<node>_ed25519` | Node SSH host key | Still in the node's `/etc/ssh/`; a new one from `make config` mismatches until the node is reinstalled |

Only `VeleroBackupTooOld` notices a backup that silently stopped ([Velero](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/index.md#configuration>)), and only whoever Alertmanager tells — see [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md>).

## Velero

[Velero](<https://velero.io/>) backs up Kubernetes objects and volume data nightly. Chart values and why each is set are in [Velero](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/index.md>).

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Schedule | The `schedules` block in `payload/platform/velero/application.yaml`: nightly, an hour after etcd so the two never contend for the object store, with a `ttl` long enough that a bad backup is noticed before the last good one expires |
| Scope | All namespaces except `kube-system` (rebuilt from Git, and large) and `trivy-system` (rescanned), minus `events` (they expire anyway) and any PVC labelled `velero.io/exclude-from-backup`, which is only Prometheus's |
| Destination | `offsite/backup.velero/` in the [Ceph object store](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md>), written as its own [backup writer](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>) |
| Volume data | CSI snapshot, streamed into the object store by the data mover (Kopia), snapshot deleted; the durable copy is the one in the object store |
| Encryption | Volume data only, with a password from OpenBao a restore needs; Secrets in the resource backups are plain JSON — see [Repository password](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/velero/index.md#repository-password>) |

The `velero` CLI defaults to the `velero` namespace; this install is in `backup`, so pass `-n backup` every time.

```bash
kubectl -n backup get backups.velero.io
kubectl -n backup get backupstoragelocation     # should be Available

velero -n backup backup create manual-$(date +%s) --include-namespaces my-app
```

## etcd

Velero restores *through* the API server, which is no use with no API server left (lost quorum, a corrupted data directory). For that a CronJob snapshots etcd.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Schedule | `payload/platform/backup/etcd-backup.yaml`: nightly, before Velero |
| Where it runs | Any control-plane node, on the host network: etcd listens on `127.0.0.1` and its client certs are on the node. It mounts the CA certificate and the healthcheck client pair, never the directory, which also holds the CA and server keys |
| Verification | `etcdutl snapshot status` before upload, so a truncated snapshot fails the job instead of replacing a good backup |
| Destination | `offsite/backup.etcd/`, separate from Velero's because it is restored by different means; the job keeps the newest snapshots and deletes the rest, the count is in the manifest |

Two settings there are easy to undo by accident: the DNS policy for a host-network pod (the node's `resolv.conf` cannot resolve the RGW Service), and the AWS CLI config file selecting path-style addressing (no environment variable sets it).

```bash
kubectl -n backup get cronjob etcd-backup
kubectl -n backup logs job/<most-recent-job> -c upload
```

### Defragmentation

The API server compacts etcd's history (`--etcd-compaction-interval`), but compaction only frees pages inside the database file; the file itself never shrinks until a member is defragmented, and once less than half of it is in use `etcdDatabaseHighFragmentationRatio` fires. A second CronJob in `payload/platform/backup/etcd-defrag.yaml` runs `etcdctl defrag --cluster` nightly from the same kind of host-network pod as the backup and prints `endpoint status` before and after so the log shows the size reclaimed.

| Property | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Nightly | Sooner than this cluster's churn crosses the alert's ratio, so the alert firing means a run failed or did not help, not that the next one is due |
| One member at a time | A member blocks for seconds while it rewrites its file; the other two keep quorum |
| Fails when a member is unreachable | `endpoint status --cluster` exits non-zero, so a cluster already short of a member is not defragmented |

```bash
kubectl -n backup get cronjob etcd-defrag
kubectl -n backup create job --from=cronjob/etcd-defrag etcd-defrag-manual
kubectl -n backup logs job/etcd-defrag-manual
```

### Taking one by hand

The snapshot lands in the static pod's `/var/lib/etcd`, which is the node's; `kubectl cp` cannot fetch it, because the etcd image is distroless and has no `tar`.

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db

ssh core@<node> sudo cat /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db > ./etcd-snapshot.db
ssh core@<node> sudo rm /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db
```

Keep the copy off the cluster, like the nightly ones below.

## OpenBao

A CronJob in `payload/platform/backup/openbao-snapshot.yaml` saves a Raft snapshot nightly, between the etcd snapshot and Velero.

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Login | Kubernetes auth as the `openbao-snapshot` role, whose policy reads `sys/storage/raft/snapshot` and nothing else; `make bao-policies` writes it — see [Kubernetes auth](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#kubernetes-auth>). The token is revoked when the snapshot is saved |
| Verification | The archive must list its `SHA256SUMS`, so a truncated snapshot fails the job instead of replacing a good one |
| Destination | `offsite/backup.openbao/`; the job keeps the newest snapshots and deletes the rest, the count is in the manifest |
| CLI version | The job's image is grouped with the server's tag in Renovate, so the CLI never lags the server |

```bash
kubectl -n backup get cronjob openbao-snapshot
kubectl -n backup create job --from=cronjob/openbao-snapshot openbao-snapshot-manual
kubectl -n backup logs job/openbao-snapshot-manual -c snapshot
```

By hand, with a token that may read the snapshot:

```bash
kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- bao operator raft snapshot save /tmp/snapshot.bao
kubectl -n openbao cp openbao-0:/tmp/snapshot.bao ./openbao-snapshot.bao
```

The snapshot holds all KV data plus policies, roles and mounts. It does **not** hold the unseal keys and is useless without them — see [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>).

## Off-cluster copy

TrueNAS pulls the [`offsite` bucket](<#backup-chain>) rather than the cluster pushing, so nothing in the cluster holds a credential that could reach the NAS.

| Property | Why |
| --- | --- |
| One S3 user per backup | Each writes only `offsite/<user>/`, so a compromised workload reaches its own backups and nobody else's. A new database's user comes with its `backup.yaml` — see [Backup writers](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#backup-writers>) |
| Nothing is left out by default | [Admission](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#admission-policies>) refuses a database without WAL archiving, an object store outside its `offsite` prefix and any new bucket claim, unless it carries `homelab.wlkr.ch/backup-exempt` with the reason. Velero takes every namespace its schedule does not exclude, and `CNPGBackupStale` fires for a database whose base backup never comes |
| Credentials | The [`offsite-reader`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#off-cluster-reader>) S3 user owns `offsite` and reads every object in it; TrueNAS uses its keys. As the owner it can also delete, so the only copy that outlives those keys is the NAS's snapshots |
| `BackupCronJobStale` in `payload/platform/backup/prometheusrule.yaml` | Fires when any CronJob in `backup` has not succeeded for a day and a half, which a run that never starts does not report as a failure |
| One Cloud Sync task, `PULL` and `SYNC` | The dataset mirrors `offsite`, so the copy shrinks when a TTL or retention prunes a prefix, and a restore finds each writer under its own directory |
| Periodic ZFS snapshots of the dataset | What `SYNC` deleted, and whatever a broken cluster wrote, is still in an older snapshot. Keep them longer than the cluster's retention, so a bad backup noticed late still has a good one behind it |
| Scheduled after the nightly backups | A Kopia repository pulled while it is being written is inconsistent |
| Encrypted dataset | Velero's resource backups are plain JSON with every Secret in them |

A removed writer's prefix stays in `offsite` until it is deleted by hand. Which users the bucket policy grants:

```bash
kubectl -n backup get objectbucketclaim offsite-bucket -o jsonpath='{.spec.additionalConfig.bucketPolicy}' | jq -r '.Statement[].Resource[]'
kubectl -n backup get cronjob offsite-policy    # LAST SCHEDULE within minutes
```

### Setting up the TrueNAS pull

1. Read the reader's keys from the `offsite-bucket` claim's Secret: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` is the **Access Key ID**, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` the **Secret Access Key**.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n backup get secret offsite-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' | base64 -d; echo
   kubectl -n backup get secret offsite-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}' | base64 -d; echo
   ```
2. Under **Credentials → Backup Credentials → Cloud Credentials**, add an `Amazon S3` credential with those keys, **Endpoint URL** `https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch` and **Region** `eu-central-1`.
3. Create an encrypted dataset for the copy.
4. Under **Data Protection → Cloud Sync Tasks**, add one task: direction `PULL`, transfer mode `SYNC`, bucket `offsite`, the dataset as the target, scheduled after the nightly backups: 07:00 local time, see [Backup chain](<#backup-chain>).
5. Under **Data Protection → Periodic Snapshot Tasks**, snapshot the dataset after the Cloud Sync task, at 09:00 local time, with a lifetime longer than the cluster's retention.
6. Run the Cloud Sync task once by hand and confirm it ends `SUCCESS`.

### Checking the reader

From any machine on the LAN, with the reader's keys exported as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `offsite` is the only bucket listed and holds one prefix per writer:

```bash
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$(mktemp)    # path-style addressing, without touching ~/.aws
printf '[default]\ns3 =\n    addressing_style = path\n' > "$AWS_CONFIG_FILE"
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 ls                # offsite
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 ls s3://offsite/   # backup.etcd/, backup.velero/, <namespace>.db/, ...
```

### Copying the backups off the cluster

By hand, before a reinstall or for a copy kept elsewhere, the same keys and config as above:

```bash
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 sync s3://offsite ./offsite
```

Store it like the NAS dataset: with the unseal keys, not beside the Git clone.

### Restoring from the copy

Velero and CloudNativePG read only from the cluster's own `offsite`, so a rebuilt cluster gets the dataset pushed back first, with the keys of the new `offsite-bucket` claim. Each writer reaches the objects under its prefix whoever wrote them, since the bucket policy grants the prefix. The etcd and OpenBao restores take the file straight from the copy.

1. Once Rook has bound `offsite-bucket` again, export its keys and the path-style config.

   ```bash
   export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(kubectl -n backup get secret offsite-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(kubectl -n backup get secret offsite-bucket -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}' | base64 -d)
   export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$(mktemp)
   printf '[default]\ns3 =\n    addressing_style = path\n' > "$AWS_CONFIG_FILE"
   ```
2. Push the dataset's copy of a writer's prefix, mounted or copied from the NAS, back into the bucket.

   ```bash
   aws --endpoint-url https://s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch --region eu-central-1 s3 sync ./<user> s3://offsite/<user>
   ```

## Ceph volumes

PVCs are covered by [Velero](<#velero>). Ceph's own replication is not a backup: it spreads each block across OSDs, which survives a disk or node failing and nothing else. Almost every Application runs with `prune: true` (`kube-vip` is [the exception](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#sync-policy>)), so removing a `PersistentVolumeClaim` from Git deletes the volume.

## Restoring

The commands follow upstream; the etcd sequence has not been exercised here.

### Database restore

A PostgreSQL database restores from its own archive: [Point-in-time restore](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md#point-in-time-restore>).

### Velero restore

1. Find the backup.

   ```bash
   velero -n backup backup get
   ```
2. Restore from it, scoped to what was lost; without `--include-namespaces` everything in the backup is restored, and existing objects are skipped, not overwritten. A PVC Argo CD has already re-created empty from Git is skipped too, and its data with it; step 3 shows whether that happened.

   ```bash
   velero -n backup restore create --from-backup velero-daily-<timestamp> \
     --include-namespaces my-app
   ```
3. Watch it finish, read the warnings, and confirm the volume data came back: one `DataDownload` per restored volume, `Completed`.

   ```bash
   velero -n backup restore describe <restore-name>
   velero -n backup restore logs <restore-name>
   kubectl -n backup get datadownloads.velero.io
   ```

### OpenBao snapshot restore

Needs an initialised, unsealed cluster and a root token from [Generating a root token](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#generating-a-root-token>). `-force` lets a snapshot from a *different* cluster (a fresh `bao operator init`) load; afterwards its keys and operator login apply, not the new cluster's.

1. Copy the snapshot in.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao cp ./openbao-snapshot.bao openbao-0:/tmp/snapshot.bao
   ```
2. Restore it.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n openbao exec -it openbao-0 -- \
     env BAO_TOKEN=<root-token> bao operator raft snapshot restore -force /tmp/snapshot.bao
   ```
3. Unseal every replica with the snapshot's key shares and confirm. The script reads `output/credentials/openbao-init.json`, which now holds the new cluster's keys, so point it at the old file with `KEYFILE`.

   ```bash
   KEYFILE=<old openbao-init.json> make bao-unseal
   kubectl -n openbao exec openbao-0 -- bao status   # Sealed: false
   ```
4. Put the old key and operator files in place of the new ones, which unseal nothing any more; every later `make bao-*` reads them.

   ```bash
   mv <old openbao-init.json> output/credentials/openbao-init.json
   mv <old openbao-operator.json> output/credentials/openbao-operator.json
   ```

### etcd restore

Every etcd member restores from the same snapshot, then all three static pods come back together. Flatcar ships no `etcdutl`, so run it from the etcd image the CronJob uses. Upstream: [Restoring an etcd cluster](<https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/configure-upgrade-etcd/#restoring-an-etcd-cluster>).

1. Copy the snapshot, from `backup.etcd/` in the off-cluster copy ([Off-cluster copy](<#off-cluster-copy>)), to every control-plane node as `/var/lib/etcd-restore/snapshot.db`.
2. On every control-plane node, stop the API server and etcd by moving their static pod manifests out, and wait until neither container is listed.

   ```bash
   sudo mkdir -p /root/manifests-stopped
   sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/{etcd,kube-apiserver}.yaml /root/manifests-stopped/
   sudo crictl ps --name 'etcd|kube-apiserver'    # empty
   ```
3. On every control-plane node, pull the etcd image the CronJob uses (the tag is in `payload/platform/backup/etcd-backup.yaml`). Only the node that last ran the CronJob has it; `ctr run` does not pull.

   ```bash
   sudo ctr -n k8s.io image pull registry.k8s.io/etcd:<tag>
   ```
4. On every control-plane node, restore into a new data directory with the `--name`, `--initial-cluster` and `--initial-advertise-peer-urls` values from that node's `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml`, and one `--initial-cluster-token` that is the same on every node and differs from the old cluster's, so a member that missed the restore cannot rejoin the new one.

   ```bash
   sudo ctr -n k8s.io run --rm \
     --mount type=bind,src=/var/lib/etcd-restore,dst=/restore,options=rbind:rw \
     registry.k8s.io/etcd:<tag> etcd-restore \
     etcdutl snapshot restore /restore/snapshot.db --data-dir /restore/etcd \
       --name <node> --initial-cluster <name=https://ip:2380,...> \
       --initial-cluster-token <new-token> \
       --initial-advertise-peer-urls https://<node-ip>:2380
   ```
5. Swap the data directory in, keeping the old one and its ownership.

   ```bash
   sudo mv /var/lib/etcd /var/lib/etcd.bak
   sudo mv /var/lib/etcd-restore/etcd /var/lib/etcd
   sudo chown -R --reference=/var/lib/etcd.bak /var/lib/etcd
   ```
6. Put the manifests back on every node, then confirm.

   ```bash
   sudo mv /root/manifests-stopped/*.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
   kubectl get nodes
   kubectl -n argocd get applications     # ArgoCD reconverges from Git
   ```

### Rebuild from scratch

1. Have the Git repository, the OpenBao unseal keys and operator login, and the [off-cluster copy](<#off-cluster-copy>) of `backup.openbao/` and `backup.velero/`; an etcd snapshot from it is optional and skips re-issuing certificates.
2. Move the old `openbao-init.json` and `openbao-operator.json` out of `output/credentials/`: `make bao-init` refuses while either exists, because keys from another cluster unseal nothing.
3. Provision the cluster per the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>) from step 1.
4. When every `ExternalSecret` is Degraded, `make bao-init`, then either restore the OpenBao snapshot as above, which puts the old files back, or re-enter the typed secrets with `make bao-secrets` and let the `PushSecret`s generate the rest anew — which loses whatever was encrypted with the old keys, Velero's volume backups among them.
5. Once the platform is Synced and Healthy, push the `velero` copy back ([Restoring from the copy](<#restoring-from-the-copy>)) and restore workloads with a Velero restore.

# Control Plane VIP

The API server is reached through a virtual IP held by [kube-vip](<https://kube-vip.io/>), not through one named node: whichever control-plane node wins the leader election answers on `control_plane_vip` from `ansible/inventory.yaml`, and another takes over if it goes away. The address is fixed at `kubeadm init` — see [Known Limitations](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/limitations/index.md>); a cluster built before the VIP is [migrated in place](<#migrating-a-cluster-built-without-a-vip>).

## How it is wired

| Piece | Where |
| --- | --- |
| VIP address and interface | `control_plane_vip`, `control_plane_vip_interface` in `ansible/inventory.yaml` |
| Bootstrap static pod | Written by Ignition to `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-vip.yaml` on control-plane nodes, at `kube_vip_version`, because it must run before `kubeadm init` writes the endpoint into the certificates |
| Running kube-vip | DaemonSet in `payload/platform/kube-vip/`, synced by ArgoCD; its image is tracked by Renovate |
| Cluster endpoint | `controlPlaneEndpoint` in the generated kubeadm config, and every `kubeadm join`, from `control_plane_endpoint_host` in `ansible/inventory.yaml` |
| Cilium's API address | `k8sServiceHost` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml` |
| Kubelet node address | `--node-ip` in the kubelet drop-in of `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2`, so the kubelet never reports the VIP on the leader's interface as InternalIP |

kube-vip runs in ARP mode with leader election, advertising a `/32`, with `svc_enable: "false"`: LoadBalancer services belong to Cilium's L2 announcements, and two components answering ARP for the same range produces intermittent, host-dependent failures.

## Design

The static pod is only the bootstrap: once ArgoCD syncs `payload/platform/kube-vip/`, a DaemonSet takes over, so upgrading kube-vip is a merged PR rather than a file rewritten on each node. kube-vip's chart is not used: it has no hook for the `adopt` init container below. A DaemonSet can hold the VIP here because the control-plane kubelets use their own node's API server (`server:` in `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf`) and so does kube-vip (`KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` is the host IP, which is in the certificate SANs), so both start after a full power loss without the VIP or Cilium. `kube_vip_version` in the inventory is therefore the bootstrap version only, and the VIP settings in the inventory and `daemonset.yaml` must be kept in step. kube-vip's ServiceAccount may only get and update its own Lease, and the Application does not prune and its objects carry `Delete=false`, because removing them takes the API away from the workers and from every kubeconfig.

### The handover

| Detail | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `pull` init container | Fetches the kube-vip image first, so the gap between old and new process has no registry round trip. Keep its image in step with the main container |
| `adopt` init container | Deletes the static manifest and waits for the static kube-vip to release `:2112`; both use the node name as leader identity and the same `plndr-cp-lock` Lease, so they must never run side by side |
| `/etc/kubernetes/manifests` mounted as a directory | A hostPath mounted as a single file is a bind mount and cannot be removed |
| 120 s timeout in `adopt` | The kubelet rescans manifests every 20 s; giving up leaves a visible stuck `Init` rather than a second kube-vip on the port |
| `maxUnavailable: 1`, no surge | An old and a new pod would fight over `:2112` and the lease |
| Tolerates every taint | A NotReady or pressured control-plane node is when the VIP has to move |
| Capabilities identical to the static pod | The first sync replaces all three at once; untested hardening takes the VIP down everywhere |
| Liveness probe on `/metrics` | Every kube-vip serves it, leader or not, so a hung process holding the Lease is restarted instead of keeping the VIP dead until another node's renew fails too; the long failure window keeps a slow API server from recycling a healthy pod |

### The `adopt` trade-off

`adopt` and its writable hostPath stay after the handover: they do nothing on an adopted node, but a reinstalled control plane gets the static manifest back from Ignition and needs adoption again, or two kube-vips contend for the VIP. The cost is a container on every pod start that can delete the static pod manifests, limited to the pinned image.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **If the DaemonSet pods do not come up**
>
> The static manifests are already gone, so nothing holds the VIP, and every kubeconfig and Cilium's `k8sServiceHost` point at it. Running pods keep their networking, but no Cilium agent sees the API server until the VIP is back. Point `kubectl` at a control-plane node's `ansible_host` from `ansible/inventory.yaml` with `--server https://<address>:6443`, write `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-vip.yaml` back onto one control-plane node from `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` so that the VIP answers again, then read `kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-vip -c kube-vip` and fix the DaemonSet in Git. The static pod holds the VIP only while the broken DaemonSet pod merely restarts; if that pod is deleted or recreated, `adopt` removes the file again.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Since Kubernetes 1.29, `admin.conf` is not usable until `kubeadm init` finishes, so the bootstrap unit points kube-vip's `hostPath` at `super-admin.conf` during init and moves it back afterwards. Inside the container the file stays at `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf`.

## Endpoint name

The next cluster build uses a DNS name as `controlPlaneEndpoint`, so moving the VIP later no longer means rewriting every node's kubeconfig; `certSANs` still needs regenerating for the new address. The running cluster keeps the bare VIP: there is no migration, because its certificates and stored configuration do not carry a name.

| Piece | With a name | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/etc/hosts` from Ignition, every node | Resolves the name to the VIP | The API endpoint must not depend on LAN DNS |
| `apiServer.certSANs` | Holds the VIP | Cilium's `k8sServiceHost` and `make kubeconfig` keep using the VIP |
| `make kubeconfig` | Writes the VIP as `server` | Only the nodes resolve the name |
| `make config`, `make reinstall` | Refuse a name the answering cluster does not publish | A node rendered with it fails certificate verification on join, after its disk is wiped |

To build with a name:

1. Set `control_plane_endpoint_host` in `ansible/inventory.yaml` to the name, before the first `make config` of the build, and keep it there.

   ```yaml
   control_plane_endpoint_host: k8s-api.<lan domain>
   ```
2. Continue with the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>). Everything else follows from that variable.

Once the first control plane is up, check the nodes and the cluster agree.

```bash
kubectl -n kube-public get configmap cluster-info -o jsonpath='{.data.kubeconfig}' | grep server
```

## Choosing the address

A free address on the nodes' subnet, outside any DHCP range, and distinct from the Cilium LoadBalancer pools. Nothing validates this: a collision leaves the API server unreachable, or reachable only from some machines.

## Migrating a cluster built without a VIP

A cluster provisioned before the VIP has its first control plane's address in the API server certificates, so this is no config change to sync.

### Rebuild (simplest)

Reprovision from the [Quickstart](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/quickstart/index.md>); the VIP is in place from `kubeadm init` onwards. Restore state per [Backups & Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md>).

### In place

One node at a time, with a second terminal holding a working kubeconfig, since several steps can lock you out.

1. Confirm the address is free.

   ```bash
   ping -c2 <vip>        # must not answer
   arping -c2 <vip>      # from a node on the segment
   ```
2. Add the VIP under `apiServer.certSANs` in the stored `ClusterConfiguration`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system edit configmap kubeadm-config
   ```
3. On **each** control-plane node, regenerate the API server certificate from the config `make config` rendered for it, which carries the VIP and the join token, hence the `rm`; kubeadm does not read the edited ConfigMap. The SANs must list the VIP.

   ```bash
   scp output/tmp/kubeadm/kubeadm-config-<node>.yaml core@<node>:/tmp/kubeadm.yaml
   ssh core@<node> 'cd /etc/kubernetes/pki && sudo mv apiserver.crt apiserver.crt.bak && sudo mv apiserver.key apiserver.key.bak && sudo kubeadm init phase certs apiserver --config /tmp/kubeadm.yaml; rm /tmp/kubeadm.yaml'
   ssh core@<node> sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A1 'Subject Alternative Name'
   ```
4. Deploy the kube-vip static pod to each control-plane node, generated from the template's values or copied from a node provisioned with the new configuration, and verify the VIP answers.

   ```bash
   curl -k https://<vip>:6443/healthz
   ```
5. Repoint the cluster: update `controlPlaneEndpoint` in the `kubeadm-config` ConfigMap, then on every node rewrite the server address in `/etc/kubernetes/*.conf` and `/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig` and restart the kubelet.
6. **Only now** change `k8sServiceHost` in `payload/platform/cilium/values.yaml` to the VIP and commit. The merge rolls every agent, so the VIP must answer before it lands; watch the rollout.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system rollout status ds/cilium
   ```
7. Re-fetch your kubeconfig so it uses the VIP.

   ```bash
   make kubeconfig
   ```

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Danger**
>
> Cilium replaces kube-proxy, so if `k8sServiceHost` names an address that is not answering, every Cilium pod loses the API server and the cluster's networking goes with it, including the networking you would fix it through. Do not commit step 6 until `curl -k https://<vip>:6443/healthz` succeeds.

## Verifying

```bash
# which node currently holds the VIP
kubectl -n kube-system get lease plndr-cp-lock -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}'; echo
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kube-vip -o wide

# the endpoint your kubeconfig actually uses
kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}'; echo
```

Test failover once: have Kured reboot the leader per [Rebooting a node](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/nodes/index.md#rebooting-a-node>) and confirm `kubectl` keeps working after a few seconds.

# Encryption Key Rotation

The API servers reload `/etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml` whenever it changes (`encryption-provider-config-automatic-reload` in `ansible/templates/kubeadm.yaml.j2`), so a rotation is a file edit on each control plane and one rewrite of every Secret; what the key protects and how it is generated is in [Encryption at rest](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/security/index.md#encryption-at-rest>).

The first key in the list encrypts, every key in the list decrypts, and a Secret's ciphertext names the key it was written with. Two things follow: the new key goes in *above* the old one, and the cluster has to end up with the new key under the name the Butane template renders (`key1` in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2`), because a control plane provisioned later gets exactly that file and can read nothing written under another name. That is why the Secrets are rewritten twice.

Reading or writing the file from a shell fires `TetragonSensitiveFileAccess`; that is the alert doing its job, not a problem to fix.

## Runbook

1. Generate the new key beside the old one, in the shape `config.yaml`'s `password` lookup produces: 32 letters and digits, stored in plain text, and base64-encoded where it goes into the config.

   ```bash
   LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' </dev/urandom | head -c 32 > output/credentials/encryption_key.new
   base64 < output/credentials/encryption_key.new    # the secret for key2 below
   ```
2. On every control plane, add the new key as `key2` **above** `key1` in `/etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml`; the rest of the file stays as it is.

   ```yaml
   providers:
     - secretbox:
         keys:
           - name: key2
             secret: <new key, base64>
           - name: key1
             secret: <old key, base64>
     - identity: {}
   ```
3. Wait for every API server to reload. Each reloads its own file, so ask each one by its `ansible_host` rather than through the VIP; a `status="failure"` count means the file did not parse and the old config is still in effect.

   ```bash
   kubectl get --raw /metrics --server https://<control-plane address>:6443 | grep apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reloads_total
   ```
4. Rewrite every Secret so it is encrypted with `key2`. A conflict on a Secret something updated mid-stream is harmless: run it again.

   ```bash
   kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
   ```
5. On every control plane, replace `key1`'s secret with the new key and move it back above `key2`; both entries now hold the new key. Wait for the reload as in step 3.

   ```yaml
   keys:
     - name: key1
       secret: <new key, base64>
     - name: key2
       secret: <new key, base64>
   ```
6. Rewrite every Secret again, so every ciphertext names `key1`.

   ```bash
   kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
   ```
7. On every control plane, remove `key2`. The file now matches what Ignition writes for a new control plane, and nothing on any node holds the old key.

   ```yaml
   keys:
     - name: key1
       secret: <new key, base64>
   ```
8. Make the new key the one `make config` renders, and verify that the Butane config of every control plane carries it as `key1`; `config.yaml` reads the file back instead of generating a new value, so nothing else changes. The Ignition JSON cannot be grepped, since Butane gzips file contents, so the check reads the Butane YAML it was transpiled from in `output/tmp/`.

   ```bash
   mv output/credentials/encryption_key.new output/credentials/encryption_key
   make config && grep -c "$(tr -d '\n' < output/credentials/encryption_key | base64)" output/tmp/butane/butane-*.yaml
   ```

   One match per control plane, none per worker or installer config.
9. Confirm against etcd that a Secret's ciphertext names the new key, with the same `etcdctl` flags as [Taking one by hand](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#taking-one-by-hand>); the value starts with `k8s:enc:secretbox:v1:key1:`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key get /registry/secrets/kube-system/ --prefix --limit 1 | head -c 120
   ```

Store the new key with the rest of `output/credentials/` wherever the old one is kept, and keep the old one next to the etcd snapshots taken before the rotation: those restore only with the key they were written under.

# Host Firewall Inventory 2026-10-30

`ss -lntu` and the established peers of each listening port on all ten nodes, read before the [host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) selected any of them. "Cluster" is every node and pod; "LAN" is everything else, Cilium's `world`.

## Listening on a node address

| Port | Listener | Nodes | Connections seen from | Admit from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 22/TCP | sshd | all | Workstation | LAN, cluster |
| 6443/TCP | kube-apiserver, kube-vip's address on the holder | control plane | Workstation, every node, pods | LAN, cluster |
| 2379/TCP | etcd client | control plane | Loopback only | Cluster, node range |
| 2380/TCP | etcd peer | control plane | The other members | Cluster, node range |
| 2381/TCP | etcd metrics, plain HTTP | control plane | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 10250/TCP | kubelet | all | API server, Prometheus, metrics-server | Cluster |
| 10257/TCP, 10259/TCP | controller-manager, scheduler | control plane | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 4240/TCP | Cilium health | all | Agents and health endpoints | Cluster |
| 4244/TCP | Hubble peer | all | Hubble Relay | Cluster |
| 9100/TCP | node-exporter | all | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 9962/TCP, 9965/TCP | Cilium agent and Hubble metrics | all | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 9963/TCP | cilium-operator metrics | The two operator nodes, moves with the pod | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 9964/TCP | Envoy metrics | all | Nothing; the Prometheus egress policy does not name it | Cluster |
| 2112/TCP | Tetragon metrics | all | Prometheus | Cluster |
| 6789/TCP | Tetragon | all | Nothing | Cluster |
| 8472/UDP | VXLAN | all | Other nodes | Cluster |
| 51871/UDP | WireGuard | all | Other nodes | Cluster |
| 68/UDP | DHCP client | all | Router | LAN |
| ICMP echo | Kernel | all | Not measured | LAN, cluster |

## Not filtered, or not listening

| Traffic | Why no rule |
| --- | --- |
| Loopback: 2379, 2381, 10248, 9878, 9879, 9890, 8118, 30003, DNS on 127.0.0.53 and .54, Envoy's and containerd's dynamic ports | Loopback never crosses a device the firewall is attached to |
| NodePorts of the two Gateway Services | Translated to the backend before the firewall |
| The two Gateway addresses | Not node addresses; the firewall checks only packets addressed to one |
| BGP | The agent dials the router and nothing listens on 179, so only replies arrive |
| Ceph mon and OSD ports | Rook runs them on the pod network; the only host-networked Ceph pod, the RBD node plugin, listens on nothing |
| DHCP server, TFTP, PXE | The boot server is off-cluster; a node's PXE boot happens before any agent runs |
| kube-vip | ARP mode: gratuitous ARP passes the firewall, and leader election goes through the API server |

## Findings

| Finding | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Services bound to `*` answer on each node's global IPv6 address: `curl` on port 9100 from the workstation returned `200` | The firewall cannot filter IPv6 with `enable-ipv6: false`; it [drops it all](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#pitfalls>). No IPv6 connection other than loopback was established on any node; each node's second resolver is IPv6, used only after the first fails |
| Prometheus's scrapes arrive from its node's address, not the pod's | Masquerading, see [Host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>). Prometheus-only is held by the pod egress policies: besides the API server rules, only Prometheus, Hubble Relay and metrics-server name a node as a destination, each with its ports |
| Tetragon holds 2112 on the control planes, the port kube-vip also wants | kube-vip logs `bind: address already in use`, and its liveness probe is answered by Tetragon. Fixed since: Tetragon serves its metrics on [its own port](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/tetragon/index.md#configuration>) |
| 6789 is Tetragon, not a Ceph monitor | Nothing on a node needs a Ceph rule |

# Host Firewall Rollout 2026-11-18

The [host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) ran in audit mode on all ten nodes from 2026-10-31, held there by a DaemonSet that re-enabled audit after every agent restart. On 2026-11-18 each node in turn was switched to enforcing by restarting its agent, then rebooted through Kured.

## Method

The verdicts below were read with the query in [Changing the host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#changing-the-host-firewall>).

## Audit verdicts

Six in eighteen days; no rule was added.

| When | Source → node:port | What it was | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10-31, three | Workstation → two workers :9100 | node-exporter from the LAN, the exposure the firewall exists to close | Refused |
| 11-04, three | Router → control planes :179 | The router opening BGP after a reconnect; the agent dials out and nothing listens on 179 | Refused; the session still comes up |

## Enforcing

| Order | Nodes | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One worker, then a second | Each rebooted alone before the next was touched |
| 2 | The other five workers | Switched together, rebooted one at a time by Kured |
| 3 | The control planes | The one holding the control-plane address last |

Every node came back `Ready` within about two minutes of its reboot with audit off, SSH, its pods and, on control planes, etcd, the API server and the BGP session working. The only drops after a boot were a few seconds of replies to one connection opened before the agent started; see the behaviour table in the [host firewall](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#host-firewall>) section.

## Found on the way

| Finding | Where it went |
| --- | --- |
| A drain moved Prometheus onto an 8 GB worker that its 2.3 GiB request fitted and its 4.4 GiB working set did not; the node swapped into `NotReady` | Request raised to the measured median, [Monitoring](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/monitoring/index.md#grafana>) |
| A drain of the Authentik database primary failed over instead of switching over, three minutes without sign-in | Replicated clusters keep their PodDisruptionBudgets, [the contract](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md#the-contract>) |
| Drops on a node's own address mailed with no node or source | `HostFirewallDrops`, [Logging](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/logging/index.md#alerting>) |
| Kured waited up to half an hour between reboots | `period` and `drainTimeout` from measured reboots, [Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) |

# Network Policy Audit 2026-09-27

One week of `AUDIT` verdicts from every namespace, read at the end of the [rollout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#rollout>), kept so the flip to enforcement starts from the disposition rather than the raw count. 25k verdicts, 21k of them one missing pair of rules.

## Rules added

| Flow | Disposition |
| --- | --- |
| Prometheus and the CloudNativePG operator to Authentik's database on 9187 and 8000 | **Rule.** The database moved in \#906 and the policy's spec never followed its description: \#927 |
| Every `http: [{}]` with a machine caller | **Tightened** to the methods and paths the week recorded: `GET /metrics` for every scrape, the four calls External Secrets makes at OpenBao, Loki's `POST /api/v2/alerts`, Grafana's `GET /loki/api/v1/…`: \#928, apps \#59. UIs behind the Authentik outpost stay open |

## Config switches

| Flow | Disposition |
| --- | --- |
| Authentik server to `goauthentik.io`, twice per pod start | **Switched off.** `disable_startup_analytics`: \#929 |
| Authentik server to `www.gravatar.com`, 117 times | **Not a switch the repository holds.** `AUTHENTIK_AVATARS` seeds the tenant once; the live value is a system setting and the database still says `gravatar,initials`. Set `initials` under System → Settings; the upstream ask is [goauthentik/authentik\#26470](<https://github.com/goauthentik/authentik/issues/26470>), the PR [\#26471](<https://github.com/goauthentik/authentik/pull/26471>) |
| Nextcloud to `updates.nextcloud.com` and `pushfeed.nextcloud.com` | **Switched off** in the startup hook: apps \#60 |
| Trivy scan jobs to `check.trivy.dev`, Authentik worker to `version.goauthentik.io`, Alloy and Loki to `stats.grafana.org`, Grafana to `grafana.com` and `secure.gravatar.com` | **Already off**, by \#861, \#883 and the values that predate the week; every record is from before the switch landed |

## Nothing to do

| Flow | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A name a `toFQDNs` rule allows, one `SYN` audited now and then: Alertmanager to the mail relay 14 of 254 mails, the repo-server to `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`, Home Assistant to `alerts.home-assistant.io`, scan jobs to the registries | The destination identity in the record is `world`, so the IP was not yet, or no longer, in the name's set when the `SYN` left. Eight fresh lookups from the Home Assistant pod were all allowed. Under enforcement the first `SYN` drops and the retransmit a second later decides it, so the `DROPPED` records after the flip say which: one drop per connection is the DNS proxy's 100ms hand-off, a run of drops on one source port is an application connecting to an address it cached past the TTL |
| Replies on high ports, pod addresses classified `world`, `openbao-N.openbao-internal` during a restart | Answer halves and identities of pods that had just gone; the export marks the first `is_reply` |
| `ceph-object-controller-detect-version` to its own node's API server, 3 times on thor | The host identity there carries `reserved:kube-apiserver`, and the same Job reached the other control-plane nodes hundreds of times; not at an agent restart. Watch for it as `DROPPED` |
| Home Assistant to the node's `cilium_host` address on UDP 53, 3 times; SSDP to `255.255.255.255` before apps \#44; `argocd-redis-secret-init` before \#871 | Predate their fix, or too rare to name |

## Consolidation

Not done, recorded: `argocd-server` and `argocd-server-oidc` select the same pods and could be one policy; the intra-namespace pair and the node rule are in 18 of 19 namespaces and are the next cluster-wide candidates after DNS, at the cost of the per-namespace file no longer being the whole record. The Prometheus rule is worded identically in 17 files, which is the point.

# Network Policy Audit 2026-10-16

Two weeks of `AUDIT` verdicts, 195k records, read before `policyAuditMode` went off. The method is the [rollout](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/security-policies/index.md#rollout>); the first reading is [Network Policy Audit 2026-09-27](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/network-policy-audit-2026-09-27/index.md>). No namespace with pods is without a policy, and every pod endpoint on the nodes checked is selected in both directions.

## Fixed

| Flow | Disposition |
| --- | --- |
| Velero and its data movers to `s3.infra.k8s.wlkr.ch`, 3.7k requests a day since 2026-10-04 | **Rule.** Not an audit verdict: the Gateway's Envoy checked Velero's egress against the RGW pod and answered `403` itself, which audit mode never sees. The backup location was Unavailable and every daily backup `FailedValidation`. Egress to the RGW pod on 8080 in `backup.yaml` |
| Pods in their first seconds, under the `init` identity: Trivy scan jobs' lookups and their calls to the Trivy server, the kubelet's probes, lookups landing on a CoreDNS pod that had just started; 27k records | **Cluster-wide policy** `init`: the node, DNS out and DNS in. A scan job's call to the Trivy server in the same seconds retransmits until the identity arrives |
| Every header of every proxied request in the export, `X-Vault-Token`, bearer tokens and cookies included | **Redacted** with `hubble.redact`; see [Cilium](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cilium/index.md#configuration>). Records written before the change keep them until Loki's retention drops them |

## Nothing to do

| Flow | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Rook mons, mgrs and crash collectors to `10.108.70.163`, `10.108.19.154` and `10.102.93.197` on 3300, 50k records from 2026-10-13 to the restarts of 2026-10-16 | Service addresses of mons that no longer exist; the daemons kept them until they restarted. A connection to an address with no backend fails with or without a policy |
| OSDs and RGW to pod addresses on 6800–6808 classified `world`, after an OSD restart | Addresses of pods that had just gone |
| The CloudNativePG operator to every instance on 8000, a few dozen at a time, and other in-cluster flows at agent restarts and node joins (2026-10-10, 2026-10-16) | The rule exists; the peer's identity had not reached the agent yet |
| A name a `toFQDNs` rule allows, one `SYN` now and then: Authentik to `www.gravatar.com`, the repo-server to the chart repositories, Dependency-Track to its package registries, scan jobs to the registry CDNs, Alertmanager to the mail relay | The DNS proxy's hand-off, as in the first reading. Gravatar stays a database setting |
| Prometheus and metrics-server to the five new nodes as `world`, 2026-10-10 | The nodes joining |
| Rook's mgr and detect-version Job to a control-plane node's API server as `host`, a handful a day | The node identity briefly without `reserved:kube-apiserver`; watch for it as `DROPPED` |

| Agent sessions to `http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com` | The `claude-agent` chart allows Claude Code's error reporting by name; telemetry here is switched off at the source, not allowed |

# Node Lifecycle

Everything you do to one machine, and the cluster's way back after a power loss.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Two of these destroy data and two do not**
>
> [Rebooting](<#rebooting-a-node>) and [adding](<#adding-a-node>) are safe and routine. [Replacing](<#replacing-a-failed-node>) destroys one node's OSD. [Rebuilding](<#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>) destroys the disk it runs against, and doing it to every node in turn destroys every replica of everything.

## Rebooting a node

[Kured](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/kured/index.md>) does every reboot: its lock keeps one node down at a time, and it waits while a Ceph, etcd, node or API alert fires. A hand reboot skips both, so it is kept for a node being wiped or dead. Flatcar is installed to disk, so the node boots without the boot server and keeps `/etc/kubernetes`, `/var/lib/etcd` and `/var/lib/rook`. A change made with `make config` is *not* picked up by a reboot; that takes a [rebuild](<#rebuilding-or-repartitioning-a-node>).

1. Set the sentinel; Kured acts on it at its next `period` check.

   ```bash
   make reboot-all LIMIT=<node>
   ```
2. Watch it cordon, reboot and uncordon the node.

   ```bash
   kubectl get node <node> -w
   kubectl -n kured logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kured --tail=50 -f
   ```

   Done when the node is `Ready` without `SchedulingDisabled`. Never cordoned: the log names the alert or lock holding it; fix that instead of rebooting by hand. A drain failing on a `<name>-db-<n>` pod's disruption budget is a CloudNativePG cluster with its budget still on — see [the contract](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/cloudnative-pg/index.md#the-contract>).
3. **Unseal OpenBao** if the node hosted a replica (below).

## After any node reboot: unseal OpenBao

OpenBao comes back sealed, looks healthy while sealed, and nothing unseals it for you — see [OpenBao](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md>) for what that costs.

```bash
make bao-unseal                      # idempotent: unseals whatever is sealed
for pod in openbao-0 openbao-1 openbao-2; do
  kubectl -n openbao exec "$pod" -- bao status | grep Sealed   # false
done
```

With `openbao-init.json` moved to a password manager, unseal [by hand](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/openbao/index.md#unsealing-after-a-restart>).

## After a power loss

The nodes boot network-first, so the PXE menus decide every boot.

1. Before starting the boot server, check every menu says `localboot`: an armed node wipes its disk on this boot. Disarm anything else.

   ```bash
   grep -H '^DEFAULT' output/tftp/pxelinux.cfg/01-*
   make reinstall-cancel    # if any says install
   ```
2. Wait for the control planes, then the workers, to report `Ready`.

   ```bash
   kubectl get nodes -w
   ```
3. Wait for Ceph's `HEALTH_OK`.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- ceph status
   ```
4. [Unseal OpenBao](<#after-any-node-reboot-unseal-openbao>), every replica.

   ```bash
   make bao-unseal
   ```
5. Wait for every Application to be `Synced` and `Healthy`; failed syncs [retry](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/gitops/index.md#sync-policy>).

   ```bash
   kubectl -n argocd get applications
   ```

## Adding a node

1. Compare `kubernetes_version` in `ansible/inventory.yaml` with `kubectl version`: a node installs the inventory's version, and `kubeadm    join` refuses a kubelet newer than the API server, so a merged minor has to be [walked onto the cluster](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/upgrades/index.md#upgrading-a-minor-version-deliberately>) first. Then add the host to the inventory and regenerate and serve the boot files.

   ```bash
   make config && make serve
   ```

   In the same commit, add the node name to `providerRegex` in `payload/platform/kubelet-csr-approver/application.yaml`, and let that PR merge and sync before the node boots: a node the regex does not name has its kubelet certificate denied and [silently drops out of `kubectl top`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/metrics-server/index.md#pitfalls>).

   Against a running cluster, `make config` also re-creates the bootstrap token baked into the Ignition configs (`ttl` in `ansible/templates/renew_join_credentials.sh.j2`) and re-uploads the control-plane certificates for kubeadm's shorter fixed window, on [whichever control plane answers](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md#playbooks>), so the node joins on its own.
2. Arm the node: the generated menu defaults to the local disk, so an unarmed node never installs, per [Switching back to local boot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#switching-back-to-local-boot>).

   ```bash
   make reinstall LIMIT=<node>
   ```
3. Network-boot it within those windows, the shorter one for a **control-plane** node. `bootstrap-k8s.service` runs the join once and only while `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf` is absent, so it does not interfere with a node that has joined.
4. If the window has passed, run `make config` again, then retry the join on the node.

   ```bash
   ssh core@<node> sudo systemctl restart bootstrap-k8s
   ```

## Replacing a failed node

1. Remove it from the cluster. A dead node is the exception to [Kured](<#rebooting-a-node>): there is nothing left to reboot.

   ```bash
   kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
   kubectl delete node <node>
   ```
2. Let Ceph re-replicate. With `useAllNodes: true` the OSD on that disk is gone for good; wait for `ceph status` to return to `HEALTH_OK`.
3. If it was a control-plane node, remove its etcd member; a dead member still counts toward quorum.

   ```bash
   kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-<healthy-node> -- etcdctl \
     --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
     --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
     --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
     member list
   # then: member remove <id>
   ```
4. Reprovision the replacement per [Adding a node](<#adding-a-node>): the inventory and regex change, then arm, then boot.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **Danger**
>
> On a cluster provisioned before the [Control Plane VIP](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/control-plane-vip/index.md>), `odin` is not an interchangeable control-plane node: its address is baked in as the API endpoint and as Cilium's `k8sServiceHost`, so losing it breaks node joins and Cilium's API connection everywhere. Check which endpoint your kubeconfig uses first.

## Rebuilding or repartitioning a node

The disk layout in `ansible/templates/butane_node_config.yaml.j2` is applied by Ignition once, on the first boot after install, and the Ignition config is embedded in the OEM partition at install time, so no change under `ansible/` reaches a running node. `rook-osd` is the last partition and deliberately raw: move its start by a sector, which any insert or resize above it does, and every OSD on that node is gone. Only the last partition can grow without a reinstall, and `rook-osd` cannot shrink in place because Ceph has already written across the space.

> [!CAUTION]
>
> **The backups are inside the thing being wiped**
>
> Every backup CronJob and Velero write to the Ceph object store this destroys — see [Backups & Recovery](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#what-is-not-covered>). Copy anything you intend to restore from **off-cluster** first.

1. Confirm the [off-cluster copy](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/operations/backups/index.md#off-cluster-copy>) ran after the last nightly backup, and copy anything in a PVC not reproducible from Git.
2. Edit whatever needs editing under `ansible/`.
3. Regenerate both Ignition configs and serve them.

   ```bash
   make config && make serve
   ```
4. Drain the node by hand: [Kured](<#rebooting-a-node>) would reboot it into the installer before it has left the cluster. A **control-plane** node also leaves the cluster (steps 1 and 3 of [Replacing a failed node](<#replacing-a-failed-node>)): it comes back with an empty etcd under its old peer URL, which kubeadm treats as joined.

   ```bash
   kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
   ```
5. Arm the nodes you are rebuilding. Arming is the only way in (the menu shows no prompt), a later `make config` keeps a node armed, and the boot server disarms it once it has the image, so the reboot at the end of the install does not start a second one — see [Switching back to local boot](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/boot-process/index.md#switching-back-to-local-boot>).

   ```bash
   make reinstall LIMIT=odin   # `make reinstall` alone asks, then arms every host
   ```

   Every control plane joins the running cluster; only [`bootstrap_cluster`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/architecture/ansible/index.md#inventory>) renders `kubeadm init`, and arming refuses while it is set and the VIP answers.
6. Network-boot the node. The installer wipes the disk, runs `flatcar-install`, and reboots into the installed system, which then runs `kubeadm`. The node keeps the SSH host key `make config` generated, so `output/known_hosts` still matches.
7. Leave the boot server up until the node is `Ready` (the sysext images are fetched from it on that first boot), then stop it.
8. Wait for `ceph status` to report `HEALTH_OK` before the next node: the OSD is new and backfills from the other two copies, and [`make storage-check`](<https://homelab.wlkr.ch/platform/rook-ceph/index.md#is-storage-ready>) proves it took the disk.
9. [Unseal OpenBao](<#after-any-node-reboot-unseal-openbao>) if a replica moved.
